- list 3 of 3Why has North Korea fired a missile before US-South Korea drills?
Pyongyang routinely denounces military drills in the south as a provocation that heightens tensions.
The drills – named “Ulchi Freedom Shield” – are due to start on August 17 and will last until August 27. They will incorporate exercises to counter drones, GPS disruption, and cyberattacks as the US and its allies adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities.
“The US announced that the forthcoming exercises are quite different from the ones of the past five years and intended to master the ability of fighting a war on the basis of the new aspects of modern warfare,” the North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in the statement.
“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” the statement, published by KCNA, added.
Lessons learned in Russia-Ukraine
North Korea sent an estimated 12,000-15,000 soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine, and the country is now thought to be preparing the deployment of another 10,000.
Thousands died, but the deal provided North Korea with valuable battlefield experience, as well as payment in arms, energy and direct financial support, according to reports.
Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesperson for the US and South Korean Combined Forces Command, said this week that North Korea’s deployment to the European war had changed the threat his soldiers may face on the Korean Peninsula.
“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea,” he told reporters. “Our training accounts for that threat.”
Pyongyang’s Foreign Ministry statement said the US-South Korea drills are being staged “at a time when military and political situation is becoming more serious with each passing day in Europe, the Middle East and other parts of the world”.
North Korea also said on Friday that it would further strengthen its nuclear deterrence, accusing the US of lowering its threshold for nuclear weapons usage and pushing the world “to the brink of nuclear war”.
On Wednesday, North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea off the Korean Peninsula’s east coast, just six days after firing another missile.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield drills will include 18,000 South Korean soldiers and counterparts from the 28,500-strong US contingent in the country.

Farage wins UK by-election to return to parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:39:02 UTC
14:39:02 KST

British politician Nigel Farage retains his seat in parliament after resigning last month over an investigation into his finances that triggered a by-election.
British politician Nigel Farage has comfortably won a local by-election on Friday after all the main political parties boycotted the vote in protest.
The former MEP had declared a "resounding victory" early Friday but said he would not attend the official result announcement that pitted him against Count Binface and a list of independent candidates.
Farage picked up over 22,000 votes in an election that saw a 44% turnout.
"The verdict is in and it is a convincing and overwhelming win," he said as supporters chanted his name at an event in Essex, which was broadcast on X.
Farage triggered the vote by resigning his parliamentary seat, which he had held since 2024, over an investigation into his finances in the constituency of Clacton in the county of Essex.
The vote had been shunned by Britain's main political parties, including the ruling Labour Party, as a stunt by the Reform UK leader - once touted as a potential prime minister - to dodge scrutiny of his dealings.
That has left candidates such as Binface - the alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey - to seize the spotlight.
"What an upside-down world it is, where Count Binface is now the candidate of the establishment," Farage said in his speech.
He said he would not attend the count, where candidates traditionally gather for the declaration of results, saying Essex Police had warned him that an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" was planned.
The BBC reported that this was not true, quoting Essex Police in a statement that read: "We have a proportionate and robust policing operation to ensure the safety and security of all participants in the count."
Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said election officials had worked with police to ensure the process was "completed safely and securely", adding there was "no reason not to proceed with the count process at this time".
Analysts expected a win for Farage, but forecast that the self-styled "intergalactic space warrior", who campaigns wearing a rubbish bin on his head, could secure an uncomfortably large share of the vote, possibly approaching 20 percent.
Binface took to social media after the result to declare himself the winner "of the candidates that 'bothered to turn up for the results'" and, in a video, suggested Farage had been "humiliated" as one in four people in Clacton would prefer him to the Reform UK leader.
Turnout reached about 44.7 percent, down from 59 percent in the 2024 general election.
In the coastal community, many voters appeared unenthusiastic about the poll, with even some Reform party volunteers describing the contest as a joke.
"It's a bit ridiculous," party campaigner Jane Embelton told AFP.
"It's all to make Nigel Farage look like an idiot, basically. But he doesn't look like an idiot to me or his supporters."
A record 33 fringe candidates, including Binface, stood in the vote, with some of the longest ballot papers in the country's history seen being unfolded at Clacton Leisure Centre, where the count was held.
- 'We can't decide' -
Farage, whose party had topped national polls for 18 months before falling behind recently, surprised voters with his July 7 resignation amid the probe into his finances.
The investigation by the parliamentary sleaze watchdog is examining allegations he and Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, failed to declare financial gifts. They deny any wrongdoing.
Farage has framed Thursday's vote as "the people of Clacton versus the Establishment", aimed at thwarting the "stitch-up" over his finances.
"The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," he said in a video released before casting his vote.
Clacton voter Phil predicted the vote was "not going to change anything", noting if Farage won as expected, the parliamentary probe would restart.
Political pundits have downplayed the vote's wider significance in a constituency that overwhelmingly backed Brexit a decade ago.
"It will be astonishing if Farage were not to win," political scientist John Curtice told AFP.
But some assessed Farage's election gambit had backfired as his Reform party slips down national polls.
"Farage's plan to turn this by-election into a serious political battle failed," Queen Mary University of London politics professor Stijn van Kessel told AFP, noting the resulting spectacle "makes Farage look rather silly".
Farage netted 46 percent of the vote in the 2024 general election to become an MP on his eighth attempt.
- Police probe -
The probe into Farage, which paused when he resigned, relates to a £5 million ($6.7m) donation from cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne.
Meanwhile, London police have confirmed starting a investigation last year into donations to Reform before the 2024 election.
UK media have reported that the police probe concerns undeclared financial support from longtime Farage ally and convicted fraudster George Cottrell and his mother.
The decision to trigger a by-election has seen a drop in support for Reform, which recently won a vast number of council elections across the UK in May.

Members of the public have been asked to call 112 (the unified emergency response centre in Latvia) if they notice anything suspicious.
Latvian officials have not so far commented officially on the drone's possible origin. However, Ukrainian drones were reported to have attacked the Russian port of Ust-Luga near St Petersburg again overnight. The shortest route to the port runs past the eastern borders of Latvia and Estonia.

Illegal gambling ads on Meta target vulnerable gamblers: BNR
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:36:01 UTC
14:36:01 KST

Illegal gambling ads on Meta target vulnerable gamblers: BNR
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Unlicensed gambling sites are running adverts on Facebook and Instagram that target vulnerable people who have signed themselves onto the national register barring them from gambling, an investigation by radio station BNR has found.
More than 100,000 people in the Netherlands have registered with Cruks, the self-exclusion scheme set up when online gambling was legalised, which requires every licensed casino, arcade and betting site to turn them away.
BNR found that searching Facebook for terms such as “Cruks”, geen Cruks or zonder Cruks (without Cruks) – surfaces a stream of adverts from casinos that hold no Dutch licence, promising large bonuses and offering routes around the register.
The adverts follow a consistent pattern, BNR reported: they suggest Cruks is restricting the user, then point them towards unlicensed alternatives. One features an AI-generated woman who tells viewers that international casinos do not consult the Dutch register and invites them to play the same day.
The accounts placing them carry names such as Betrouwbare Spelsites (reliable gaming sites). Users who encounter the adverts on Facebook go on to see them on Instagram and Threads.
Addiction specialists told BNR they were concerned that people registered with Cruks were being singled out, because seeing gambling adverts can trigger strong urges in addicts.
Meta removed adverts
 Meta pulled a large number of the adverts from its public ad library after BNR put questions to the company, and the accounts that were identified were taken offline.
In a written response, Meta said it takes enforcement seriously and that advertisers must comply with the law. It declined to tell BNR what it earns from the adverts.
An estimate published in May by two gambling industry bodies KVA and VNLOK put Meta’s annual revenue from illegal gambling adverts aimed at the Netherlands at between €7.3 million and €13.6 million.
The figure is modelled from publicly available advertising data rather than confirmed by Meta, and the report states that it is not suggesting Meta knowingly allows the adverts.
VNLOK took Meta to court in June in an attempt to force it to act faster, and complained to the European Commission that the company is not meeting its obligations under the EU’s Digital Services Act.
The cabinet set out plans in June for a complete ban on online gambling advertising and bonuses. Junior justice minister Claudia van Bruggen has said the rise in gambling addiction, particularly among young people, is deeply worrying.
If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s gambling, OpenOverGokken, the national gambling helpline run by regulator the Kansspelautoriteit, can be reached free on 0800 24 000 22, day or night.

Fewer tuberculosis cases prompt Estonia to rethink universal vaccination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:32:00 UTC
14:32:00 KST

Fewer tuberculosis cases prompt Estonia to rethink universal vaccination
Estonia's declining tuberculosis rate has prompted the Social Affairs Ministry to prepare to replace universal newborn vaccination with targeted TB shots for at-risk children.
Under the current national immunization schedule, all newborns in Estonia are vaccinated against tuberculosis (TB) within five days of birth.
In June, however, the ministry's Immunoprophylaxis Expert Committee backed launching preparations to move from universal to targeted vaccination.
Department of Public Health adviser Maia-Triin Kanarbik said that the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends vaccinating all newborns in countries with a high incidence of TB, while low-incidence countries can limit vaccination to defined risk groups.
"Estonia is now among those countries with low tuberculosis incidence, and the incidence here has been steadily declining," she said.
Kanarbik noted that several European countries including Finland and Sweden have shifted from universal early childhood TB vaccination to risk-based vaccination without increasing TB cases among children.
According to the adviser, preparations will include defining risk groups, updating guidelines, training healthcare workers and establishing procedures for the new system.
While ministry communications have indicated the change is unlikely to take effect before 2028, Kanarbik said that with experts yet to discuss the necessary details, it's still too early to predict when universal TB vaccination will end.
Until then, the Social Affairs Ministry continues to recommend TB vaccination for all children.
"Although TB incidence in Estonia has declined, the share of drug-resistant cases remains high, accounting for nearly 20 percent of all pulmonary TB cases," the official noted.
TB vaccine coverage down
A Health Board handbook for new parents describes tuberculosis as "a serious disease that requires long-term treatment and can affect the lungs and other organs. In young children, it can even cause severe meningitis," or inflammation of the tissues surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Estonia recorded 28 new tuberculosis cases in the first six months of 2026, according to the National Institute for Health Development (TAI), with no initial cases among children under 14.
Including recurrent cases, 86 people were diagnosed with TB last year and 88 in 2024, down significantly from 316 in 2011.
According to Health Board figures, TB vaccine coverage among the country's newborns stood at 87.6 percent in 2025, down significantly from over 98 percent in 2011.

- Farage faced strong competition from comedian Count Binface, who gained 26.7% of the vote, highlighting public criticism and political risks.

CLACTON-ON-SEA, Britain - Reform UK leader Nigel Farage won his self-triggered by-election in Clacton on Aug 14 but saw his strategy to silence critics backfire when his main rival Count Binface, a comedian dressed as a trash can, took more than a quarter of the vote.
Farage, one of Britain’s leading Brexit campaigners, in a highly unusual move, did not turn up at the vote count in the southern English seaside resort of Clacton.
He said the police had advised him that there was a campaign to disrupt the result.
He also cancelled a victory speech planned for later on Aug 14.
“I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies,” Farage told supporters at a party before the result was announced.
The election was triggered after Farage resigned from Parliament in July to seek a fresh mandate from voters in what he described as a war against an establishment bent on discrediting him over taking undeclared gifts from donors.
The result, while a victory, underscored the political risks of Farage’s gamble.
With a parliamentary investigation into his finances set to resume, the vote may have done little to remove a threat he wanted to sideline.
Reform’s momentum shows signs of slowing
After Britain’s main parties pulled out of the race, calling it a self-serving stunt, Farage’s main challenger ended up being Count Binface, a figure created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has become a fixture of fun at British elections.
While Farage took 62.8 per cent of the vote, Count Binface, whose policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using a speaker phone on public transport, secured 26.7 per cent.
The turnout was 44 per cent.
After enjoying a lengthy lead in national opinion polls, Reform has seen its popularity wane.
That has been driven partly by the funding accusations made against Farage, who is under investigation in Parliament over whether he should have declared a £5 million (S$8.64 million) gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire investor.
Laura Richards-Gray, a politics lecturer at Birkbeck University in London, said the absence of major-party opponents undermined Farage’s attempt to turn it into what he called a “people versus the establishment” contest.

Since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July, Labour has been enjoying a bounce in ratings, with the party leading Reform 28 per cent to 25 per cent.
Burnham has dominated the airwaves and social media in his first few weeks in office, and while the next national election is expected in three years’ time, he appears to be consolidating a left-leaning bloc around Labour.
Reform, on the other hand, is competing for a divided right-wing vote with the Conservative Party and the anti-immigration party Restore Britain gaining in support.
Gift from billionaire crypto investor
While Farage was always expected to win the election, his share of the vote was lower than forecast by a Survation poll conducted in July, which predicted he would secure 73 per cent of the vote, with Count Binface on 20 per cent.
Shortly after the result was declared, the parliamentary standards investigation into his financial declarations – suspended after his resignation from Parliament to fight the election – was listed once again as active.

Under parliamentary rules, Members of Parliament must declare any donations received in the year preceding an election within one month of taking office.

Five years of war have narrowed to two cities: why the battle for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk will likely decide when — and how — Russia’s invasion of Ukraine ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:27:34 UTC
14:27:34 KST

Five years of war have narrowed to two cities: why the battle for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk will likely decide when — and how — Russia’s invasion of Ukraine ends
Recently, Meduza invited readers to send the Razbor desk any questions about the war in Ukraine. This is the second time we’ve done this, and like last year’s round, it drew considerable interest — we received hundreds of responses (thank you!). Answering every message individually is impossible, so we’ve again grouped them into thematic blocks, from questions about when the war might end to an analysis of the current phase of the conflict, in which mutual drone strikes have come to the fore. If your letter isn’t mentioned in this piece, don’t be discouraged: the topic is most likely still addressed in one of the sections. Below is the first installment of our answers. It consists of two parts: the first covers the war’s strategic outlook, and the second examines strikes behind the lines. We’ll publish the second installment in the coming days. It will include answers to questions about the situation on the front, mobilization, and other aspects of the conflict.
Meduza has condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine from the very start, and we are committed to reporting objectively on a war we firmly oppose. Join Meduza in its mission to challenge the Kremlin’s censorship with the truth. Donate today. 
When and how will the war end?
Before turning to your questions, here’s a recap of the strategic context behind the war between Russia and Ukraine.
In recent years, Meduza has often written about modern theories of armed conflict — see this piece, for example — the kind studied not only by military experts but also by economists, political scientists, and historians.
One of the leading theories, the so-called bargaining (or negotiation) model, holds that wars begin when one or both rational actors conclude they cannot obtain resources through peaceful means. The combatants remain rational — their actions aim to maximize utility — but they lack complete information about the risks and rewards ahead. War becomes a way of gathering that information through a series of battles. Peace arrives once one side has firmly seized the contested resource, or once both sides recognize that continuing to fight will only leave them weaker.
Seen through this lens, a protracted war over Ukraine’s sovereignty — the “resource” at stake here — is nothing unusual. Years of fighting have taught both sides that the goals they went into the full-scale war with are unattainable.
- Vladimir Putin understands that he cannot install a puppet government in Kyiv or seize most of the country’s territory, including Odesa, which he specifically named when he formally announced the start of the ”special military operation.”
- Kyiv, for its part, has recognized that for now it remains far from restoring full sovereignty within its 1991 borders.
The negotiations that Donald Trump forced upon both sides in 2025 had the effect of crystallizing new positions.
- Putin continues to press for a further violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty — one that Kyiv itself would acknowledge. He wants Ukraine to accept the loss of the entire Donbas, along with part or all of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions.
- Ukraine, in turn, is trying to persuade Putin to abandon that plan.
The means of imposing one’s will can vary, from outright victory on the battlefield to wearing the enemy down and inflicting unacceptable damage on its economy and society.
Now, on to your questions
When will the war end? — Danil
Why does Putin keep fighting a war that’s obviously going badly? Does he really not know how things actually stand? Or is he happy gaining a few kilometers a month? By hook or by crook, is he still fighting just to finish grinding down the Donbas, even if it takes 10 years? — Draviden
In coverage of recent talks between the American and Ukrainian presidents, journalists emphasized that Volodymyr Zelensky managed to convince Trump that Ukraine’s armed forces could win the war against Russia. But what would actually count as a Ukrainian victory? Liberating most of the occupied territory? Advancing into Russian territory itself? Signing a peace treaty? If the latter, on what terms should it be signed? — Alexey
As the strategic context above makes clear, this war can end only once both sides are convinced that their goals have been achieved or are unattainable at an acceptable price. For the war’s current phase, which has been under way for the past two years, that goal is what one reader called Putin’s drive to “finish grinding down the Donbas” — that is, to capture the sprawling urban area of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in the northern Donetsk region.
Putin is pressing on with a war that went wrong for him as early as 2022. He does so because he believes he can take this territory in far less than 10 years. Below, we examine what’s behind that confidence.
Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, with a prewar combined population of 250,000, obviously can’t be the point of such a long war on their own. But as a result of the 2025 negotiations, they came to symbolize the preservation of Ukraine’s sovereignty. Numerous sources indicate those talks boiled down to a formula centered on the Donbas:
- Putin regularly invokes the “spirit of Anchorage,” a reference to his 2025 talks with Trump in Alaska, where, according to sources on both sides, the discussion centered on a “compromise”: Ukrainian forces withdrawing from the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, with the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions divided along the front line. The Kremlin insists that a ceasefire would take effect immediately under those terms. Putin’s representatives at the talks, Kirill Dmitriev and Yuri Ushakov, said as much: transcripts of their conversations with American counterparts, obtained by Bloomberg, show them discussing “handing over the Donbas and exchanging some other territories.” Still, the Kremlin has never officially confirmed it would limit itself to the Donetsk and Luhansk regions and split the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, which the Russian Constitution designates as sovereign Russian territory.
- Zelensky and other Ukrainian sources have repeatedly said they’re under pressure specifically to give up the Donbas. Other major issues — such as guarantees against future Russian attacks — have been described as “almost settled,” a characterization Kyiv found unconvincing. Ukraine has flatly refused. The wording matters here: Ukrainian society won’t accept such a decision, since withdrawing troops from the Donbas would split the country and trigger a political crisis. Putin was likely counting on exactly that political outcome.
Even while the negotiations were deadlocked, some argued that the Kremlin was only playing along to distract Trump, and that Russia actually intends to keep fighting until it captures Kyiv and Odesa and installs a friendly government in Ukraine. That interpretation contradicts everything we know about the balance of forces, not just on the front but in the other arenas where this war is being fought.
- Russia has tried, and failed, to destroy Ukraine’s military infrastructure. That’s an extremely difficult task even in more clear-cut cases: in six months of bombing Iran, a country with no reliable allies, the world’s most powerful military machine — the combined forces of the United States and Israel — failed to achieve a decisive result. Ukraine is a harder case still: much of what sustains its war effort sits outside its own borders, its military facilities are often well hidden from reconnaissance, and Russia has far fewer weapons for the job than the United States. The goal looks entirely out of reach.
- Russia has also tried, and failed, to use strikes on civilian infrastructure to break Ukrainian society’s will to resist and cripple the economy sustaining its war effort. We examine the theory and practice of this kind of “suppression” in a separate section below, covering strikes by both Ukraine’s and Russia’s armed forces.
- Judging by Kremlin-controlled media and statements from experts, Russian authorities have likely long hoped for a critical shift within the coalition of states backing Ukraine — one unfavorable to Kyiv. If Western countries were to abandon most of their military and financial aid, that could indeed upset the balance of forces, and the Kremlin may still be counting on it. But building a strategy for victory on such shaky ground, in an arena the Kremlin doesn’t control at all, is irrational, to put it mildly. Ukraine, meanwhile, has had years to learn it shouldn’t expect a dramatically greater level of Western involvement in the war either.
- Finally, on the front itself, the current balance of forces and prevailing tactics all but rule out breakthroughs capable of routing either army. Both sides can only “gnaw through” tactical defenses, hoping to force the other to abandon its own “vision of victory.”
Even if Putin still harbors hopes of destroying present-day Ukraine, he lacks the tools to carry it out — and his own actions make it reasonably clear that he knows it:
- For several years now, faced with a choice between pushing deeper into Ukraine toward strategically vital cities such as Dnipro or continuing to press in the Donbas, Russia’s leadership has chosen the Donbas. That was clearest in early 2025, when Russian forces captured the southern part of the Donetsk region — Kurakhove and Velyka Novosilka — and had an opening to advance toward Dnipro against a weakened Ukrainian force along the Donetsk–Zaporizhzhia highway and farther north. Instead, the Russian General Staff redeployed an entire army, two divisions strong, from the Kurakhove area to Kramatorsk, later sending reserves from around Kherson and Sumy there as well. Putin, in short, isn’t currently planning to crush Ukraine outright; his immediate goal, one that has stretched on for years, is occupying the Donbas. More than half of Russia’s forces in Ukraine are now involved in the advance on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from multiple directions.
- Kremlin sources quoted by Western media outlets have said that Putin is focused specifically on the Donbas and treats every other front and every other arena of the war as secondary, and Putin himself has said as much.
The odds of the war ending would rise sharply if Russia closed in on that main objective — or if Ukraine’s armed forces convinced the Kremlin that seizing it is impossible or would cost Russia too much. Ukraine’s problem is that Putin appears to have decided to pursue “victory” at any cost, while remaining willing both to raise the stakes and to adapt as circumstances change. So Ukraine has to prove — on the battlefield itself — that further Russian advances are impossible.
It can’t be ruled out that the war will continue even after the battle for the Donbas ends. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that if Ukraine doesn’t surrender these territories voluntarily, the terms of any peace could change. Kyiv, too, could keep fighting even if it loses the battle for the Donbas. But for now, the fight for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk looks decisive; everything else, including the strikes each side aims at the other’s infrastructure, is largely a backdrop. Zelensky effectively matched that bet when he refused to surrender the Donbas, citing the danger of a national split.
The Ukrainian side claims there has been a turning point on the front, while Russia continues its offensive in the Donbas. What specific military indicators — territorial control, logistics, reserves — allow the Razbor desk to confirm or refute a strategic turning point in Ukraine’s favor at this point? — Mara
It’s clearly too early to call this a turning point, but over the past year, Ukraine’s armed forces have made real gains on two fronts: they have slowed the Russian advance and are hitting targets deep inside Russia. Those successes are especially notable given how long the Kremlin has tried to show that the war hasn’t disrupted ordinary life in Russia. Putin will of course have to reckon with changed circumstances as the offensive at the front fails to go according to plan — something he himself acknowledges and that we return to below. But the Kremlin still appears to believe it can capture the Donbas in the not-too-distant future, allowing it to end the war on its own terms, however far those terms have drifted from its original aims.
Can we be sure that Putin has an accurate picture of what’s happening? That he has a firm grip on reality? In your view, what could make Putin stop? — Alexander Schmidt
From what I’ve been reading, there’s a “vertical of lies” running through the Russian military, where towns clearly not under the full control of the Russian army — Kupiansk, Lyman, Orikhiv, and partly Kostiantynivka — are regularly presented to Putin at briefings as captured. Is he really that easy to fool? Or does he know exactly how it is and just not care? — Draviden
There’s no reliable data on this, but indirect signs suggest Putin isn’t entirely satisfied with how the Kramatorsk operation is going. Even so, he’s behaving rationally by his own logic, since he’s prepared for “victory” to take more time and effort than he’d hoped.
Last week, Putin unexpectedly called Colonel Abdulaziz Shikhabidov, commander of the 76th Air Assault Division, which has spent six months trying to break through to Dobropillia, north of Pokrovsk and one of the most important intermediate objectives in the Donbas offensive. Coverage of the call focused on the fact that social media users in Dagestan had declared Shikhabidov dead a year earlier, even though it was already known that he was alive and still in command. But the content of this strange conversation is far more interesting.
Putin pressed Shikhabidov on exactly which towns and villages his division had reached. The colonel’s answers were fairly accurate: video, including video published by Ukraine’s armed forces, backed up his account that Russian forces were fighting in villages on the southern outskirts of Dobropillia. Putin, with evident irritation, said that other advancing units were faring worse.
The conversation, which bypassed the General Staff, likely reflects an internal dispute over the situation east of Dobropillia, where the 51st Combined Arms Army reported a breakthrough into the city itself — even though published video shows its forces have been stuck roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away for months.
The conversation continued like this:
Putin: Are the tasks being assigned achievable within the time frames and deadlines that have been set?
Shikhabidov: Yes, sir. The deadlines being set are all realistic.
Putin had previously said that “everything is working out for us — not as quickly as we would like, but we’re still advancing every day.” It’s quite likely, then, that Ukrainian intelligence is right when it says Russian forces regularly miss the deadlines set by their own command.
Conversations like this one suggest the Kremlin is tracking the front in granular detail, and the last few weeks may have brought it some encouraging results. The current phase of the offensive on Kramatorsk, which began in May, started out with extremely slow progress, but the pace has picked up lately — though not in every sector of the 300-kilometer (186-mile) front, from the city of Lyman to the border with the Zaporizhzhia region.
- Russian forces launched an unsuccessful assault on Lyman, northeast of Sloviansk, but closed to within 13 kilometers (8 miles) of the city from the east, an advance of 17 kilometers (11 miles) since January. A second Russian force has closed to 7 to 9 kilometers (4 to 6 miles) from the southeastern outskirts of Kramatorsk, an advance of about 14 kilometers (9 miles) over the same period.
- Kostiantynivka, south of Kramatorsk, has been almost entirely captured.
- Russian assault troops have been spotted on the outskirts of Oleksiivo-Druzhkivka, the next town along the highway to Kramatorsk, 13 kilometers (8 miles) from the city — an advance of about 10 kilometers (6 miles) since January.
- Meanwhile, Russian forces are trying to push toward Druzhkivka, behind Ukrainian lines, from both the west and the east, from about 10 kilometers (6 miles) out.
- Near Dobropillia, the advance since the start of the year has totaled about 12 kilometers (7 miles), but only in one sector, the southern one, where the 76th Air Assault Division has been operating since late winter.
Seen through Putin’s eyes, fixated as he is on occupying the Donbas, this picture suggests Russian forces could reach the outskirts of the urban area’s two main cities in early 2027 and then attempt to storm them in the months that follow. But there are also signals that should worry the Kremlin, though it’s unclear how rationally Russia’s leadership is actually weighing them:
- The Russian army constantly runs into trouble holding territory its assault troops have already reached. For the army to push farther, every breakthrough requires weeks of work — clearing the area, preparing supply routes, moving drone operators closer to the front line, setting up new artillery positions farther back, and more, all of it under drone strikes. Then the enemy’s own fire support assets — drone operators, artillery, electronic warfare systems — have to be suppressed all over again. There’s no longer any stretch of the front where Russian forces, or Ukrainian forces for that matter, can string together one tactical operation after another while keeping up a relatively high pace of advance. As recently as a year ago, Russia’s “Vostok” grouping of forces in the Zaporizhzhia region was covering up to 10 kilometers (6 miles) per week for several weeks in a row. But on the main Donbas axis, slow advances and small, “discrete” tactical operations have been the norm since late 2024.
- Russian military losses are steadily rising, a subject we address in more detail in a later section of this piece. That’s also visible in the army’s own structure: in 2024, Russia was forming entirely new divisions and even larger formations — corps and armies — from scratch, drawing on an influx of new recruits and reactivated Soviet-era equipment. Now, commanders can only expand existing brigades into divisions, using already-formed reserve regiments. The rate at which those losses are replaced clearly isn’t outpacing them by much.
All of this suggests the Russian army will struggle to reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, even though Putin clearly cares deeply about the pace of the offensive and doesn’t want to keep fighting for the Donbas for years.
When does this war of attrition end? It’s been five years and both countries still have enough soldiers to hold the line. That just seems unrealistic. — Eva
Both armies have built mobilization systems that keep feeding reinforcements to the front, whatever the systems’ flaws.
- In Russia, the main problem is that each new recruit costs more over time. But deeper issues loom too: the pool of people willing to risk their lives for relatively modest sums of money could eventually run dry, and the army isn’t entirely satisfied with the caliber of new contract soldiers either. We address all of this in a separate section on mobilization.
- Ukraine’s mobilization has its own problems. To keep pace with the number of reinforcements Russia sends to the front, Ukraine’s armed forces have to draft a far larger share of the population — several times larger. Forced conscription also opens the door to abuse and violence, which take a psychological toll on the population and drive desertion before recruits ever reach the front.
But overall, neither country has come close to running out of men to call up. Even in Ukraine, several million potential recruits remain available.
For years Russia bragged about weapons that supposedly had “no equal” anywhere in the world, rolling out new ones every year and saying it could beat anybody almost instantly. So why, after five years, can it still not take all of the Donbas? I think about this almost every day. — Andrei
Most of Russia’s prewar weapons systems haven’t proven effective. That’s only partly a matter of quality, which is often perfectly acceptable. The bigger problem is that the war itself didn’t unfold the way Russian commanders had envisioned — a pattern seen in other protracted wars as well.
Ukraine deserves considerable credit here, too: its army evolved quickly — and forced its opponent to evolve — in ways that give it a chance to match Russian forces or even surpass them. Today’s fighting is built around superiority in communications, reconnaissance, and cheap precision weapons — mainly drones.
By your estimate, how many more months of money and strength does the old shithead in his bunker have left to keep waging this war? — Yuri
That’s a many-trillion-ruble question, and there’s no precise answer. The war’s current cost is still affordable for the Russian state, so long as it keeps gradually extracting resources from the population. Over nearly five years, the government has built a resilient system for doing that, though one already running into difficulties as the conflict grows more expensive. Oleg Itskhoki, an economist, has said Putin operates on a “principle of optimization” that serves the main political project of his life: the war. Under that principle, all the “screws” are tightened as little as possible, but evenly — the state gradually squeezes what the war needs out of ordinary Russians through inflation, tax increases, pulling workers out of the economy and into the army, and more. In that sense, the Kremlin has acted quite rationally since putting the country on a wartime footing in the fall of 2022, and that could continue for a long time yet.
It’s hard to say what the price will be in the future, or whether Russian authorities will be able to pay it. That depends on many unknowns, from the price of oil and the scale of Russian military losses to which new targets Ukraine’s armed forces choose for long-range strikes.
I have a theory that where Russia is right now already suits the people making the decisions just fine (those in power and among the “elites”). The war has become a tool that grants the authorities freedom of action they wouldn’t have without it. In its current form, it could go on for a long time — 10-plus years. Since occupying all of the Donbas doesn’t look like an endpoint for the war and can’t “secure” Russian territory in any way, the goal (at minimum) appears to be the destruction of Ukraine — on any timeline, at any pace of advance, and at any cost. If that’s the case, it seems Russia has all the resources it needs for that task. […] 1. Am I badly mistaken? 2. In your view, what could make Russia stop firing and halt its military operations (no copium, please)? — Ahmed Abad
If Putin achieves the “goals of the special military operation” by reaching the borders of the Donetsk region and declares the “operation” over, why does he think Ukrainians will consider it over too? What are the odds the Russian army digs in along the Donetsk region’s borders while Ukraine’s forces keep pounding it along those same lines? Or will Ukraine’s partners intervene and force Ukraine to stop? — Mikhail
Consider a thought experiment. Suppose Russia captures the entire Donbas through prolonged, bloody fighting, rather than gaining it, say, by Trump pressuring Kyiv into concessions. If the Kremlin then decides to keep fighting with the goal of “destroying” its opponent or seizing new territory, it would hand Ukraine a reason to keep resisting — and its allies a reason not to withdraw their support.
Continuing the war as it is now being fought, with such ambitious goals, could take many more years, or even decades, of fighting. That would create enormous risks for the Kremlin, risks that keep accumulating: the economy’s “screws” could strip their threads, for instance, as the national debt inevitably grows and becomes costlier to service. The level of engagement by the international “coalitions” backing each side — the West on one side, and China and Russia’s other allies of convenience on the other — could also shift in a direction unfavorable to Moscow. It’s hard to predict how the next American administration will behave, and that’s only a little over two years away. International relations theory, specifically the security dilemma, suggests that as Russia grows stronger — that is, as it draws closer to the destruction of Ukraine — the West should increase its support for Kyiv. And we’ve already mentioned the risk that the pool of people willing to die for money could run dry, which would force a shift to less popular mobilization methods.
The war, it turns out, doesn’t give the authorities absolute freedom, even though they have the tools to tighten various screws and crack down at home.
An alternative to a protracted battle would be sharply increasing the resources the country spends on the war. Russia’s current military spending reaches 8% of GDP, more than double the prewar level. In Ukraine, the figure exceeds 55% of GDP, though a significant portion of that spending is covered by Western countries through direct military and financial aid. In absolute spending, Russia is ahead, but not by much: very roughly, the figures work out to $150 billion a year versus $100 billion, based on 2024 data. Small wonder, then, that Russian forces don’t hold a decisive advantage in this war of attrition.
Could Russia spend several times more? Probably, but that would require a radical overhaul, one that draws far more of the population into the war effort. Putin could have taken that path earlier, but so far he’s preferred to “optimize” the process little by little. That likely reflects his own calculation of the trade-off between the benefits of fighting a “war to a victorious end” and the domestic and external risks that come with it. For now, he appears to prefer taking a “small victory” in the Donbas and negotiating sanctions relief in exchange for a ceasefire, rather than waging an endless war.
It can’t be ruled out that the Kremlin’s assessment will change. For Ukraine, voluntarily surrendering the Donbas would raise the risk that Putin would decide to keep fighting. A Ukrainian victory in the battle for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk — say, through a major counterattack — would lower that risk instead.
Either way, ending the war promises to be complicated. Beyond the territorial dispute, questions about security guarantees for Ukraine and Western sanctions against Russia remain unresolved.
What are the two sides’ strikes behind the lines achieving?
You sent us many similar questions on the most sensitive topic for both Ukrainians and Russians: the strikes each side launches on the other’s businesses and infrastructure behind the lines, which kill civilians.
To answer these together, we’ll first lay out, once again, the context in which they should be understood.
- By 2026, Ukraine had amassed enough drones of two types: one for strikes deep inside Russia, hundreds or even thousands of kilometers from the front, and another for closer targets, 20 to 150 kilometers (12 to 93 miles) away. It quickly launched a campaign that came to be known in Kyiv as the “40-day operation to influence Russia,” “bringing the war back to where it came from,” and “long-range sanctions.” The strikes first targeted the largest oil refineries, as far away as Western Siberia, and then the warehouses of the Russian online marketplace Wildberries.
- Medium-range drones equipped with cameras for homing in on moving targets, such as trucks, have struck vehicles in occupied territories, mainly — though not exclusively — on roads connecting the Rostov region with Crimea.
- The campaign, then, as the names Kyiv has given it suggest, is meant to affect Russia through two channels: first, by worsening the country’s economic situation, in particular by reducing budget revenues; and second, by making it impossible for Russian society to keep pretending the war doesn’t concern it.
The campaign aligns substantively with proposals from Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s former defense minister, who believed that the economic and social costs of such strikes would help push Putin to abandon the war. On the front itself, he proposed more than doubling Russian military casualties with drones, so that Russia couldn’t recruit contract soldiers faster than it was losing them — forcing Putin either to end the war or to introduce additional, coercive mobilization measures.
This concept, which wasn’t fully trusted even inside Zelensky’s office or Ukraine’s armed forces, has flaws — and not just theoretical ones. Statistics on the outcomes of air campaigns in the 20th and 21st centuries show such plans don’t succeed on their own. The evidence isn’t conclusive, though: there are few cases suitable for analysis, and it’s difficult to separate out the role of any single factor in success or failure.
The idea of strategic bombing capable of knocking an opponent out of a war entirely originated with the Italian general Giulio Douhet after World War I. Under his doctrine, an attacker must first strip the enemy of aircraft and seize air superiority; the defender would then have nothing left to fight off bombers capable of reaching any target on its territory. Douhet argued the preferred targets shouldn’t be military ones, but rather sites whose destruction could break the will of the state and society to resist. In his view, using aviation this way would eventually make armies and navies unnecessary.
A century of theorizing and practical implementation hasn’t produced very good results: air campaigns unsupported by other branches of the military have failed, and their contribution to overall success has been relatively small. The United States, the leading practitioner of strategic bombing, has failed in the same pattern each time, according to American military experts who have studied the question — and the same conclusions hold for other practitioners, such as Britain and Germany:
- Even overwhelming air superiority didn’t make bombers invulnerable at every altitude and every hour of the day or night, because of air-defense countermeasures — forcing campaign tactics and targets to be adjusted to preserve aircraft.
- Targets and priorities were consistently chosen in ways ill-suited to the overarching objectives.
- Identified targets ran out quickly, requiring a constant search for new ones.
- Each time, a race developed between the pace of strikes and the enemy’s pace of repairing damaged facilities.
- When strikes on industrial and infrastructure targets failed to produce the desired political effect, target selection shifted steadily toward maximizing psychological impact on the population.
- Strategic bombers were increasingly diverted to hit tactical military targets instead.
- Strategic air commanders would insist every time that their mission failed only because politicians wouldn’t let them bomb the “right” targets with the necessary intensity — otherwise, they claimed, victory would have come quickly.
Until the late 1990s, the underlying problem was thought to be insufficient bombing accuracy, and the fix seemed obvious: adopt precision-guided munitions on a wide scale. But once those weapons arrived, things didn’t get better. In Yugoslavia, the air campaign’s outcome was, on balance, positive, though that can’t be fully attributed to strategic bombing alone. In Libya, a second, prolonged wave of strikes on tactical military targets and direct air support for opposition forces proved necessary. In Iran in 2026, the campaign failed spectacularly, partly because it followed the same familiar “recipe” described above.
There’s another problem: this part of the war carries its own escalatory logic. Any participant in an air campaign against an enemy capable of retaliating should expect strikes behind the lines on both sides not just to continue, but to intensify. Civilian casualties in Ukraine are rising again after a long lull — the toll had been declining every year since it peaked in 2022 — while in Russia, unsurprisingly, they’re at their highest level yet.
Your questions about strikes behind the lines, and our answers
It’s often said that, with rare exceptions, bombing alone doesn’t have a decisive impact on the course of a conflict. I’d like to hear more about those exceptions: obviously there are the strikes on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, but is there anything else? If so, what do they have in common? — Alexander from Moscow
The exception usually cited is NATO’s campaign against Yugoslavia during the conflict in Kosovo. But how successful those bombing and missile strikes actually turned out to be remains unclear, given exaggerations from both sides. Yugoslavia had some success repairing damaged infrastructure between strikes, though how much isn’t precisely known either. And the impact of strikes on strategic targets is hard to separate from other factors in that war’s outcome: it’s widely believed Slobodan Milosevic’s government surrendered because a NATO ground operation had become inevitable and because Belgrade was internationally isolated and had no allies.
The part the atomic bombings played in hastening Japan’s surrender is less clear-cut, too. The widespread view, including among Western researchers, holds that the Red Army’s rapid advance into Manchuria, the empire’s main resource base, drove home to Tokyo that it had reached a strategic dead end. The emperor, in fact, used this as a pretext to persuade the military to surrender, on the condition that he remain on the throne.
How effective and justified is it to spend missiles and shells on civilian utilities like heating and power plants, creating humanitarian problems for the civilian population, rather than trying to destroy strategic targets like bridges and rail junctions, even if those are harder targets to hit? — Clausewitz
The fact that the bridges across the Dnipro remain undamaged, and that there have been no strikes on other bridges, tunnels, or rail junctions deep inside Ukraine, suggests some unspoken agreement between the warring sides. Can you shed any light on this? — Femistoklius
Supplies to Ukraine’s armed forces cross the Dnipro River, meaning literally around 10 bridges would need to be damaged to create serious problems [for Ukraine]. Dams are very hard to damage remotely, but railway and road crossings, for instance, are far less fortified. Why doesn’t Russia want to concentrate its strikes on these targets? It might be difficult, but it’s easier than fighting a fifth year of war. — Ruslan
Russia has struck, and continues to strike, both railway infrastructure and bridges — with mostly unsuccessful results.
- Most railway infrastructure, aside from rolling stock and electrical equipment, is fairly easy to repair.
- Bridges are also repairable, unless their spans are brought down or their supports damaged — which is far from easy to do.
The troubled history of the rail-and-road drawbridge across the Dniester estuary at Zatoka, in the Odesa region, is well known. It connects Ukrainian territory to the right bank of the Danube and to Romania. Despite its relatively fragile design and numerous strikes with a wide variety of weapons, the structure still hasn’t been fully destroyed. Since 2022, the bridge has been hit with ballistic missiles and glide bombs — and, in single raids, dozens of drones. Ukraine has consistently repaired the damage quickly, only for Russian forces to strike it again. In early August, according to Russian sources, a massed strike finally brought down one span of the bridge.
In 2024, a Russian missile strike damaged the overpass at the Dnipro hydroelectric station, known as DniproHES, but Ukraine quickly restored traffic across it as well.
The number of bridges still standing across the Dnipro in Ukraine — not counting the pedestrian bridge or those linking Ukraine to Belarus — isn’t “around 10,” but 23. Five of them run across reservoir dams. Many of these bridges are extremely difficult targets if the goal is to destroy them outright, rather than simply damage them temporarily.
In 2024, German missile officers discussed a possible strike on the Crimean Bridge with a Taurus missile. Russian intelligence services apparently intercepted the conversation, whose authenticity was later confirmed. The officers concluded they could not train Ukrainian troops fast enough for such a mission. “They’ll just make a hole in it, [not destroy it],” one Bundeswehr representative said. A launch from a French fighter jet, they said, might also be needed for more precise targeting. In the conversation, the officers estimated that destroying the Crimean Bridge would require 10 to 20 missiles in total. Taurus is accurate enough to strike a support pillar directly, while Russian missiles aren’t as “precise.”
The United States destroyed bridges across the Danube in Yugoslavia using laser-guided missiles for precision and glide bombs for their heavy payloads. Applying the same methods to targets in Kyiv, Dnipro, and Kremenchuk would require the launching aircraft to be inside the range of Ukraine’s air defenses at the moment of release.
In short, a serious attack on the bridges across the Dnipro would require hundreds of missiles — with no guarantee the targets would even be fully destroyed.
Why do the two sides gladly inflict damage on each other’s infrastructure and civilians, while the political and economic leaderships of both countries remain completely unharmed? — Clausewitz
Why don’t the two sides strike each other’s decision-making centers? Is this some kind of backroom deal? — Oleg
And why don’t Russian forces actually bomb Bankova Street, the seat of Ukraine’s presidential administration? — Andrei Vasilyevich
We answered similar reader questions back in 2025.
This time, though, we received far more questions on strikes against “decision-making centers.” That’s partly because Israel and the United States legitimized this kind of attack by killing Iran’s political and military leaders — while also demonstrating that such strikes can fail to achieve strategic goals.
In the case of Russia and Ukraine, the “unspoken arrangement” theory may well be right, though it’s unlikely anyone actually agreed to anything explicitly. Both sides simply understand that the enemy can respond in kind, as periodically happens with assassination attempts against lower-ranking politicians and military officials, or that a strike on top officials could send the situation spiraling into uncontrolled escalation.
Why are Wildberries warehouses considered a legitimate military target? Pointing to the body armor [for sale] at the warehouses seems like a stretch. I don’t understand why such things become acceptable when one side does them but unacceptable when the other side does. — Dobrynya
How does the postwar reckoning work in terms of international law? Suppose the war ends or freezes, and the international community sees thousands of violations of international law by both sides. Who tries the people responsible, and how? What sentences can they get, and who actually enforces these “measures of accountability”? — Vladislav Kuznets
Wildberries warehouses, like those of Nova Poshta and other similar companies in Ukraine, don’t qualify as legitimate military targets under the conventions governing the laws and customs of war — even if they contain not just body armor but components of lethal weapons, such as devices for dropping grenades from drones.
The argument that Ukraine, as the victim of aggression, has the right to respond symmetrically to such Russian strikes doesn’t hold up either: the conventions classify these kinds of attacks on civilian targets as “reprisals,” and they’re prohibited.
But failing to observe the rules of target discrimination isn’t the most condemned or discussed of war crimes. Many of the world’s armies that have fought over the past 80 years have committed this violation in one form or another, even after the conventions now in force had banned it.
One more thing: everything points to this war ending in a stalemate, with no clear winner. That will likely mean each side prosecutes those it considers criminals within its own jurisdiction. The International Criminal Court could also prosecute Russians, though many countries are not parties to it. Russia itself will almost certainly keep convicting Ukrainians on “terrorism” charges rather than on war crimes charges, since war crimes are harder to “prove” — especially in cases where no crime was actually committed at all.
Why do drones roam around Russia like it’s a buffet? How did they get this kind of edge, and why has nobody in Russia managed to do anything about it in over a year? Do we even still have design bureaus, research institutes, and other organizations? — Oleg
Drones are difficult to detect, to track along their entire flight path, and to distinguish from friendly aircraft. They’re also expensive to shoot down, and a large enough swarm can overwhelm any air defense system, whose capacity to track and destroy multiple targets is inherently limited.
Armies around the world are working on this problem, but no one can guarantee complete success so far — and attack drones are improving faster than the defenses meant to stop them.
Why doesn’t Putin strike Ukrainian oil refineries and large stores as a matching response? Do Ukrainians not have oil refineries, or have they defended them well? If they’ve defended them, why can’t we do the same? If they haven’t, why isn’t anyone striking them? — Oleg
Putin has struck Ukrainian “stores” before, along with what was then the country’s only working major refinery, in Kremenchuk. Russian forces reportedly “completely destroyed” the plant back in 2022. It resumed refining several times afterward, only to be struck again — most recently in the summer of 2026, according to Russia’s Defense Ministry. Other major Ukrainian oil refineries were shut down before the war, destroyed in the fighting, or occupied — the front line, for instance, ran near the Lysychansk refinery for several years.
As a result, Ukraine today depends almost entirely on imported petroleum products. Russian forces are trying to disrupt that trade too, striking fuel depots and hundreds of gas stations, and, like Ukraine’s armed forces, using drones equipped with cameras and machine-vision guidance to hit fuel trucks behind the lines.
Russia has also struck warehouses belonging to civilian companies in Ukraine, and continues to do so.
Why doesn’t Russia destroy all the infrastructure through which weapons are supplied to Ukraine’s armed forces? Do we really not have such weapons? Or do we have such serious intelligence problems that Ukraine knows everything about us while we know nothing about them? And why do Ukrainian strikes on Russia have an economic and social effect, while all we hear about Russian strikes is that an apartment building or something similar was destroyed? — Andrei
Russia simply doesn’t have enough weapons and intelligence assets to destroy “all the infrastructure.” Ukraine does have an intelligence advantage, partly thanks to the West, but that’s not the main factor here. Ukraine has been at war for years: it hides its military plants and imports much of what it needs or receives it as aid. Finding important, vulnerable targets inside Ukraine isn’t easy.
Russian forces, for their part, have yet to develop any systematic campaign to affect Ukrainian society beyond strikes on energy facilities in winter — though they clearly want to. In summer, Ukraine’s power grid doesn’t experience shortages.
Russia, meanwhile, is trying to carry on with ordinary life: businesses keep operating quite openly, from military plants to airports and refineries. That lets Ukraine pick the most painful targets — and the ones least protected against strikes by drones with small warheads.
Russian forces, meanwhile, rely on large numbers of missiles with powerful warheads but low reliability, especially in terminal-phase targeting — so every error can turn into a catastrophe for civilians. Ukrainian censors are also far more effective at concealing the aftermath of strikes on military targets than their Russian counterparts, even though both countries have similar rules banning the publication of videos showing strike “impacts.”
Why doesn’t Ukraine strike Alabuga and the “Shahed” drone production workshops there? It seems like one of the most important targets in Russia, militarily and politically both, given all the publicity surrounding the site. After Ukraine’s recent successes with long-range strikes, it’s surprising there haven’t even been attempts to damage production, destroy it, or temporarily halt operations. — Alexander
Ukraine has struck those workshops and a workers’ dormitory several times, but the attacks have disrupted operations for at most a few days. Factory workshops are difficult targets for drones carrying small warheads; hitting them effectively requires missiles capable of carrying hundreds of kilograms of explosives.
How has Russia’s gasoline crisis affected supplies to the army? How likely is it that the military actually runs short of fuel? — Andrei
If it’s had any effect, it’s been minimal so far. The government decided that state agencies, including the military, get priority access to motor fuel: gas stations come last, while even farms rank only second. Some units of the “Dnepr” group of forces, fighting in the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, may be facing supply disruptions because they received supplies via the “Novorossiya” highway, which has come under large-scale strikes by Ukrainian drones, as well as via neighboring roads. Russian “military correspondents” — even those who regularly report on the army’s problems — aren’t currently flagging any shortage.
Why hasn’t Putin used nuclear weapons yet, even tactical ones? Why does he just silently put up with Russia being hit by drones as if it were a shooting range? — Oleg
- First, he likely considers it taboo.
- Second, the Kremlin’s main partners on the international stage — the leaders of China and India — also consider it taboo, and have told Putin as much, though that’s known only from Western media reports.
- Finally, gaining a real strategic advantage through tactical nuclear weapons isn’t easy, while escalating tensions with the West and triggering global ostracism would be all but guaranteed.
Bombing rattles a population, but that doesn’t mean people blame their own government and military for it, rather than the enemy. If anything, innocent victims of Ukrainian strikes already have some grounds to start genuinely wanting the other side to lose, not just say so out of habit. So what does this supposed turning point in Ukraine’s favor actually amount to? Or is it just a propaganda line? — Pomor
The question describes a well-known effect of strategic bombing. The authors of the article “When Does Aerial Bombing Work? Quantitative Empirical Tests, 1917–1999” say they obtained statistically significant results across various air campaigns showing that a population under attack either doesn’t blame its own government at all or shifts the blame onto the enemy — regardless of the form of government or other characteristics.
For now, it’s more accurate to describe the Ukrainian campaign not as a turning point in the war, but as an attempt to use a newly available resource to pressure the enemy — and, of course, as a response to the enemy’s own strikes.
I don’t understand why Ukraine’s armed forces don’t try to paralyze operations at major Russian airports on an ongoing basis. Is it really that hard? It seems like you could just launch drones several times a day into the area around, say, Domodedovo, to have them loiter there. Airports closed all the time would cause real problems and start shifting how people feel. — Alexander
Experience — that of Gulf countries whose airports have come under attack from Iran, as well as Russia’s own — shows it’s difficult to paralyze air travel this way for long. Doing so requires a constant threat of strikes, which means launching large numbers of drones on a regular basis, and most of them won’t even reach their targets.
Why is the attack aimed specifically at Wildberries warehouses? Why hasn’t the infrastructure of, say, Ozon been targeted? — Andrei
No one but Ukraine’s leadership has a definitive answer to that. On paper, though, Wildberries warehouses meet every criterion for a Ukrainian strike target.
- They’re poorly defended facilities that can be destroyed with just a few drones carrying small warheads.
- They hold large quantities of valuable goods that also burn easily.
- Destroying Wildberries as a business would hurt government budgets, including the federal budget, by reducing value-added tax payments.
- Finally, what sets Wildberries, founded by Tatyana Kim, apart from Ozon is its sheer scale — larger by every measure, from market share to total warehouse floor space.
Exactly how Ukraine’s military commanders drew up their target list is unclear, though military AI may have played a role. Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, an American company that leads the field globally, has said the company’s AI model actively helps select targets for Ukraine’s armed forces. Ukrainian intelligence said that this includes building a database of targets deep inside Russia. Palantir did similar work under contract to the Pentagon before the war with Iran.

The Reform UK leader won with 22,239 votes. His nearest rival, a comedian styling himself as Count Binface, came second with 9,455 votes. Farage got 1,014 more votes this time around than in 2024 — a 17-point swing in his favor — albeit against no real competition. Turnout was 44.37 percent.

Advertisement
The right-wing populist has faced mounting questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, received before he became Clacton’s member of parliament in 2024, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

The interior of the Karasun Manuk Armenian Church is seen.
Restoration has officially begun at the 150-year-old Karasun Manuk Armenian Church in Hatay, following structural and altar damage sustained during the devastating 2023 earthquakes.
The project receives 5 million Turkish Liras ($130,000) in support following decisions by the Hatay Cultural Heritage Preservation Board and the Monuments Board, with contributions from the Culture and Tourism Ministry. Built in 1876, the historic church sits in the İskenderun district.
Karasun Manuk Armenian Church Foundation Chairman Yusuf Tabaş noted that while the Feb. 6, 2023, earthquakes spared the church from total destruction, severe ground movement bulged its walls and compromised its main structure and altar. He added that heavily damaged outbuildings will be rebuilt from scratch, while the church’s income-generating shops are also slated for full restoration.
The church will close to religious services this weekend to allow crews to begin the structural interventions safely and quickly.
“As part of the restoration, the roof of the church will primarily be renewed, the floor will be restored and the existing drainage problem will be solved. Altars will be rebuilt, and necessary works will be carried out on walls requiring repair and exterior facades,” Tabaş said.
The twin earthquakes centered in Kahramanmaraş claimed more than 53,000 lives across 11 provinces in southern Türkiye. The mainshocks leveled entire urban centers and inflicted severe damage on hundreds of registered cultural assets, including historic mosques, churches and ancient monuments spanning centuries of human history. Authorities continue to prioritize the rapid restoration of all affected cultural.

Generations discover underwater world together

Two women from different generations communicate while scuba diving.
Scuba diving in Türkiye has become a shared family pursuit, following the Turkish Underwater Sports Federation’s decision to lower the minimum age limit to 12 under its “Young Diver” initiative.
At an event in Karaburun, İzmir, participants ranging from 12-year-old children to first-time divers aged 65 took part in introductory dives under the supervision of certified instructors.
Diving instructor Ece Yanaray, who accompanied her 65-year-old mother Nilgün on her first dive, said the experience showed that enthusiasm for exploring underwater life transcends age.
“We put both a 12-year-old and a 65-year-old into introductory dives. Despite the 53-year age gap, we saw the same excitement and enthusiasm in both,” Yanaray said.
Yanaray said she had long wanted to dive with her mother. After completing the dive comfortably, Nilgün was presented with a red ribbon by her daughter — a gesture recalling the ribbon her mother had given her when she first learned to read at primary school.
“It was an emotional moment,” Yanaray said. “There really is no age for the underwater world. From the age of 12, anyone who is medically fit to dive can discover its beauty.”
Karaburun Diving Center official Hamdullah Aras said the new age limit had allowed young people who were previously unable to begin training to enter the sport earlier. Participants can receive a one-star diving certification from age 14, while there is no upper age limit, provided their health permits diving.
For families, the program offers a new way to spend time together. Huriye Ersen, who dived with her family, said having an underwater family photograph had become a memorable addition to their album and that diving had strengthened their bond.
Sixteen-year-old diver Kuzey Karalom, who has completed around 50 dives, said he had encountered groupers, moray eels and octopuses. For young people curious about marine life, he described diving as a passion made more accessible by programs and centers such as Karaburun’s.

Artisan preserves root dyeing tradition with 500 natural colors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:25:22 UTC
14:25:22 KST

Şükran Kara has spent years experimenting with different fabrics, yarns, plants and boiling times, producing more than 500 shades of color.
40-year-old artisan from the central province of Kayseri’s Sarız district is working to preserve the traditional art of natural root dyeing she learned from her grandmother as a child by documenting hundreds of recipes and color samples for future generations.
Şükran Kara, who was introduced to root dyeing at the age of 6 or 7 at her family home in the rural Tekneli neighborhood, has spent years experimenting with different fabrics, yarns, plants and boiling times, producing more than 500 shades of color.
Kara has compiled recipes and color catalogs to ensure that traditional dyeing techniques, which are increasingly practiced by fewer people, are not forgotten.
Kara told state-run Anadolu Agency that she has been professionally involved in kilims, weaving and root dyeing for 15 years.
Describing the process as labor-intensive, Kara said wool is sheared in season, washed in a river and dried before being beaten with thin sticks. The wool is then spun into yarn using a spindle before being naturally dyed with plants collected from nature.
Kara said interest in root dyeing has increased over the past two years, which she described as encouraging.
She also works as a master instructor at maturation institutes and has conducted her own research on natural dyeing.
“I have a book titled ‘From Root to Color’ that I wrote on this subject. I also prepare fabric color charts and recipes. I am creating these recipes so that this root dyeing culture will not be forgotten and can be transferred to future generations,” she said.
“Not many people practice this art anymore. I am doing my best to introduce it to more young people and future generations. Interest in root dyeing has increased over the past two years.
“People from across Türkiye and even abroad contact me and ask for recipes. I have prepared root dyeing recipes for the maturation institutes in Adana and Kayseri. Friends from Paris have also contacted me, and I have taken part in some of their projects.”
Kara said she obtains brown from walnuts, yellow from barberry roots, green from nettles and beige from acorns.
“I see this as my own culture and essence. I believe every person has a color of their own and finds that color at the dyeing pot. I recommend that all young people try it because it is an art and craft that requires effort and patience and tells the story of a person’s roots and past,” she said.
Kara said she created her catalog through trial and error by experimenting with plants collected from nature.
“I prepared my color chart with visuals and recipes showing which colors different fabrics and types of yarn produce and how they turn out. I have more than 500 recipes,” she said.

1,600-year-old bathhouse emerges at ancient city of Nysa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:25:13 UTC
14:25:13 KST

The ancient city of Nysa is known as the ‘city with two sides’ because it was built across a valley.
Archaeologists excavating the ancient city of Nysa in the western province of Aydın are uncovering a 1,500- to 1,600-year-old bathhouse believed to have served as a place where people washed and cleaned themselves before entering the city.
Excavations at Nysa, known as an educational and cultural center during the Roman period, are being conducted under the direction of Professor Serdar Hakan Öztaner of Ankara University’s Department of Archaeology, with the support of the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
Known as the “city with two sides” because it was built across a valley, Nysa is home to one of the best-preserved ancient libraries in Anatolia, a theater with a capacity of around 10,000 people, a stadium, three bridges bearing traces of Roman architecture and engineering and a tunnel.
Excavations among the olive trees are currently focusing on the Late Roman Bath, which dates to the fourth century A.D., to determine the full boundaries of the structure.
Öztaner told Anadolu Agency that excavations were continuing at the approximately 1,600-year-old bath as part of the “Heritage for the Future” project.
He said teams were working along the southern and western sides of the bath to better understand its layout.
“This year, we are continuing excavations along the arched section extending along the southern edge of the structure and on its western facade. We are also investigating the relationship between the western facade and Street 8 to establish its exact place in the city plan,” he said.
A place to wash before entering the city
Öztaner said the bathhouse was located along a street connected to the road leading to Nysa from the ancient cities of Ephesus and Tralleis.
“The Late Roman bath appears to have been a place where those arriving in the city washed and cleansed themselves before entering. We have not yet determined the full dimensions of the structure, but we have identified its main rooms,” he said.
“We are investigating its western and southern sides. It is located in the insula south of the library. Therefore, we are uncovering an important public building from the Late Roman period on the western side of Nysa, the city with two sides.”
Öztaner noted that bathhouses were often built near city entrances during the Roman period and afterward as part of urban planning and construction.
He said the team aims to determine the full boundaries of the bathhouse this year.
Öztaner said they plan to carry out conservation and restoration work alongside incorporating the structure into the city’s archaeological plan.
“We aim to clearly understand the plan of the bathhouse and introduce it to the archaeological literature. Since this is the first structure visitors to the city see, its visual appearance is also very striking,” he said.

Settlers returned the following day, blocked a road with rocks and clashed with soldiers, according to footage recorded by residents.

Qusra Mayor Abdel Azim Wadi said the settlers remained elsewhere in the village after the outposts were removed. Families evacuated during the military operation had not returned to their homes as of Aug. 13, residents said.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry separately accused Israeli authorities of using settler violence to advance forced displacement and the annexation of the West Bank. It called for international intervention and sanctions against those carrying out or supporting the attacks.
The U.N. humanitarian office said in April that Qusra had recorded 27 settler attacks causing casualties or property damage in 2026, the highest number documented in any single West Bank community at that point.
One Palestinian had been killed and eight others wounded in those attacks.

Tunnel collapses at an Indian hydropower project, killing at least 7
