Builders, bakers and cheeseburger-makers: the UK workers struggling in extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:00:19 UTC
14:00:19 KST

In the sweltering kitchen of the Plimsoll pub in north London, the head chef, Joshua Swinney, has a frozen tea towel wrapped around his neck to combat the heat.
As temperatures exceeded 35C (95F) in the capital, workers who were not lucky enough to be in air-conditioned offices sweltered in the heat.
To cope, Swinney said the pub tried to put more dishes on the menu that did not require ovens or stoves. That is tricky, however, when it is most famed for its cheeseburger, the making of which entails standing over a grill.
“Suddenly you realise you have seven salads on and can’t get enough raw fish dishes in there,” he said. “As for the heat itself, fans help, but mostly just blow the hot air around, and you can’t have them in the service kitchen.” He said kitchen staff had been known to keep cool a number of ways: “I’ve even seen someone take an ice bath in a flexi bucket.”
Swinney is just about managing, but bakers, construction workers, bus drivers, paramedics and teachers all say heatwaves are becoming incredibly dangerous for them. A campaign for a maximum working temperature, to bring England into line with other European countries, is gathering pace.
Spain is the gold standard: the maximum working temperatures for sedentary work, such as office work, is 27C, while for light physical work it is 25C. In Belgium, it is 29C for light physical work, 26C for a moderately heavy physical work, 22C for heavy physical work and 18C for very heavy physical work.
Kenny Dinsdale, a construction worker, said there was a risk to life from working in extreme heat. “If you’re not careful, you run the risk of significant injury, either through dehydration or through heat stroke or, you know, the ultimate thing is death.”
He said the demographics of the construction industry meant workers like him were particularly at risk. “We’re an older workforce. I’m 65 years of age coming up this birthday, I’m still working in the industry.” He suggested construction should adopt more “Mediterranean-style hours” to avoid the heat of the day.
Bakers, with their large, hot ovens, often working in small unventilated spaces, were also struggling. Sarah Woolley, the chair of the Bakers, Food and Allied Workers’ Union, said: “As it heats up outside, an already hot workplace with ovens and provers is going to get hotter still.” Her union has been calling for a maximum working temperature for a decade.
She said that rather than just putting regular fans in their bakeries, some employers had implemented extra measures, such as relaxing the uniform guidance without impacting food safety standards, providing cold water and offering additional breaks. “But others, where we haven’t got [union] recognition, stay open and expect workers to continue as normal. Some employers have provided isotonic drinks rather than just ice pops, reduced lines running, and instructed unnecessary equipment, like hot holds, to be turned off rather than adding to the heat.”
It is difficult for essential workers, such as paramedics, to stop working in intense heat, but they are asking to be allowed to shed their sweltering uniforms when temperatures reach a certain level.
An ambulance medical technician in Birmingham said: “Working in the heat has been awful. It’s vile. It’s also ridiculously busy when it’s hot. We have one uniform, whether it’s -10C or 30C. You’re sweating even when you’re just driving. I could have cried during my last shift. I often think: ‘I can’t do this again’.”
A London paramedic said of his uniform: “I love the good weather, but the minute I put my uniform on, it’s unbearable. I recently had to carry someone down from the seventh floor, and I don’t think I’ve ever sweated that much in my life. I work at capacity, both physically and mentally. The physical demands of working in the heat are extreme.”
Unison’s head of policy, Sampson Low, said: “Paramedics, cleaners and other public sector workers have no choice but to carry on when the mercury rises. Extreme heat not only brings a rise in demand for care but can also affect the health of staff. What’s needed are thresholds based on evidence. This is for jobs where work can’t simply stop when a temperature is reached.”
Bus drivers have been voicing their frustration about the greenhouse-like effect in their cabs, where air conditioning, if it exists, often does not work and temperatures can exceed 40C. Some have recently gone on strike to protest against their conditions.
One London bus driver said: “The buses are at the poorest state ever. The aircon barely works, the heatwave is icing on the cake. I feel we as bus drivers are treated extremely unfairly and we just add up numbers, to the companies we mean nothing.’
Another added: “The buses don’t have AC, they think putting a little fan in the cab helps. It doesn’t. The cab’s temperature is hotter than being outside, it’s ridiculous. Something needs to be done. I have suffered with migraines and when it’s hot they get worse.”
The Trades Union Congress’s health and safety lead, Huma Haq, said: “The experience from other countries is clear: maximum workplace temperatures can work. If they work in Spain, where summers are far hotter than in the UK, they can work here too. Unions are calling for rules that require employers to take action to reduce temperatures when they exceed 24C, and for work to stop when temperatures reach 30C, or 27C for strenuous jobs.
“Unions have been leading this campaign, and right now workers are taking action to keep themselves safe as temperatures climb to extremes again. From bus drivers in north London to front of house at the V&A Museum, workers are using their collective power to bring about the changes needed for cooler and safer workplaces.”

‘We feared we’d all be drowned’: the Indian floods that killed more than 100 and left thousands homeless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:00:19 UTC
14:00:19 KST

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

Helen Goh’s recipe for frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:00:18 UTC
14:00:18 KST

I love the glorious unruliness of Eton mess, all billowy cream, crushed meringue and tumbling fruit. This frozen version captures all of that charm but in a sliceable, make-ahead dessert that’s perfect for August entertaining. The fruit can even be cooked a day in advance, leaving little more to do than whip everything together before freezing. Thanks to the condensed milk, the cream freezes surprisingly softly, while the meringue keeps its gentle chew and the toasted coconut adds a welcome crunch and nuttiness. Late summer plums bring a lovely tartness that balances the sweetness beautifully, though apricots, peaches and nectarines would also work well.
Frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry
Prep 10 min
 Cook 40 min
 Freeze 8 hr+
 Serves 8
For the fruit
  400g red plums (about 5 medium fruit), stoned and quartered
40g caster sugar
  2 tsp lemon juice
  1 pinch fine sea salt
  120g raspberries, plus a few extra to decorate
For the ice-cream
150g coconut condensed milk, or regular condensed milk
  250ml double cream
  1 tsp vanilla extract
  ½ tsp fine sea salt
  120g shop-bought meringues, roughly broken
50g toasted coconut chips, plus 15g extra to decorate
Start by cooking the fruit, as it needs to cool completely before being folded into the ice-cream. Put the plums, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a medium pan on a medium heat. Cover partially with a lid and leave to cook gently for about 10 minutes, until the plums soften and collapse. Add the raspberries, stir gently for about a minute, just until they begin to soften, then take off the heat.
Strain the fruit through a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl, reserving both the fruit and its juices separately. Return the juices to the pan and simmer on a medium-high heat for three to five minutes, until reduced to a lightly syrupy consistency. Pour into a small jug and leave both the syrup and the fruit to cool completely.
Line a 20cm x 10cm loaf tin with baking paper, leaving plenty of overhang on all sides. Put the condensed milk, cream, vanilla and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk on medium-high until the mixture holds firm peaks. Fold in the broken meringues and toasted coconut chips, until evenly incorporated, then add the cooled fruit. Fold gently a few times, just so the fruit remains in generous ripples, rather than becoming fully incorporated.
Spoon the mix into the lined tin and smooth out the surface with a spatula. Tap the tin firmly on a work surface a few times to knock out any air pockets, then fold the paper overhang over the top and freeze overnight, or for at least eight hours.
To serve, briefly wrap the outside of the tin with a hot, damp tea towel, then use the paper overhang to lift the ice-cream on to a platter. Spoon over the reserved fruit syrup, scatter with the extra toasted coconut and decorate with a few extra raspberries. Slice thickly and serve immediately with any remaining syrup alongside.

SMIC weighs more capacity as AI-related chip demand exceeds forecasts
China’s largest foundry says shortages are spreading to mature-node chips, with some AI-driven demand visible through the end of 2027
Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) is actively looking at adding equipment in its factories after demand for mature-node chips used alongside AI processors surged beyond expectations, according to company management.
“Future wafer starts are far exceeding our previous expectations,” co-CEO Zhao Haijun said during an earnings call, referring to the volume of new chip batches entering the production line.
Zhao said SMIC was adjusting its expansion plans and may install additional equipment at existing sites where space was available, with further details to be disclosed in upcoming announcements or briefings.
Demand was particularly strong for supporting chips in AI servers and data centres – including logic chips, power-management products and optical module components. Orders for BCD (bipolar-CMOS-DMOS) power-management products were visible through the end of 2027, Zhao added.

Northern Lights travel bucket list: Unique trips and experiences to book in 2026-2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:00:05 UTC
14:00:05 KST

Witnessing the Aurora Borealis is top of the bucket list for many travellers. In this guide, we pick out some of the best Northern Lights trips and experiences to book in 2026 and 2027.
For people around the world, seeing the Aurora Borealis – better known as the Northern Lights – is high on many a travel bucket list.
Typically visible in regions near the Earth’s poles, the spectacular phenomenon occurs when electrically charged particles from the Sun reach Earth and interact with its magnetic field and atmosphere, creating vivid ribbons of green, red, blue and purple light across the night sky.
Do you have the Northern Lights on your travel bucket list? Here’s some of the top trips and experiences to book in 2026 and 2027.
Best places and time to see the Northern Lights
While you can see “the world’s greatest light show” in both polar regions, the viewing is “better in the northern hemisphere”, said Bucket List Travels. In the so-called “Aurora Belt”, it appears with the “most intense light and greatest colour variations”.
Top destinations to see the Northern Lights include Iceland, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Lapland, Alaska and the Yukon in Canada.
It’s well known that the Aurora Borealis is an “elusive spectacle” and “sightings can’t be guaranteed”, said Exodus Adventure Travels. However, during prime weather conditions, you are “more likely to catch a glimpse” between the months of September and March when the skies are at their darkest.
Spectacular hotel stays
Hotel Rangá in south Iceland is a popular place to stay for guests seeking to see the Northern Lights or to go stargazing, due to its own advanced on-site observatory and remote location. By turning off the external lights, the hotel provides “optimal conditions to view the night sky” and travellers can also relax in geothermal hot tubs while starbathing.
The Kakslauttanen Arctic Resort, a wilderness retreat in Finland, offers “infinite stars” with guests sleeping under the Northern Lights in its iconic glass igloos.
Another property to offer “sky views from the comfort of your bed” is Aurora Village Ivalo in Finnish Lapland, which has a range of igloo cabins available.
The Santa Claus Express, Finland
Autumn and late winter are the best times to spot the Northern Lights, and if you’re lucky you could combine seeing them during certain journeys on the Santa Claus Express in Finland.
One of the most magical rail journeys in Europe, this Finnish overnight sleeper train takes travellers from Helsinki and Turku all the way north into the Arctic Circle to Rovaniemi, through frozen lakes and snow-dusted woods.
Horse riding on the Northern Lights Trail in Iceland
Horse riding holiday company Saddle Travel has a four-day trip on the "Northern Lights Trail" in Iceland. Starting from £1,179 (€1,375) per person, guests can spend around four hours per day for three days riding Icelandic horses on volcanic mountain slopes, before relaxing in thermal swimming pools and watching snow fall from the outdoor hot tub in a cosy winter wonderland.
Yukon's Aurora360 experience: Fly through the Northern Lights
One of the world's rarest Northern Lights experiences is returning to the Yukon, with an exclusive Aurora360 flight taking to the skies in February 2027. It offers travellers the opportunity to witness the Aurora Borealis from 30,000 feet aboard a private Air North charter aircraft.
Unlike traditional Northern Lights holidays, the Aurora360 flight lifts guests above cloud cover, dramatically increasing the chances of witnessing the dancing lights in all their brilliance. With every passenger guaranteed a window seat, the flight provides an unrivalled perspective of the aurora.
Canada As You Like It offers a seven-night Yukon's Northern Lights Resort & Spa Aurora360 holiday from £7,735 (€9,021) per person, including return international flights, two nights in Vancouver, four nights at Northern Lights Resort & Spa, one night in Whitehorse, and an exclusive Air North Aurora360 flight.
Reykjavík and the Northern Lights, Iceland
Travellers on this five-day trip with Newmarket Holidays can explore Iceland’s capital Reykjavík before heading out of the city to search for the Aurora Borealis. There’s also the option of a dip in the mineral-rich warm waters of the Blue Lagoon, and a Golden Circle tour to see Þingvellir, the dramatic open expanse where Iceland's ancient assemblies came to set the laws of the land.
Available from October 2026 to March 2028, it costs from £1,056 (€1,231) per person and includes return flights from various airports in the UK.
Havila Voyages’s Northern Lights ‘promise’
Norway-based cruise operator Havila Voyages is so confident that passengers will see the Northern Lights on its sailings that it’s made this promise: “If the lights don’t show up, your next voyage is on us – free of charge.”
For passengers that book on a 12-day round voyage between 1 October and 31 March, Havila Voyages promises that the magical Aurora Borealis will “make an appearance”. However, “if nature plays shy" and the lights "don’t grace the skies", passengers will receive a complimentary six-or seven-day voyage, Havila Voyages said.

Busta Studio evokes the elegance of New York townhouses for Kimpton Ashbel hotel

LRT English Newsletter: Enduring sins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – August 14, 2026.
For 23 years, one man moved through parishes in southeastern Lithuania – and, prosecutors say, quietly kept a secret nobody at his own Church or parishes ever suspected. But now that secret became a criminal case, and a national reckoning over how the Catholic Church, and the state, handle allegations of sexual abuse against children.
Vilnius prosecutors have referred to court a priest accused of sexual crimes against minors over two decades – from 2002 to 2025 – 34 charges, including two counts of raping a minor, with 11 recognised victims aged 12 to 18 at the time. In a separate but related case, a second priest faces a charge of possessing child pornography.
Neither prosecutors nor the Archdiocese have named either man publicly, though Lithuanian outlet Delfi has identified them as 56-year-old Tadas Švedavičius and 51-year-old Ryšardas Peciunas, respectively. The Archdiocese says one has admitted guilt, but didn’t say which.
Critics are confused over the prosecutors’ decision to withhold the names, since they’re easily identifiable using publicly available information. They also argue that withholding the names makes it harder for other potential victims to come forward, even as they acknowledged the counter-risk of vigilante backlash if names were released.
The Archdiocese has opened its own canonical investigation and notified the Vatican, while also cooperating, it says, with law enforcement. But that self-policing model isn’t convincing human rights activists. The Catholic Church is known to follow a long-standing practice of quietly reassigning problem priests to new parishes for a “fresh start” – historically covering everything from broken celibacy vows to, campaigners warn, more serious misconduct that can hand an abuser access to a new, unsuspecting community. Whether either priest here was ever moved this way, the Archdiocese won’t say.
The case also raised questions about the lack of a public sex offender registry in Lithuania. The country’s only existing safeguard against former abusers is a policy started in 2024, whereby anyone working directly with children – including priests running catechism classes, youth groups, or camps – must hold a QR code confirming they have no conviction for sexual offenses against children. But the policy has huge gaps. Purely religious duties, like saying Mass or hearing confessions, are exempt. Furthermore, nobody tracks how many priests actually hold the code, and most critically, it only screens people already convicted.
That last gap cuts to the heart of why this case went unnoticed for so long. Both the Archdiocese and the communities affected have either refused to respond or claimed they never received any prior reports or suspicions about either priest. Even the Church’s own 18 months of safeguarding training, which one of the priests went through, ultimately proved useless here. Prosecutors say that’s not unusual: it’s a pattern seen worldwide, where such cases stay hidden for decades because victims rarely come forward.
MORE ON SEXUAL ABUSE
But how could victims be expected to come forward when Lithuanian institutions across the board are riddled with similar gaps when it comes to handling sexual assault? A separate story regarding drug-facilitated sexual assault paints much the same picture. Comedian and advocate Vita Žiba, who was drugged and assaulted a decade ago, described the disorientation that followed – and the wave of victim-blaming she faced after speaking publicly, even when her story helped surface roughly 800 other accounts from women with similar experiences.
But turning those stories into justice is another matter. Specialist care exists in only five hospitals, all in major cities, forcing rural survivors through a maze of queues and transfers. Worse, Lithuania doesn’t currently preserve forensic evidence for any set period, meaning survivors who aren’t ready to report immediately may find it harder to prove their case later. Advocates are pushing for a clear referral pathway and a mandatory evidence-retention window, whereas the Social Security Ministry says reforms – including a 24-hour notification requirement for healthcare providers and a longer-term protection order – could reach parliament this autumn, with an eye toward taking effect next June.
ABUSE IN WASHINGTON?
Moving onto a different kind of abuse: a brewing scandal at Lithuania’s embassy in Washington has spilled into political warfare at home, with Ambassador Gediminas Varvuolis facing complaints from his own staff and now – a formal review.
The story surfaced in early August, after embassy employees complained to the Foreign Ministry about Varvuolis’ conduct, citing shouting, disrespect, and excessive hours. Staff reportedly spoke with the ministry’s inspector general, but no formal investigation followed – the Ministry dismissed the complaints as unverified rumours, and Varvuolis said he wasn’t aware of any inquiry.
That didn’t hold. By mid-August, opposition conservatives – led by deputy foreign affairs committee chair Žygimantas Pavilionis – were trying to arrange informal talks with staff about the ambassador. Pavilionis said he’d heard nothing but complaints about Varvuolis for six months, even suggesting US officials were growing reluctant to deal with him.
That’s when it turned political. Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys accused the conservatives of “provocation” and harming Lithuania’s relations with the US, while PM Mindaugas Sinkevičius urged politicians to stop interfering. The Ministry itself is now scrutinising whether Pavilionis himself has a conflict of interest, acting for his party rather than as a lawmaker.
The Ministry now also says it will form a commission to formally assess the allegations, with findings due before the parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee on August 26. Varvuolis has served as ambassador to the US for only a year.
LEIPZIG DRONE
A drone carrying explosives shut down part of one of Europe's busiest cargo hubs on August 4, and the trail runs straight back to Lithuania.
The drone was spotted near a fleet of Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, prompting German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt to call it “a new threat scenario” in the ongoing wave of hybrid warfare hitting Europe. Hours later, a separate cargo plane near the same airport struck an unidentified object midair and had to divert to Hanover, landing with only minor damage. The incidents were serious enough that Germany has since summoned Poland, the Baltic states, and the Nordic countries for security talks.
The Lithuanian connection emerged days later, when German investigators matched a DNA trace from the drone to evidence in an unrelated but ongoing case: incendiary parcels shipped from Lithuania to the UK and Poland in 2024, at least two of them via DHL. One of those parcels ignited at – of all places – Leipzig airport; another caught fire in a British warehouse. Five people already face charges over the parcels, a mix of Lithuanian, Ukrainian, and Russian nationals.
Who’s actually behind either incident remains officially unconfirmed. The Wall Street Journal has reported, citing intelligence sources, that the drone has been tied to Russia, but German authorities have named no suspect, and the investigation is still open.
EDITOR’S PICKS
– With US troop presence in Lithuania still in question, Vilnius is carefully navigating Washington’s conflict with the ICC.
– It’s been five years since Lithuania’s migration crisis began, and the country’s own ombudsperson says its reception centres still don’t meet basic standards.
– Century-old search for our national hero’s grave might be nearing the end.
– Check out the photos of partial eclipse over Lithuania.
– Learn about Lithuania’s Oscar selection.

Kyle Schwarber can’t wait to watch ‘Field of Dreams’ with his kids. Dad hit a pair of homers there
DYERSVILLE, Iowa (AP) — Kyle Schwarber grew up in Middletown, Ohio, played college ball at Indiana and spent his first six major league seasons with the Chicago Cubs.
The 33-year-old Philadelphia Phillies slugger added another thoroughly Midwestern highlight to his well-decorated career Thursday night, hitting two home runs into an Iowa cornfield.
Schwarber led off the Field of Dreams game with a homer and then connected for a two-run shot in the fourth inning to spark the Phillies in a 7-1 victory over the Minnesota Twins.
“We all watched the movie as kids, so it was really cool to be able to see exactly where it was and just kind of the full ceremony of it, too,” said Schwarber, who leads the major leagues with 37 home runs. “Just an unbelievable experience.”
After helping the Cubs win the World Series in 2016, making the postseason 10 times in his first 11 years and being selected to four All-Star teams, Schwarber has been building quite the resume. With 377 career home runs and counting, perhaps he’ll one day join the club in Cooperstown like the 26 members of the National Baseball Hall of Fame who took part in the pregame pomp at the newly constructed ballpark.
For now, Schwarber has an unforgettable night to share with his family forever. His two children are too young to watch or understand the movie now, but he can’t wait to watch the 1989 film with them down the road.
“You might not ever get to play another big league baseball game here, so to be able to have that experience, it’s a unique thing for you and it’s something you’re going to bring up to your kids,” Schwarber said. “We’re going to watch that movie together with my kids one day and be able to say, ‘Hey, dad got to play there,’ or, ‘See that house in this movie? I got to see it.’ So it’ll be really cool.”
Twins right fielder Luke Keaschall, who homered in the loss, nearly caught Schwarber’s second home run above the wall, but the ball glanced off his glove and into the dark green sea of corn.
“It was up there a while. In a perfect world, I think I should catch it,” Keaschall said. “I didn’t today.”
The Phillies moved a half-game ahead of idle Arizona into the third and final wild-card spot for the NL playoffs. So Schwarber’s big swings meant more than just a page in his personal memory book.
“To have a good season a lot of guys have to have good years, but the aircraft carriers have still got to carry you,” Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. “That just takes pressure off of everyone.”
Having entered the night just 10-15 since the All-Star break, the Phillies needed a bit of a jolt like the magic of the movie site and game location can produce — and their star designated hitter can provide.
“I feel like some people could take that for granted because he’s done it so many times, but we definitely don’t,” Phillies pitcher Aaron Nola said. “There’s no moment ever too big for him.”

Luigi Mangione set to appear in court for expected guilty plea in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO

Luigi Mangione set to appear in court for expected guilty plea in killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO
NEW YORK (AP) — Luigi Mangione is scheduled to be in federal court Friday for a hearing at which he’s expected to plead guilty in connection with the 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Mangione could still change his mind about the plea, said the person, who was not authorized to talk publicly about the case and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity. Previous plea talks in June broke down.
Lawyers for Mangione and the Justice Department declined comment prior to the late-morning court hearing, which was hastily requested by prosecutors and defense lawyers earlier this week.
Mangione, 28, was charged by both federal and state prosecutors with ambushing Thompson, 50, outside a New York City hotel on Dec. 4, 2024, as the insurance executive walked to UnitedHealth Group’s annual investor conference.
A trial on state murder charges is scheduled to start next month. It is unclear whether that trial would go forward if Mangione pleaded guilty in the federal case.
Mangione faces two federal charges that he stalked Thompson to cause his death. Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed Mangione to a potential death penalty.
Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”
Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first. The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.
In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.
U.S. District Judge Margaret M. Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defense, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.
They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.
In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defense in the state case but reversed course a day later. The defense, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.
Surveillance video of the killing showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims.
Mangione, a University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, was arrested five days later at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pennsylvania, about 230 miles (370 kilometers) west of Manhattan.
He has become a cause célèbre for some people upset with the health insurance industry.

A look at the history and beliefs behind Japan’s controversial shrine to the war dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:53:02 UTC
13:53:02 KST

A look at the history and beliefs behind Japan’s controversial shrine to the war dead
Emperor Meiji first visited the site that would become one of Japan’s most controversial shrines in 1874. He vowed that the names of those who died for their country would live there forever.
More than 2.4 million people are now honored at Yasukuni, a memorial and Shinto shrine in central Tokyo. Among them are 14 war criminals who are also commemorated each Aug. 15, when Japan’s surrender ended World War II.
The shrine provides spiritual comfort for some who mourn relatives and others who visit to express gratitude. Yet for Asian countries that endured Japanese imperial rule and expansion, Yasukuni remains a symbol of Japan’s militarism.
Visits by Japanese leaders frequently draw criticism from China and South Korea, which see them as a sign of insufficient remorse for Japan’s wartime aggression.
Here’s a look at the history and religious background of a shrine that is both a sacred place of remembrance and a source of controversy.
Yasukuni’s foundation followed a historic transformation
Imperial rule was restored in Japan in the 19th century after the fall of a military government that ruled for more than 250 years. A year into the new imperial era, in 1869, Emperor Meiji ordered the construction of the shrine that would later be renamed Yasukuni.
The name derives from two Japanese characters that can be translated as “peaceful country,” and its purpose was to honor those who fell defending the imperial cause.
“Yasukuni Shrine was initially conceived as a way to send a message to the Japanese people,” said Akiko Takenaka, a professor of history at the University of Kentucky. “The message was about the emperor; the message was about a new Japan.”
In that Japan, Takenaka added, Meiji became the one who could bestow the highest honor on those who died fighting for the empire and men were expected to consider it an honor to sacrifice their lives for him.
Religion and government became intertwined
Japan’s emperors have long been regarded as descendants of the sun goddess Amaterasu under Shinto beliefs. However, the notion of the emperor’s divine origins strengthened during the Meiji era, when the concept of State Shinto arose.
On one hand, that meant the government exercised control over the shrine’s practices and finances. Beyond that, the line between patriotism and religion blurred.
“The Meiji reformers believed that they were establishing an ideal nation in which the people and the sacred emperor maintained a spiritual union,” wrote Susumu Shimazono, a scholar specializing in religion and modern Japan, in the Japanese Journal of Religious Studies.
The separation of religion and state came after Japan’s surrender in WWII.
In December 1945, U.S. Gen. Douglas MacArthur issued an order that abolished State Shinto. The measure effectively cut off government funding for shrines and removed Shinto practices and teachings from public institutions.
Yasukuni subsequently became a private religious corporation. Official visits have raised questions about the constitutional separation of religion and government.
Enshrinement at Yasukuni has long stirred controversy
Yasukuni is not a cemetery. Rather than bodies or graves, those remembered there are enshrined as “kami” — divinities or sacred spirits in the Shinto tradition.
They include soldiers, women who provided battlefield relief, students mobilized to support wartime production, and foreign nationals who died while serving Japan.
Yasukuni’s most controversial kami are 14 Class-A war criminals, a designation applied to Japanese leaders accused of “crimes against peace” by planning and waging the war. Among them is wartime Prime Minister Hideki Tojo, one of the masterminds behind the attack on Pearl Harbor.
Their enshrinement was carried out in secret by Yasukuni’s head priest in 1978, three years after Hirohito last prayed at the shrine.
“Emperor Hirohito did not go again after he found out,” said Mark R. Mullins, professor of Japanese and religious studies at the University of Auckland. “He didn’t want to get caught up in criticism surrounding that.”
Hirohito’s successors have sent emissaries to Yasukuni for its key annual rites, but neither has visited the shrine in person as emperor.
Other controversial enshrinements include Buddhists, Christians, Koreans and Taiwanese whose families say they were included without their consent, Mullins said.
Some have taken legal action, but Japanese courts have rejected efforts to have relatives removed from the shrine.
Yasukuni means different things to different people
“For some of those in the bereaved families’ association, the focus may be on the personal grief,” Mullins said. “But for those who are keen to restore what they feel was lost by the loss of the war and the foreign occupation, it means something more.”
Adjacent to the shrine is the Yushukan Museum, which displays wartime artifacts. Scholars have underscored how its account of Japan’s military history leaves out the experiences of China and Korea under Japanese imperialism.
“By eliminating the enemy, the Yushukan remembers a war that was only ever glorious,” wrote John Breen, a professor at the International Research Center for Japanese Studies, in a paper called “Yasukuni Shrine: Ritual and Memory.”
Some visitors say paying respects at Yasukuni carries a spiritual meaning that should not be equated with endorsing war.
Kana Shindo, a member of Tokyo’s Minato City Assembly, said she regards the shrine as a place where she purifies her mind, gives thanks to the kami and reflects on herself.
“I have absolutely no intention of glorifying war,” said Shindo, who added that politicians also have freedom of religion and conscience. “I visit because I believe that the peaceful Japan in which we live today exists upon the lives and accumulated history of the people who lived before us.”
Bereaved families maintain ties to Yasukuni
Before leaving for war, Japanese soldiers were told that if they died, they would be enshrined at Yasukuni.
“They told their families: ‘I want you to come see me at Yasukuni Shrine,’” said Toshiei Mizuochi, president of the Japan War-Bereaved Families Association.
His father, who served in the Japanese navy, was killed in a bombing six days before the end of the war, on Aug. 9, 1945.
More than 2.4 million Japanese soldiers died overseas during WWII. The remains of approximately 1 million have yet to be recovered.
“For that reason, the vast majority of bereaved families who received neither remains nor personal belongings believe that the spirits of the war dead are at Yasukuni Shrine,” Mizuochi said.
Relatives like him visit Yasukuni beyond Aug. 15. They attend major ceremonies, commemorate death anniversaries and report family milestones — entering school, starting a job, getting married or having a child.
“I visit Yasukuni Shrine more times than I can count in a year,” Mizuochi said. “Every time I put my hands together in prayer, the face of my father in his portrait naturally comes to mind.”

Salvage work begins on tanker leaking oil off Oman, risk firm says

Salvage work begins on tanker leaking oil off Oman, risk firm says
Environmental NGO Greenpeace warns that spill has rapidly expanded to 1,300 square kilometres, threatening ecosystems.
A salvage operation is under way to stabilise the stricken tanker behind a major oil spill off Oman, the risk management company coordinating the effort has said.
The announcement by Ambrey on Thursday came a day after Oman’s environmental authority confirmed that oil from the Caroline Bezengi had reached beaches along the sultanate’s central coast.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4AI escapes confinement
- list 2 of 4Talks between government and opposition mark a new chapter for Venezuela
- list 3 of 4Bodycam captures lightning striking metres from US police officers
- list 4 of 4Could Trump actually run for a third term as president?
The tanker, a suspected member of Russia’s shadow fleet used to transport sanctioned Russian oil, has been leaking crude into waters near the Hallaniyat archipelago since June, when the ship’s crew reported an unidentified explosion.
Ambrey said it was working with Omani authorities and that its services had been engaged as part of a “significant international response” that included salvage vessels, aircraft and specialist personnel.
Apart from Oman and an unnamed “leading international oil spill response company”, Ambrey did not elaborate on which other countries or firms were involved in the effort to salvage the vessel, which has flown the flags of states including Cameroon, Palau and Liberia.
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) – the United Nations maritime agency – said on Thursday that it was “closely monitoring” the situation and would “continue to support ongoing efforts”, without providing further details.
The International Oil Pollution Compensation Funds, a pair of intergovernmental organisations established to provide compensation for oil pollution, said it would not be involved in the cleanup operation after determining that the incident likely resulted from an act of war.
Ambrey, based in Hereford in the United Kingdom, said it expected salvage vessels to reach the Caroline Bezengi soon and that specialist personnel had already boarded the vessel to begin stabilising its cargo.
Ed Wollaston, director of global response at Ambrey, said the “extremely challenging situation” had been complicated by adverse weather from the annual Khareef monsoon.
“However, we have deployed the leading experts in each aspect of the response and have mobilised the appropriate supporting equipment, aircraft and vessels,” Wollaston said in a statement.
“We are working around the clock to mitigate the environmental impact of the situation.”
The oil spill has expanded dramatically in size over the past week, according to analyses of satellite imagery, raising fears for coastlines and ecosystems in the region, including a marine reserve established last year off the Hallaniyat archipelago.
Environmental NGO Greenpeace said on Thursday that, based on satellite imagery, the spill had grown from 45 square kilometres (17sq miles) in late July to about 1,300sq kilometres (502sq miles) as of Wednesday.
Omani authorities as recently as Monday estimated the size of the spill at approximately 400sq kilometres (154sq miles).
Hanen Keskes, Greenpeace’s head of campaigns for the MENA region, said the circumstances of the spill made it “especially challenging” to respond to.
“Given the scale of this – a damaged tanker in a remote location, during monsoon season, with no clear owner or verified insurer to compel a rapid response – this is a case where international assistance should be mobilised urgently,” Keskes told Al Jazeera.
“Capabilities like specialised salvage equipment and expertise can exceed what any one country has on hand, and every day of delay allows more oil to disperse.”
Najmedin Meshkati, an expert in oil spills and a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Southern California, said that authorities should have moved faster to contain the spill.
“That two-month interval was the response window, and it closed. In spill response, source control on day three is worth many multiples of source control on day 60,” Meshkati told Al Jazeera.
Meshkati acknowledged, however, that Omani authorities had been dealt a difficult situation.
“It was handed an orphaned wreck with no responsive owner, no verifiable insurer, no functioning flag state, and a compensation regime containing a war exclusion that may void it entirely,” Meshkati said.
“No mid-sized maritime administration on earth is resourced for that. But that is precisely the argument for escalating harder and earlier.”
Damilola S Olawuyi, a professor of energy and environmental law at Hamad Bin Khalifa University in Qatar, said the spill highlighted the need for stronger international mechanisms to hold polluters accountable.
“The obligation of the entity responsible for pollution to pay for the cost of cleanup and remediation, ie, the polluter pays principle, has for long been a bedrock of international law,” Olawuyi told Al Jazeera.
“However, in an era of increasing geopolitical realignments, identifying the responsible polluter has become complex, therefore complicating effective risk reduction, response and remediation measures,” he said.

Finnish study links coffee drinking to leaner physique
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:51:46 EEST
13:51:46 KST

Coffee-loving Finns may have another reason to enjoy their daily brew. A new study from the University of Oulu suggests that higher coffee consumption is associated with a leaner body composition.
The study is particularly relevant in Finland, one of the world's highest coffee-consuming countries, where annual consumption averages around 11.8 kilograms per person.
People who regularly drank coffee tended to have a leaner body composition than those who did not, the study found.
The study analysed data from more than 2,200 participants in the 1966 Northern Finland Birth Cohort. The analysis focused on data collected when participants were 46 years old. The researchers examined associations between coffee consumption and circulating metabolites and sex hormones.
The study found that coffee consumption was associated with lower total body fat and visceral fat, as well as greater skeletal muscle mass.
There were other benefits, too. Men who consumed more coffee had higher levels of testosterone. The researchers suggest that hormonal mechanisms may partly explain the association between coffee consumption and metabolic health.
"Coffee is consumed by millions of people every day, yet we still know surprisingly little about how it relates to our metabolism and hormones," said the study's lead author, Luca Verroest, in a press release.
The study does not, however, establish a causal relationship between coffee consumption and the observed changes.

Scientists map how spacecraft design could affect astronauts’ mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:51:29 UTC
13:51:29 KST

Could the design of a spacecraft affect astronauts’ mental health? Scientists have mapped how everything from lighting and privacy to shared spaces could shape wellbeing on long missions to the Moon and Mars.
Scientists have mapped how different features of a space habitat could affect astronauts’ mental, emotional and social well-being, in a new study.
Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the University of Colorado Boulder in the United States examined links between features such as lighting, privacy and the layout of living spaces, and experiences including anxiety, homesickness, fatigue and relationships between crewmates.
The idea is to give engineers a clearer way to consider astronauts’ mental health when designing habitats for long-duration space missions.
“The awareness has been there for some time that living in space is difficult,” Mich Lin, a lead author of the study and a PhD candidate in the Human Systems Lab and the Engineering Systems Lab at MIT, said in a press release.
“We’ve come a long way from the human in a tin can. As our priorities shift toward long-duration exploration missions, making sure a crew is safe, healthy, happy, and productive becomes even more important,” she added.
In extreme environments, habitats are usually built primarily for survival. Submarines, Antarctic bases and spacecraft must protect people from immediate physical dangers, often with very limited space.
Spaceflight can put astronauts under considerable psychological strain. Isolation and confinement can affect sleep, mood, cognitive performance and relationships within a crew, while living without normal day-night cycles can disrupt the body's circadian rhythm.
But as humans prepare for longer missions to the Moon and eventually Mars, astronauts could spend months or even years confined with the same small group of people, far from family and friends and with little opportunity to leave their surroundings.
How much can design help?
Researchers carried out an extensive, iterative review of scientific literature on habitability in space and other extreme environments to find evidence linking physical surroundings with behavioural health.
They used the research to build a map containing 68 factors and 167 connections showing how aspects of an environment could influence behavioural health and performance.
They focused on 14 emotions and experiences that could be affected by habitat design, including anxiety, autonomy, curiosity, fatigue, nostalgia and kinship.
They then mapped how different design factors could contribute to these outcomes.
Lighting, for example, can affect sleep and circadian rhythms. The amount of privacy available to crew members could influence stress and autonomy, while the arrangement of shared spaces, corridors and entrances can shape how often people interact with one another.
Meanwhile, access paths, stairs and entrances can contribute to friendships and social cohesion because they influence how often people naturally encounter one another.
Researchers also suggest looking at features that can help astronauts develop a stronger attachment to where they live in order to reduce homesickness. These could include greater privacy and spaces that crew members can reconfigure or personalise.
“The connection between habitat and behavioural health has not been made in this format before,” Lin said. “So we made those connections for the first time.”
The research team says the same approach could also be applied on Earth, including to submarines, oil rigs, Antarctic expeditions and other environments where people spend long periods isolated and confined.
Researchers have also made the findings available through an interactive website called the Human-Environment Connection and Interaction Atlas (HECIA), where designers can explore the different connections.
However, the researchers stress that the tool and the ideas behind it are not a one-size-fits-all guide to designing extreme habitats. The appropriate design will depend on each habitat’s particular specifications and constraints.

Estonians defrauded of €13.2 million in first 6 months of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:42:00 UTC
13:42:00 KST

Estonians defrauded of €13.2 million in first 6 months of 2026
In the first six months of this year, police received 1,816 reports of telephone and online scams. Scammers defrauded Estonian residents of €13.2 million.
Jaagup Toompuu, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) fraud prevention and investigation center, said the number of people making scam calls continues to grow. Although people may be more aware of scammers' activities overall, they continue to fall victim to the same schemes as they did a year ago.
More than half of the cases involve multi-stage phone scams. This means the victim receives a call purportedly from a service provider and is then directed to take another step.
One common scheme involves a scammer calling the victim and saying there is a package for them from, for example, Tartu County Court. The victim is told they need to confirm an action to receive the package. The scammers do not ask for the victim's PIN but instead send them a confirmation code. "The person hangs up and a few minutes later they get another call from the so-called bank security department," Toompuu explained.
The scammers then ask whether the victim has entered their details anywhere. If the person says they have, the caller tells them a police operation is underway. The victim is then given instructions by a scammer posing as a police officer.
"The story then continues depending on where the person has their money and how it can be moved," Toompuu said. Where possible, the scammers take remote control of the victim's computer or phone or send a courier to collect cash. Ultimately, the victim becomes involved in the supposed "police operation."
Use of famous faces
Another common scheme is investment fraud. "Fake websites and news stories have been created online using the faces of well-known Estonians who talk about how they invest," Toompuu said. These have featured people including composer Arvo Pärt, politician Helle-Moonika Helme, former deputy police chief Koit Pikaro and rally driver Ott Tänak.
Victims then enter their details on the fake website themselves. They are contacted by an investment broker who instructs them on how to transfer money to the platform. The initial amounts are usually around €250. From there, the victim is instructed on where to take out loans so they can invest more.
"One characteristic of investment scams is that they last quite a long time, sometimes for months," Toompuu explained. They only end once all of the victim's money has been taken or when the person first tries to withdraw their virtual funds from the platform.
Sometimes, after falling victim to an investment scam, a person becomes the victim of another scam. "Once victims have lost their money, they start searching online for ways to get it back," Toompuu said.
Through sponsored posts, victims may come across law firms or so-called ethical hackers who promise to recover the money. The victim is required to pay additional fees, resulting in them being defrauded again.
Scammers do not know in advance how much money they will be able to get from a particular victim. While they may get €40 from some people, scams involving companies can yield millions of euros. "Scammers take everything they can get," Toompuu said.
If someone has fallen victim to fraud, the first thing they should do is call their bank and have their cards and accounts blocked. If they still have money left, they should also disable their electronic identification tools. Only then should they contact the police. "The police certainly do not conduct their operations via WhatsApp video calls, as scammers do," Toompuu said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Black Forest coolcation: tourism in Germany surges in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:40:23 UTC
13:40:23 KST

In Spain and Italy, the Black Forest is an extremely popular holiday destination. But Germany has set a different record with other visitors.
Most tourists in Germany come from the country itself. The trend towards travelling to all kinds of regions, from the Baltic Sea to the Alps, has continued in recent years. According to the Federal Statistical Office, hotels, guesthouses and campsites recorded 223.8 million overnight stays in the first six months of this year, a new record for Germany.
And the growing number of guests booking holiday flats online is not even counted. Germans also top the rankings for online bookings of holiday rentals, followed by visitors from the Netherlands, Poland and the United States.
Southern Europe turns to the Black Forest
Regionally, however, there are some striking trends. The Black Forest is particularly popular in Spain and Italy. That has less to do with its delicious Black Forest gateau, which has long since made a name for itself internationally, and more with the search for cooler climes.
With the 1,493 metre Feldberg and the picture-postcard Titisee, the Black Forest, like Scandinavia or Scotland, is regarded in this era of climate crisis as a "coolcation", in other words as a particularly cool holiday destination. The fact that summer 2026 in south-west Germany, as in neighbouring France, was marked by heatwaves has so far done little to dent that image.
According to Schwarzwald Tourismus GmbH, the number of visitors from Spain coming to the Black Forest has risen particularly sharply, by 64 percent since 2015. The State Statistical Office of Baden-Württemberg counted 199,000 overnight stays by Spanish guests last year.
Italians are close behind, with 194,000 overnight stays in the Black Forest.
The famous fairy-tale brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm grew up in the 19th century not far from the Black Forest and collected stories from all over Germany. The slightly eerie atmosphere of "Hansel and Gretel" and "Little Red Riding Hood" draws visitors not only at Halloween, but can also be relived on a summer walk through the forest in its more mystical corners.

Taiwan legislature passes drone development and procurement spending without cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:39:21 UTC
13:39:21 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The KMT legislative caucus on Friday withdrew proposals to freeze the Cabinet’s NT$44.2 billion (US$1.38 billion) comprehensive program for developing Taiwan’s drone industry and another NT$19.2 billion in drone-related spending, citing its support for the industry.
The KMT had initially proposed cutting NT$63.4 billion in combined spending from the two items before changing its proposal to freeze the spending, per Liberty Times. The move drew criticism from the DPP, which argued that freezing the funds would delay the country's drone development and harm the industry in the long term.
The KMT withdrew the freeze proposal Friday and called on the Cabinet to phase in its drone industry development program to ensure stable funding for the industry, per ETtoday. The party said support for national defense should not be used as an excuse to avoid legislative oversight and called on the Cabinet to subject future programs to oversight mechanisms.
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) said Friday that the Legislature could pass the 2026 budget with fewer opposition-proposed cuts than in previous years, per CNews. She said that after speaking by phone with Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) and KMT Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁), the proposal to freeze the drone-related spending would be withdrawn.
Lu called on the government to allocate drone-related funding to Taichung, Changhua County, Miaoli County, Nantou County, and Yunlin County, saying that approving the spending without cuts would help secure funding for local industries. She said the government had not allocated drone-related funding to the five areas and argued that they should have received funding as potential drone development hubs.
Lu also called on the government to establish drone flight-testing areas in central Taiwan, saying that requiring local companies to send prototypes to southern Taiwan for testing has caused inconvenience for businesses. Taichung Deputy Mayor Cheng Chao-hsin (鄭照新) had previously called on the government to allocate a similar amount of drone funding to Taichung as was allocated to Chiayi and Tainan, at roughly NT$10 million, per China Times.
Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) questioned the government’s plans to allocate robotics development funding to Tainan and drone development funding to Chiayi, per Storm Media. He said that while he supported the government’s efforts to promote balanced regional development, Taichung has one of the most complete supply chains for both industries and should play a leading rather than supporting role.
Chiang said focusing on southern Taiwan while neglecting central Taiwan would weaken Taiwan’s ability to compete in international markets.

Trump announces tariffs on drone imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
04:38:45 UTC
13:38:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – US President Donald Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation saying he will impose tariffs up to 100% on imported drones and components, citing national security concerns and over-dependence on foreign suppliers, Reuters reported.
The White House said the measure mandates a 100% tariff on larger UAVs or drones with certain capabilities that are particularly sensitive to national security, including those with a combined weight over 25 kilograms and thermal imaging capabilities, as well as their docking stations and key components.
Smaller drones without capabilities sensitive to national security will face a 25% tariff. For non-sensitive drone components, the tariffs will take effect 180 days after the signing.
Drones and components from Taiwan, the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, and Switzerland will face a 15% tariff. Drones from the UK will see a lower 10% tariff.
Trump said an investigation by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick found that foreign producers of drones and components pose security risks. Trump added that the US does not produce enough to meet its Drone Dominance goal.
The White House said that tariffs are to take effect in 21 days. The White House added that for products that the Pentagon has approved for exemption from the Federal Communications Commission's Covered List within 20 days of signing, the tariffs will take effect 180 days after signing.
