BAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:35:47 UTC
02:35:47 KST

The UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breaching US arms exports regulations more than 100 times.
The US Department of State announced on Thursday that it had reached an administrative settlement with the US arm of BAE to resolve 104 violations of the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
The breaches included the unauthorised exports of technical data to multiple countries, including China, and violations of directorate of defense trade controls authorisations involving various countries.
BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations, which helped it avoid a higher penalty. It also persuaded the state department to suspend half of the penalty, on the condition that the $18m was used to strengthen BAE’s compliance programme.
BAE Systems said it remained committed to ensuring full compliance with all applicable export control laws, and had “thoroughly cooperated” with the state department’s review.
“We have been working diligently to implement improvements to our BAE Systems Inc compliance programme over the last several years, and we will continue to do so. We take seriously our responsibility to protect critical information and support all our customers’ security,” the company added.
The state department said the settlement highlighted “the importance of exporting defence articles pursuant only to appropriate authorisation from the department”.
BAE was accused of sending technical data related to printed wiring boards for use in global positioning system (GPS) to a manufacturer in China in December 2023. According to the state department, the company “recognised its supply chain team did not fully understand the export control and compliance regulations” and that its secure file transfer networks did not highlight export control warnings before the data was sent.
The company also sent data related to printed wiring boards for use with military GPS to Canada in September 2021, after a licence agreement had expired, and the technical specification of an “explosive mixture” to the UK. In another breach, technical data related to a US navy guided-missile destroyer were sent to Germany.
A BAE subcontractor also “furnished defence services without authorisation” on more than 17 separate occasions in Italy and France, and also in Indonesia, according to the state department.
The company also accidentally exported without authorization a control system for a military gas-turbine engine to Switzerland.

====================================================================================================

The Mecca Pact is the latest sign of the U.S.’s declining influence in the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:34:29 UTC
02:34:29 KST

Last week, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signed a defense pact that raised eyebrows around the globe. Although the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement had been discussed publicly for some time, its actual conclusion raises questions about its implications for the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the longer-term security playing field in the region.
Israel and its supporters reacted with consternation to the deal, while both Iran and the United States downplayed it. What exactly the agreement will mean in practice remains an open question, despite some grandiose statements that it is a NATO-like agreement.
The deal probably won’t change a lot in the short term. There are scant details about what would trigger the mutual defense agreement, and what would be required of partner countries if it were triggered.
But it reflects the increasing sense that the United States cannot be relied on as a guarantor of security and that small and medium-sized powers will have to take security architecture more into their own hands. While U.S. concerns and interests will not be ignored for the foreseeable future, the American role is shifting more towards arms merchant than strategic partner.
The U.S. has only itself to blame for this decline in its reliability. It has not only made remarkably poor decisions of its own, but it has also helped Israel to emerge as an even greater threat to regional security than it historically has been, while neglecting all its other allies in favor of guarding Israel’s aggression and occupations.
No trust in the United States
The second term of Donald Trump’s presidency has predictably been far more disastrous than the first. His foreign policy, in particular, has been marked by foolish decisions, massive corruption, and blunders that will have ramifications for many years after Trump’s departure from office.
Trump has directly endangered his allies in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, and Bahrain with his reckless attacks on Iran. His actions have raised the specter of real disaster in those countries. Their vulnerability to Iranian retaliation is acute. Iranian attacks, at their worst, could destroy the region’s oil industry and its desalination systems, effectively making those states uninhabitable. The UAE has reacted to this by doubling down on its partnerships with the U.S. and Israel, but the other nations have moved away, slowly, from the American orbit.
Trump’s arming of Israel and encouragement of its most radical nationalists has led to Israel expanding its zone of occupation back into Lebanon and farther than ever into Syria, while permitting escalating atrocities against Palestinians that recall the worst episodes of human history.
Making matters worse, Trump didn’t do these things by himself. He built on both his own first term in office and Joe Biden’s own reckless and immoral policies to magnify mistrust.
As I’ve noted in the past, much of the Saudi loss of faith in the U.S. can be traced back to Trump’s refusal to act after Saudi oil fields were attacked by Ansar Allah. For Riyadh, that was the first major sign that the U.S. could not be counted on to keep its side of the long-held “oil-for-security” pact on which American-Saudi strategic relations were built.
Biden’s support of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, its attacks on Lebanon, and its invasion of Syria reinforced concerns over his lack of action to restore the Iran nuclear deal, which, at that time, could have built upon Iraqi and Chinese efforts that successfully lowered the tensions between Riyadh and Tehran. That was evidence that the United States, not just Donald Trump, was willing to sacrifice Gulf stability to support Israeli aggression.
The attack on Iran further undermined Arab confidence in the U.S. American allies had pressed for a diplomatic resolution to the tensions with Iran, despite some reports to the contrary. Riyadh and other Arab capitals were concerned that the attack on Iran was conceived and executed without taking their security needs into account or any consultations with them.
This loss of confidence in Washington is serious. It is not solely about Trump or Biden, but grows out of the capricious nature of American domestic politics and a proven inability for one president to promise the next will keep to their agreements. That loss of confidence will not be easily reversed by future administrations.
Iran and Israel
Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia all insist that this new pact is not meant to be directed at any other state in particular. While that is no doubt technically true, the deal is meant to deter attacks from potential enemy states, and the two states that are most likely to be of concern are Iran and Israel.
Publicly, Iran has not seemed worried. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said, “Any plan that is based on the geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy and its allies.”
Iran has certainly considered what the pact might mean to its strategy of retaliation against its Gulf neighbors in the event of an attack by the United States. Yet the calm that Baghaei expressed is likely genuine.
That’s because Iran can game out the implications. First, just because there is a NATO-style guarantee in the agreement doesn’t necessarily mean there will be an immediate, collective response to any Iranian attack. Ansar Allah attacked Saudi oil fields after the pact was signed, but Islamabad and Ankara did not respond.
More importantly, the pact raises the stakes of an American attack on Iran. Should Washington attack Iranian infrastructure in an escalation of the existing conflict, it must take into account the concern that Türkiye and Pakistan might respond to Iranian retaliation, even if by non-military means. That would risk a wide expansion of the war, and it is not at all clear who would shoulder the blame, especially if China felt that such expansion warranted its involvement.
But the main focus of the agreement is less on concerns about Iran than on establishing a regional security regime. The trio of countries was very explicit about leaving the door open for other countries to join the defense pact; they hope to change the very nature of security strategy across the entire region.
It is Israel, not Iran, that requires the region to rethink its entire security structure.
Türkiye had been reluctant to enter into a formal defense pact with the Saudis and Pakistanis, fearing international complications as its own regional ambitions grew. But American fickleness and rapidly increasing Israeli belligerence toward Ankara changed their mind.
Correctly identifying the source of regional stability as coming from Israel, not Iran, the three states came together to create a defense strategy focused on Israel, the one country the U.S. can’t even consider defending them against.
For Saudi Arabia, this is a very clear message that Israel can forget about any notion of normalizing relations with Riyadh without ending the denial of Palestinian rights. Both Türkiye—due to its regional ambitions—and Pakistan—due to its rivalry with India, which is drawing ever closer to Israel—have a stake in backing Saudi Arabia in this regard.
The deal brings together three powers with unique capabilities: Türkiye’s military capabilities and vast arms production, Pakistan’s nuclear umbrella, and Saudi Arabia’s considerable resources. That makes the alliance a significant regional power, one that is capable of confronting even Israel militarily.
The obvious goal is to deter Israel from its growing belligerence toward Türkiye, which Israeli officials have ominously labeled “the next Iran.” But more than that, the alliance, especially if it grows, creates a defense structure that is not just independent of the U.S. but independent of any concern about Israel’s interests, domestic or international.
That’s no small consideration. It was enough to scare Egypt away from joining the pact, even though it has been the fourth guest at many gatherings of the other three for strategy meetings and summits over the past year.
Egypt has developed a deep dependence on the U.S. and Israel. It receives the second most annual military aid from Washington, behind Israel, and depends on Israel for a good deal of its energy supply in the form of natural gas.
Because Egypt’s economy is in perpetual crisis, it would take considerable resources and time for it to be in a position where it could abandon Israel and anger Washington in this manner. The day that it does so may come, but not for some time.
Egypt’s potential inclusion was controversial. Türkiye very much wanted Egypt in, due to its alignment with Cairo in several North African arenas. Saudi Arabia was opposed, due to growing tensions between Riyadh and Cairo, especially over Egypt’s relationship with the UAE, which is fast becoming a bitter regional rival to Riyadh.
In the end, Egypt rendered the point moot by choosing to avoid choosing between Washington, Tel Aviv, and Abu Dhabi on the one hand, and Ankara and Riyadh on the other.
The Mecca Agreement also strives to make it harder for Israel to continue its dominance over the Palestinians and its invasions of its neighbors in Lebanon and Syria.
An American-based security regime allowed Israel total impunity. That was tolerable for some in the region when it was believed that the U.S. offered at least some mild restraint on Israeli excesses and protected its Muslim and Arab allies from attack. Those beliefs no longer hold.
The United States cannot even get Israel to go along with a plan for disarming Palestinian armed groups that would leave Gaza under effective American control and pacified, a deal that was clearly favorable to Israel. It has proven unable to move Israel out of its deadly occupation of southern Lebanon, and has not even tried to get Israel out of Syria, despite the fact that Washington has been supporting Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s efforts to reunite the country.
For the past 50 years, the American-based security regime in the region has encouraged partnership with Israel, as pioneered by Egypt and Jordan in the 1980s, as the road to regional stability. That was followed by the disastrous Oslo Accords, increasing clandestine trade and cooperation between Israel and other Arab countries, and, finally, the Abraham Accords.
All of these efforts at creating “partners for peace” only reinforced Israel’s belief that it could achieve peace and regional integration without ever compromising on Palestinian rights.
With Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s decision to refuse to cooperate with Trump’s “Board of Peace” and the agreement to disarm Palestinians and have Israel withdraw from Gaza ahead of its reconstruction, the U.S.-Israel relationship is at a low ebb, despite the fact that many American leaders continue to insist on backing Israel regardless of how often it spits in Washington’s face.
The Mecca Pact can serve as a vehicle to increase pressure on Israel even as its popularity in the United States continues to wane, particularly if more countries join it.
The Iran war, the invasion of Lebanon, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the ongoing occupation of Syria, and the threat to the holy sites in Jerusalem can all be traced back to Israel’s dominance of the Palestinians. While not every problem, by any means, in the Middle East is due to Israel’s apartheid and aggression, many of them are, while others cannot be resolved because of it.
The Mecca pact is a first step toward a regional force that can stand against that, not out of concern for the Palestinian people (which, sadly, few states, if any, seem to have), but for their own interest in regional stability. If the pact expands, the pressure will increase, the potential for action will, at long last, widen. And if that coincides with the long-dreamed of shift in American policy, there is a real possibility for significant change, a force which even the obstinate nationalism of Israel could not resist.
Mitchell Plitnick
Mitchell Plitnick is the president of ReThinking Foreign Policy. He is the co-author of Except for Palestine: The Limits of Progressive Politics and maintains the Cutting Through newsletter.

Federal judge throws out Trump administration's antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:25:30 UTC
02:25:30 KST

A federal judge on Thursday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit accusing Harvard University of failing to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment and discrimination.
U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston ruled that the government had not plausibly demonstrated an ongoing violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin in federally funded programs.
The administration filed the lawsuit in March, alleging that Harvard faculty members and university leaders had “turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis.”
Stearns said, however, that the government’s allegations focused largely on incidents surrounding protests over Israel’s war in Gaza during the 2023-24 academic year.
Only a handful of later incidents from March 2025 were cited, he said, and those were “too isolated and episodic” to establish an ongoing civil rights violation.
The judge also found that the lawsuit did not adequately allege misconduct by Harvard after the government informed the university in June 2025 that it was not complying with Title VI.
The White House and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.
The case was part of a broader confrontation between President Donald Trump’s administration and Harvard, one of the most prominent targets of his campaign to reshape major U.S. universities.
In court filings, the administration said it was seeking to “recover billions of dollars of taxpayer subsidies awarded to a discriminatory institution.”
Harvard denied the allegations and previously described the lawsuit as “yet another pretextual and retaliatory action by the administration for refusing to turn over control of Harvard to the federal government.”
In a June filing seeking dismissal of the case, the university argued that the government had failed to allege any ongoing or imminent violations of Title VI.
“Harvard condemns antisemitism and is committed to ensuring that Jewish and Israeli students, like all members of the Harvard community, can learn and participate fully in campus life free from harassment or exclusion,” the university said.
The ruling marks another legal setback for the administration in its confrontation with Harvard.
In December, the administration appealed a separate ruling that found it had unlawfully terminated more than $2 billion in federal grants awarded to the university and barred it from further cutting off Harvard’s research funding on those grounds.
In another case last year, a federal judge blocked the administration’s attempt to revoke Harvard’s ability to enroll international students.

Montreal opposition party moves forward with motion to cut ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:24:31 UTC
02:24:31 KST

The opposition party at Montreal City Hall, Projet Montréal, is moving forward with a motion calling on the city to sever institutional ties with Israel ahead of the August 24 council meeting.
The motion, originally introduced in June by interim party leader Ericka Alneus and city councilors Nathalie Goulet and Alex Norris, asks the city to "recognize and denounce the apartheid regime in Palestine and the genocide being perpetrated there, and affirm solidarity with Palestinians and other civilian victims of hostilities in the Middle East."
The text further requests the suspension of official ties, calling on the city to "suspend institutional ties with Israel's current government, including by not inviting representatives of the state to official events held at city hall 'until Israel returns to its internationally recognized borders, ceases its violations of the rights of the Palestinian people, and ends its violations of international law.'" While the vote was initially delayed after Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada removed it from the agenda amid political debate, Projet Montréal has signaled its intent to bring the text back to the floor.
Proponents claim text is consistent with city's values, advocates and community leaders disagree
Proponents of the measure have defended the text as consistent with the city's values. According to statements from Canadians for Justice and Peace in the Middle East (CJPME), the motion is viewed as a concrete step after years of public appeals following the events of October 2023, with proponents arguing that municipal bodies should take a stand on human rights. CJPME has explicitly drawn parallels to the 1980s when former Montreal Mayor Jean Doré cut institutional ties with apartheid South Africa, pointing to that precedent as establishing Montreal as a pioneer city for upholding human rights.
Conversely, the motion has faced opposition from community leaders and advocacy groups.
'Montréal needs a city council that focuses on local issues'
Addressing the broader climate in a statement to The Jerusalem Post, Eta Yudin, senior vice-president for Quebec at the Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA), pointed to the recent Fierté Montreal pride parade, stating that "social peace and a discourse promoting inclusion were able to take center stage" because participants "collectively refused to import the hatred from a distant conflict."
Yudin warned that "importing a foreign conflict to appease extremists or for electoral calculations only fuels division, chaos, and violence," adding that the opposition party "must draw conclusions from the rejection of its recent motion thanks to an exceptional mobilization of Montrealers, Jewish and non-Jewish alike." Concluding that the situation "should serve as a lesson to Projet Montréal ahead of the municipal council meeting," Yudin emphasized that "Montréal needs a city council that focuses on local issues."
The motion comes amidst a series of hate incidents targeting Jewish communities across Canada in recent months, including an attempted arson attack on a prominent Westmount synagogue, the targeting of Jewish individuals, and instances of vandalism and harassment.

Hamas must be banned from Palestinian Authority elections - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:24:10 UTC
02:24:10 KST

With Hamas saying it intends to participate in the Palestinian legislative election now scheduled for November 28 as part of a broad national coalition, it suddenly feels like 2006 all over again.
Why? Because 2006 saw tensions emerge between Ariel Sharon’s government and the George W. Bush administration over whether to allow Hamas to participate in a democratic election.
The Bush administration, with Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice at the forefront, was then pursuing its “freedom agenda” – an effort to spread democracy across the Middle East, based on the belief that democratic governments would ultimately produce greater stability and less terrorism.
“Only when Palestinians are able freely to express themselves through ballots rather than bombs will we be able to get on the road to security for Israel,” Bush’s national security adviser, Stephen Hadley, declared in October 2005.
Nice idea. The only problem was that Hamas wanted both ballots and bombs.
Israel argued that allowing an armed terrorist organization committed to Israel’s destruction to participate in an election was a deeply flawed idea. Washington recognized what it called the “fundamental contradiction” between an armed Hamas taking part in democratic politics, but still did not insist that Hamas resolve that contradiction before standing for election.
The US prevailed. Hamas took part in the elections under the less menacing party name “Change and Reform” and won 44.5% of the vote, compared with 41.4% for Fatah. Because of the electoral system and deep divisions within Fatah, that slim popular-vote margin gave Hamas 74 of the Palestinian Legislative Council’s 132 seats, compared with Fatah’s 45.
An ugly, murder-strewn history
The result caught nearly everyone by surprise, including Washington. Rice acknowledged afterward that the US had failed to anticipate the magnitude of Hamas’s victory.
The rest is history. An ugly, murder-strewn history that might have turned out differently if Hamas had not been allowed to participate.
A little more than a year later, in June 2007, Hamas violently drove Fatah and the Palestinian Authority out of Gaza, turning the coastal strip into an armed fortress from which to launch rockets and, ultimately, an invasion of Israel.
The Americans, in what some may say was innocent naivete, did not imagine that a group intent not on coexistence, but rather on replacing Israel’s existence with its own, would prevail at the ballot box.
That naivete is neither uniquely American nor has it passed from the world. Nikolay Mladenov, director-general of the Trump-led Board of Peace, offered another taste of it in a recent interview with Channel 12’s Amit Segal.
Both Israelis and the people in Gaza, he declared, “have one strong shared interest, and that is to get out of this horrible cycle of violence that has cost so many lives and caused so much destruction on both sides.”
That is a noble sentiment, an echo of the familiar formulation that Israelis and Palestinians alike simply want to live side by side in peace, dignity, and security.
Were that it were only true. This phrase reflects the sentiment of most Israelis, evident in the fact that Israel, over the years – through Oslo, the Camp David negotiations, the 2005 Gaza withdrawal and the statehood proposal advanced at Annapolis by Ehud Olmert – has been willing to make far-reaching territorial compromises to live in peace with the Palestinians. The Palestinians have not shown a similar appetite.
The last Palestinian legislative election, the one in 2006, proves the point. Hamas – whose original charter calls for the destruction of Israel – won. Doesn’t that demonstrate that the phrase “both sides want to coexist in peace and security” is hollow, wishful thinking – at least at this point in history?
Some will argue that the 2006 vote was not as much a vote for Hamas as it was a sign of opposition to the corruption of Fatah and the Palestinian Authority. But that doesn’t even matter. Voters may select a movement because they like its social services, ensure that the trains run on time, or dislike its rivals, but they still hand power to that movement’s entire program, which in this case was “armed resistance” and the erasure of Israel.
The October 7 Massacre cannot be separated from public opinion
October 7 translated that program into action: murder, rape, kidnapping, and pillage on a scale of medieval savagery.
And October 7 cannot be separated from public opinion. In the most recent comprehensive Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research poll, conducted in October 2025, 53% of Palestinians said Hamas had been right to launch the attack, and of those who said they would vote in an election, Hamas led Fatah 29% to 20%.
What that all means is that if Hamas is allowed to participate in the elections – either standing alone or as part of some broader coalition – then be prepared for the fact that it may win again and use that legitimacy to further entrench its control, not only in Gaza but also in Judea and Samaria.
October 7 is not the only date from which Israel – and the world – needs to learn. January 25, 2006, is another. And the lesson is simple: Never again allow Hamas to take part in an election; never again let it play simultaneously with ballots and bullets. Because if it wins, it is clear what will come next – and it is anything but coexistence, peace, and security.

Israeli officials stunned by Iran’s rapid military recovery after 2026 war - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:23:59 UTC
02:23:59 KST

Israeli defense officials have been shocked by the speed of Iran’s recovery following the early 2026 war, The Jerusalem Post has learned.
This includes both IDF and Mossad officials, though the military was the lead evaluator of targeting and the harm from the targeting of the Islamic Republic’s defense sector.
Numerous foreign media reports have poked holes in specific aspects of Israel’s narrative of military success setting back Iran’s military industrial complex by years already dating back to March of this year, but for months, apolitical IDF expert officials held the line that the damage was so extensive that even if some specific claims were off, Israel’s general narrative of setting Iran back years held.
Four months after the main war ended in April, the Post understands that the IDF is now seeing a stunningly speedy turnaround that it did not expect and not in merely one or another specific area, but in many areas, including regarding the ballistic missile threat.
Iran's history of recovery
Part of what is surprising in this story is that the IDF was already surprised by the Iranians in this area of rapid recovery twice: in October 2024 and January 2025.
After striking 20 critical ballistic missile and industrial military targets in Iran in October 2024, the IDF claimed that it had set back Iranian future missile production by a year or more.
By early 2025, the IDF had already seen the Iranians fully recover their high-speed ballistic missile production pace, so much so that the military moved up a possible fall 2025 attack to June 2025.
After attacking around 100 missile and industrial military targets in June 2025, the IDF said it had found the formula to truly set back Iran’s missile production by multiple years.
There was reason to believe this given that five times as many targets had been struck and that the IDF had dropped an exponentially larger volume of bombs.
Yet, once again, somehow, Iran figured out ways to recover high-speed missile production, again stunning the IDF.
What was estimated as around 1,300 missiles in June 2025 became 2,500 by February of this year.
Finally, the IDF and the US together said they achieved the goal during the around 40-day war in 2026.
Over 2,600 missile and industrial military targets were attacked, and both the US and Israel collectively attacked Iran around 30,000 times.
This was an increase of 26 times compared to 2025 and over 100 times compared to 2024.
IDF officials told the Post that every large and small part of the military industry had been shattered to pieces.
How could Iran restore its missile volume to 2,500 or to much higher threatening levels with $300 b. in damage to its military?
In other words, the lesson the IDF drew from each of the three rounds of attacks was not that Iran could find shortcuts which Israel might not anticipate to rapidly rebuild specific weapons threats, while leaving other parts of the country in squalor, but that a larger number of specific targets needed to be struck.
Israeli defense officials admit Iran finds innovative ways to rebuild missiles
Yet, the Post understands that top Israeli defense officials are now admitting that Iran has figured out creative ways to focus on rebuilding the missile and other defined threats, even if massive parts of the country still remain in ruin.
The New York Times previously reported that Iran was successful in using bulldozers to undo covered underground missile cities much faster than Israel expected.
But that is only restoring access to weapons which were never destroyed, only blocked.
The Post has now independently confirmed statements by senior Iranian officials that it is now producing new weapons again at a much faster pace than expected.
Until now, there was a debate about whether Tehran retained closer to 500 or 1,000 long-range missiles which could hit Israel after this year’s war.
This was an important debate as long as the assumption was that the Islamic Republic was stuck for a few years with whatever volume it had since its new production capabilities had been mostly destroyed.
But with this new information that Iran can now speedily rebuild ballistic missiles, the debate about how much it had left post-war becomes less important than the pace at which Iran is rebuilding.
If Iran can return to manufacturing 100-300 missiles per month, then it can restore its missile arsenal to June 2025 levels by early to mid-2027 and might become a prohibitive threat in 2028.
Even if its pace does not get back to that point, steady progress now means that in a period of a couple or a few years, the Iranian ballistic missile existential threat could be back in play.
All of this will also likely influence broader Israeli strategy about when and if another attack might be necessary regardless of the status of negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz and over the nuclear issue.
Alternatively, Israel may look the other way on the ballistic missile issue given that US President Donald Trump has made it clear he does not care about the issue, and to try to achieve a reduction of Tehran’s nuclear threat.
The IDF responded to the Post's report saying, "throughout the war, the IDF substantially harmed a diverse range of central components relating to Iran's military capabilities, thereby harming both the capabilities of the regime to utilize portions of its capabilities and the ability to rehabilitate them at the same scope and pace which existed prior to the war."
"Since then, the IDF has closely and continuously followed the Iranian efforts to rehabilitate and to newly rebuild their capabilities. The IDF's evaluation and situation assessments are constantly updated and brought in line with actual developments," continued the IDF.
Next, the military concluded, "From the nature of the issues at hand, it is not in our ability to specify concrete evaluations regarding the pace of the rehabilitation, because giving such specifics could expose IDF sources and methods. The IDF will continue to analyze developments and to be prepared accordingly."

Zelensky’s missile math mistakes: A few Patriots won’t save him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:23:49 UTC
02:23:49 KST

Zelensky’s missile math mistakes: Here’s why his numbers fall far short
Vladimir Zelensky has made an unusually specific claim about what Ukraine needs to defend itself against Russian ballistic missiles.
In an interview with CNN, Zelensky said Ukraine currently has enough Patriot interceptors to amount to roughly 1% of America’s existing stockpile – itself reportedly depleted by the war with Iran and a source of some acrimony between US President Donald Trump and his secretary of war, Pete Hegseth.
Nevertheless, Zelensky used the CNN interview to call on Washington to sell Ukraine 5% of its remaining Patriot missile stockpile, which he claimed would be enough to get Kiev through the winter. The former actor went further on air, saying that 10% of the US inventory would allow Ukraine to shoot down every Russian ballistic missile fired at the country.
But the numbers quickly begin to fall apart under scrutiny.
How many missiles does the US have, and what does Zelensky want?
The total number of Patriot interceptors currently at America’s disposal is classified, but the most recent estimates put the figure at around 800, after the US reportedly burned through some 65% of its total inventory during the war on Iran.
Zelensky’s proposed 10% transfer would therefore amount to about 80 Patriot interceptors.
That may sound substantial – until it is compared with the rate at which Kiev has been using them. Zelensky adviser Dmitry Litvin told the New York Times in March that Kiev had received and used some 600 Patriot missiles over four years. There is also the rate at which Russia is firing ballistic missiles to consider.
How many missiles does Zelensky claim Russia is firing at Ukraine?
Zelensky himself told Axios in late July that Russia was firing 30 to 40 ballistic missiles in each major attack, with such strikes occurring three to five times a month.
On July 5-6, Russia reportedly launched 29 ballistic or similarly high-speed missiles in an attack focused heavily on Kiev. Ukraine intercepted none of them, with Ukrainian officials attributing the failure to a shortage of interceptors.
Less than two weeks later, Russia reportedly launched 25 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and ten Zircon missiles – 35 in total – alongside several other weapons in another barrage focused largely on Kiev. Ukraine claimed to have intercepted 17 of the Iskander/Zircon/S-400 missiles.
Does Zelensky’s missile math make any sense?
Even under the extraordinarily favorable assumption that every Patriot interceptor destroys an incoming ballistic missile, 80 interceptors would be enough to defeat only 80 targets. At the rate of 30-40 ballistic missiles per major attack cited by Zelensky himself, that would provide enough ammunition for roughly two large-scale attacks – again, assuming every interceptor hits its target.
US and NATO defense doctrine calls for launching between two and four Patriot interceptors at each incoming missile. Zelensky’s claim that a Russian barrage involves 30 to 40 ballistic missiles would therefore mean that Kiev could expend as many as 80 interceptors – or 10% of the estimated US inventory – on a single attack.
Three to five such attacks a month, involving 30 to 40 ballistic missiles each, would amount to roughly 90 to 200 incoming ballistic missiles per month. Eighty Patriot interceptors could not destroy all of them even with an impossible 100% success rate.
At a 1:1 interception ratio, 80 Patriots would cover 80 ballistic targets. At 2:1, they would cover 40. At 3:1, about 27.
Does Zelensky’s claim of protecting Ukraine through the winter add up?
In other words, 10% of America’s estimated stockpile of roughly 800 interceptors could plausibly provide enough ammunition for robust ballistic-missile defense against one major barrage, or perhaps several weeks to a month of more selective protection.
It could not literally “destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles,” as Zelensky told CNN.
There is another inconsistency, however. According to Axios, just weeks before making his 10% proposal, Zelensky said he needed 300 Patriot interceptors before winter because of the scale and frequency of Russian ballistic-missile attacks.
If the relevant US inventory is around 800 missiles, 300 would represent nearly 40% of the total. Yet Zelensky is now suggesting that approximately 80 – barely a quarter of his previous request – could accomplish something far more ambitious.
What’s the bottom line?
Moscow’s most recent ballistic-missile barrages against Ukraine have reportedly further eroded Kiev’s ability to mount even a token defense. Zelensky’s 40-day influence operation has also significantly backfired, earning him a dressing-down from Washington over attacks on shipping in the Black Sea. His apparent failure to anticipate that Russia would respond in kind and shut down Ukraine’s Black Sea ports could reportedly cost the Ukrainian economy another 1.5% of GDP.
Zelensky may be working from a different estimate of America’s missile inventory, or assuming that US production would provide a recurring supply in the future rather than a one-time delivery. Alternatively, his use of the phrase “destroy all” may simply be another example of his usual rhetoric rather than a literal claim that Ukraine could intercept every ballistic missile Russia launches.
That leaves two possible interpretations: Either Zelensky is using his own media-manipulation techniques to deliberately simplify or exaggerate the figures in an effort to strengthen his case for further depleting America’s stockpiles, or his assessment of how long such a stockpile would last is seriously mistaken.

Magnetic ‘Goody King’ toys recalled over ingestion hazard after two children receive surgery

Magnetic ‘Goody King’ toys recalled over ingestion hazard after two children receive surgery
CHICAGO (AP) — About 213,500 “Goody King” magnetic building toys were recalled in the U.S. on Thursday, due to an ingestion hazard posed that has resulted in at least two children receiving surgeries.
According to a notice published by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, these toys’ building cubes can break or open, allowing the magnets inside to become loose. That poses a serious ingestion hazard for children.
When high-powered magnets are swallowed, they can attract each other or other metal and become lodged in the digestive system, the CPSC warns — which can potentially lead to “perforations, twisting, and/or blockage of the intestines, blood poisoning and death.”
To date, Goody King seller Yi Suen Commerce is aware of two children who ingested magnets from these toys and needed surgery to remove them. The Hong Kong-based company is also aware of at least 27 reports of the cubes breaking or opening.
Consumers in possession of the now-recalled magnetic toys are urged to stop using them immediately and contact Yi Suen Commerce for a full refund. Affected model numbers and more information can be found both on the CPSC’s notice and Goody King’s recall website.
In an online FAQ, Goody King noted that it will send prepaid shipping labels to customers who successfully register for the recall — and that refunds will be issued after the company physically receives the returned products. Receipts are not required.
The recalled toys were sold online through Amazon between January 2024 and July 2026 — under a variety of themes to build 3D designs like forests, dinosaurs and unicorns. The products came in sets of 45, 56, 100, 120, 150 and 300, the CPSC noted. They were priced between $17 and $50.

ROME (AP) — The remains of an ancient bridge have emerged in Rome’s Tiber River, near St. Peter’s Basilica, as weeks with virtually no rain caused water levels to plunge.
“Nero is the most famous person linked to this area, because precisely in Nero’s circus, where the Vatican is now located, the Apostle Peter was martyred,” said Antonella Bonini, an archaeologist at Rome’s cultural heritage superintendency.
“However, scholars consider the bridge to be older (than Nero’s era) — built by Caligula, Nero’s uncle,” she said, adding that it existed as early as 39 AD.
The ruins of the ancient Roman Neronian bridge, emerge from the riverbed of the Tiber river due to drought, in Rome, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)
The ruins of the ancient Roman Neronian bridge, emerge from the riverbed of the Tiber river due to drought, in Rome, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)
The Tiber’s flow has fallen below 80 cubic meters (2,825 cubic feet) per second, about half the historic average for the month of July, according to Giovanni Giganti, coordinator of the Rome civil protection service’s center for water management.
“We are facing a major water crisis. And it is a crisis that is also due to the fact that this winter we did have quite abundant rainfall, but then the dry periods ... were quite long,” Giganti said.

Blanche seeks to rally a depleted Justice Department workforce in first speech as attorney general
WASHINGTON (AP) — Attorney General Todd Blanche sought to rally a depleted Justice Department workforce Thursday in his first speech since taking the reins of the beleaguered agency, promising rank-and-file staff that he will lead them with integrity.
Blanche’s speech inside the storied Great Hall at Justice Department headquarters represented an effort to reassure lawyers and law enforcement officials on the heels of a tumultuous confirmation battle that exposed deep concerns about the direction of the agency under Republican President Donald Trump.
Blanche vowed to uphold the rule of law “without fear or favor,” and told staff he would welcome their ideas and encourage disagreement. Without mentioning specific moves that have raised alarms from critics that Blanche is still functioning as Trump’s personal lawyer, the attorney general acknowledged he would “not get every decision right.”
“Everything that I do will not be the right path or the right decision,” said Blanche, who served as Trump’s criminal defense lawyer before entering the department last year as deputy attorney general. “No one does that, but I do promise you this: I promise you that I will work as hard as any of you. I promise that I’ll listen to you. That I will listen to the ideas that you have, or adjustments that we need to make, and if we need to make them, I will make them.”
Blanche is assuming control of the Justice Department at a turbulent time, with mass firings and resignations having hollowed out the workforce and a slew of politically charged investigations drawing concerns that the agency is being used as a weapon to target the president’s perceived foes.
He was confirmed by the Senate early Saturday by the narrowest of margins, opposed by two Republicans who expressed concerns about what they described as the politicization of the Justice Department under Trump.
Blanche told the workforce he is proud of the department’s work under the second Trump administration to tackle violent crime, illegal drug trafficking and violent gangs and cartels.
“It’s easy to focus on the negative or the news story that is critical of something we’re doing or something that we’ve done, or questions something that we’re doing or something that we’ve done,” Blanche said. “But do not forget that we have accomplished a tremendous amount of good, positive work in the past year and a half.”
Justice Connection, a network of alums, said in a statement that “Blanche’s platitudes will only resonate if his actions start matching his words.” The group noted that the department under Blanche’s leadership has pushed out employees who opposed decisions in high-profile cases or who were deemed insufficiently loyal to the administration’s agenda.
“Thousands more have left because leadership has consistently violated the principles Blanche articulated: prosecuting defendants based only on the facts and the law; holding those who attack law enforcement accountable; and respecting the courts,” the group said.

Feds issue Line 5 tunnel permit, call it ‘not contrary to the public interest’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:23:02 UTC
02:23:02 KST

Feds issue Line 5 tunnel permit, call it ‘not contrary to the public interest’
The US Army Corps of Engineers has permitted construction of the controversial Line 5 tunnel project in the Straits of Mackinac.
The project, which would divert a section of the Line 5 petroleum pipeline from the open waters of the Straits into a concrete tunnel beneath the lakebed, is “not contrary to the public interest” and would not harm tribal treaty rights, the Army Corps said in announcing its permit. Nonetheless, the Corps noted the project would have adverse effects on endangered species and archaeological sites, that it would contribute to “long-term impacts of habitat loss” and have “long-term detrimental impacts on land use.”
While the federal approval clears a big hurdle for the nearly decade-old proposal, don’t expect shovels in the ground anytime soon. The Michigan Supreme Court recently ordered state energy regulators to reconsider a separate key permit, the project remains tied up in state and federal court, and new lawsuits have been promised by opponents.
Still, Line 5 owners Enbridge Energy praised Wednesday’s decision.
The federal permit “represents the highest standard of environmental review required for major critical energy and other infrastructure projects,” Enbridge said in a written statement. “Line 5 is safe. Enbridge will continue operating Line 5 safely and responsibly, incorporating enhanced safety measures in the Straits, and protecting Michigan’s natural and cultural resources.”
A coalition of Native American tribes that has opposed the project, meanwhile, slammed the decision.
“Our federal government has a solemn obligation to uphold and protect Treaty rights and is supposed to protect American waters and sacred spaces,” Managing Attorney David Gover with the Native American Rights Fund said in a statement. “Instead, the U.S. Army Corps just rubber-stamped a Canadian oil project that desecrates a Tribal sacred space and threatens to pollute the Great Lakes.”
The tunnel project would likely “adversely affect” Houghton’s goldenrod and dwarf lake iris, which are listed as threatened species under the federal Endangered Species Act, the Corps said, but that “reductions in the overall recovery, numbers, or distribution” are not expected after mitigation efforts.
The project site is culturally and spiritually significant to the Anishinaabe tribal nations. The Corps noted there would be “major, permanent, adverse effects on historic properties, including archaeological sites” that the tribal nations said “cannot be mitigated.”
The Corps’ decision is in line with the Trump administration’s goal of bolstering fossil fuel energy and preventing renewable energy development.
“The approval of the Enbridge Line 5 Tunnel Project is a testament to President Trump’s vision to ensure our nation’s energy dominance,” said Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works Adam Telle in an emailed statement. “By cutting unneeded red tape and overhauling our regulatory process, to provide fast, clear, and consistent decisions that implement our regulatory authorities just as Congress intended, we are able to help projects like this move forward with regulatory certainty.”
David Holtz, coalition coordinator for the group Oil & Water Don’t Mix said in an email the Corps’ decision was “driven by the Trump Administration’s phony ‘national energy emergency.’”
He said the decision — which did not consider what would happen if the tunnel was not built and Line 5 was decommissioned — was reminiscent of the Michigan Public Service Commission’s permit review that the Michigan Supreme Court recently said was erroneous. The court called the review overly narrow and said it failed to consider whether it would harm public rights to the Great Lakes and that it failed to study whether Line 5 would shut down if the tunnel isn’t built.
On July 15, Michigan’s departments of Natural Resources and Environment, Great Lakes and Energy issued two key permits for the tunnel project, despite noting disruption to Native American burial sites and harm to wetlands and rare species.
Enbridge is also seeking a permit to discharge millions of gallons of treated wastewater per day into Lake Michigan during tunnel construction. EGLE is expected to rule on that by Sept. 30.
Meanwhile, the state is battling in court with Enbridge over Whitmer’s 2020 order to shut the existing pipeline down for fear that it could cause an oil spill in the Straits. A federal judge in December ruled that Michigan had no authority to order a shutdown, but the state has appealed the ruling.
Separately, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has sought a shutdown since 2019 in a case that has pingponged from state to federal court and back again. The case now sits in the 30th Circuit Court in Ingham County, where deliberations are paused pending resolution of the case stemming from Whitmer’s shutdown order.

More than 110,000 Canadians have signed a petition as of Thursday calling for the removal of controversial U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, the latest sign of deepening rifts between the neighboring countries.
Hoekstra, a relentless defender of President Donald Trump and a former Republican congressman from Michigan, has had a volatile tenure since arriving in Ottawa in April 2025.
A Globe and Mail editorial in May described Hoekstra as being "keen to channel his boss's aggressive boorishness."
"Pete Hoekstra doesn't understand why Canadians are so upset," the editorial said.
"The U.S. ambassador seems to think this nation a bunch of inexplicable malcontents for reacting as it has to President Donald Trump's threats and bluster."
The petition, which will remain open for signature until Nov. 18, accuses Hoekstra of normalizing "the Trump administration's threats to annex Canada as the 51st state."
The citizen-led effort calls for him to be declared persona non grata and removed from Canada.
More than 116,000 signatories had been confirmed as of Thursday morning, according to the Canadian parliament website.
After signatures close, the document will be introduced in the House of Commons by lone Green Party lawmaker Elizabeth May.
During his time in Canada, Hoekstra has reportedly leveled a profanity-laced tirade against an Ontario official over an anti-tariff ad that quoted former U.S. President Ronald Reagan on the merits of free trade.
The ad, produced by Ontario's provincial government, infuriated Trump, prompting him to suspend all trade negotiations.
In June, Hoekstra said the idea of the U.S. annexing Canada would be "a great discussion" for Trump to have with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
He has defended Trump's tariffs and criticized Canadians for referring to Trump's protectionist measures as being part of a trade war.
Canadian trade negotiators are in Washington this week trying to hammer out a deal that will include broad tariff relief in exchange for Ottawa dropping certain countermeasures.
The Dutch-born Hoekstra also faced controversy while serving as U.S. ambassador to the Netherlands during Trump's first term.
He was forced to apologize over 2015 comments in which he falsely claimed that Muslims had created "no-go zones" in the Netherlands and that they had "burned" politicians.

PSO-2027 for UZ below UAH 20 bln or unresolved eurobonds would trigger tough action package – supervisory board member
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
20:22:14 EEST
02:22:14 KST

Ukrzaliznytsia could avoid a tough package of measures if the 2027 state budget provides the company with at least UAH 20 billion in PSO funding, plus additional payments for 2026 PSO obligations, if the eurobond default is resolved through restructuring, and if the cash gap stays within UAH 26 billion, company supervisory board member Anatoliy Amelin said.
"Breaching any of these conditions triggers the tough package: cutting core staff by 15-20%, closing loss-making routes outside the state order, freezing CAPEX except for safety, and accelerated asset sales," according to an analytical report titled "What Is Happening to Ukrzaliznytsia?" from the Ukrainian Institute for the Future (UIF), presented Thursday by Amelin together with former Deputy Infrastructure Minister Volodymyr Shulmeister.
If budget support for Ukrzaliznytsia remains at UAH 16 billion this year, applying the tough package would reduce the annual loss to UAH 6.1 billion, while raising PSO funding to UAH 24 billion would keep the loss within UAH 5.1 billion, the report said.
"Translation for the budget negotiating table: the UAH 8 billion withheld by the government converts into thousands of jobs and dozens of canceled trains. This isn't a threat — it's arithmetic," the plan's authors said.
They added that while operating loss compensation this year accounts for only UAH 5.55 billion of the UAH 16 billion in budget support, with the rest being an investment component, the entire 2027 PSO amount should be calculated using the formula "cost of the state order minus tariff revenue."
The document states that the additional payment for 2026 should be made in the fourth quarter, noting that parliament's relevant committee had earlier requested this amount be set at up to UAH 26 billion. For 2027, in addition to UAH 24 billion in the state budget, the authors propose providing for prepaid regional contracts for suburban rail services.
The report's authors note that international service is the only profitable segment of Ukrzaliznytsia's passenger operations, expected to bring in about UAH 2.4 billion in 2026, while suburban rail is the most loss-making: an average 46-km trip costs 15-20 UAH per ticket against a cost of more than UAH 300, generating more than UAH 10 billion in annual losses. Local budgets are supposed to compensate for discounted fares, but the actual compensation rate is chronically only 15-20%.
The report's authors note that the potential for staff cuts at UZ is limited by a workforce shortage already estimated at 15-20%, as well as by the need for emergency infrastructure restoration and wartime security. Since the start of the war, UZ's workforce has shrunk by 62,800, to about 170,000, though the company remains Ukraine's largest employer.
At the same time, the authors propose obtaining about UAH 4-5 billion by completing a 25% cut to administrative staff and further reducing central office service functions by up to 50%, retraining some staff for in-demand blue-collar roles.
The authors estimate a further UAH 1.5-2.5 billion in savings from optimizing the passenger network outside the state order, including by reducing the frequency of chronically underused night trains and duplicate routes.
The anti-crisis model proposes obtaining an additional UAH 2-3 billion through optimizing repairs and the network. Major repairs, in particular, should be concentrated on corridors with proven traffic, while up to 1,200 km of infrastructure should be mothballed in "hot reserve" status in coordination with Ukraine's General Staff.
The commercial segment could provide an additional UAH 4.5-6 billion, according to the authors' estimates, through continued use of dynamic pricing, the sale of about 370,000 tonnes of scrap metal, and the development of related freight services.
The report's authors said the previously announced UAH 6.9 billion effect from dynamic pricing is overstated, since the annual ticket revenue base is UAH 7.4 billion; by their conservative estimate, this tool can provide only UAH 0.3-0.5 billion in additional annual revenue within the total cited above.
The report also proposes reviewing the portfolio of unfinished construction projects, which grew 98.5% in 2025 to UAH 24.08 billion: facilities more than 90% complete and capable of generating cash flow should be finished, while the rest should be mothballed.
On developing competition and private traction, the authors say this is a necessary condition for attracting roughly $3 billion a year in rail investment, but that it must wait until the war ends.
"We wrote this in 2018-2019, and we don't retract a word of it. This plan deliberately excludes that lever within its wartime horizon: the defense filter and network manageability matter more right now. Competition is a deferred horizon after stabilization, not a canceled idea," the document states.
Regarding the 30% freight tariff hike that took effect Aug 1, the authors estimate its stated gross effect at UAH 20-26 billion a year, but say the net effect could be UAH 17-19 billion once accounting for a possible shift of 7-11 million tonnes of cargo (out of 161 million tonnes in 2025) to road transport.
As previously reported, Ukrzaliznytsia announced in January that it would not make $45 million in coupon payments on its 2026 eurobonds (8.25% rate, $703.2 million total) and its 2028 eurobonds (7.875% rate, $351.9 million total), and said it intended to launch a comprehensive restructuring of its bond obligations with the help of financial and legal advisers. Eurobond holders have so far rejected the company's proposals, which included, among other things, a 20% writedown of face value, a deferral to June 2033, amortization starting in 2030, and a coupon reduction to 1.5% with a gradual increase to 7.75% tied to freight volumes.
The company cited the continued decline in freight revenue amid falling cargo volumes, as well as intensifying attacks on the railway — which totaled 1,195 in 2025, exceeding the combined total for 2023-2024 — as the main reasons for suspending debt service on its eurobonds.
In 2025, Ukrzaliznytsia's revenue fell 15.6% to $2.189 billion, and EBITDA fell 30.2% to $293 million, of which $270 million came from budget support. Its net debt-to-EBITDA ratio rose to 5.2.

DR Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to a sixth province
Ebola outbreak has killed 2,128 people out of around 4,566 recorded cases in the DRC, according to government figures.
The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to a sixth province after a death was recorded in previously unaffected Bas-Uele, said the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.
Jean Kaseya said on Thursday that the man died in Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele province, after travelling from Haut-Uele province.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3DR Congo Ebola outbreak set to become deadliest on record, WHO warns
- list 2 of 3Ebola outbreak caused by new ‘animal transmission’: What that means
- list 3 of 3DR Congo Ebola death toll surpasses 2,000
“If we do not stop this outbreak, it will last more than a year and will be the largest in the world,” Kaseya warned. That would also increase the risk of the outbreak spreading to other countries, he added.
The World Health Organization (WHO) says it is spreading faster than any previous one.
The latest outbreak began in the northeastern Ituri province and infections have also been recorded in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces.
It has killed 2,128 people out of 4,566 cases recorded, according to government figures. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus responsible for this outbreak.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Wednesday that “at its current pace”, the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest on record, which started over a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people.
The current outbreak was formally declared on May 15 but the virus had begun circulating in February, health officials said this week.
The WHO hopes to reverse the spread of the virus within three months, but warned that the outbreak would not end by then.
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri.
Two vaccines developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus are being tested in people for the first time, the WHO said on Wednesday.
The UN health agency also plans to test whether an existing Ebola vaccine could protect people against the latest virus after studies in animals showed promising results.

EU Urges Member States to Transfer Patriot Missiles to Ukraine from Own Stockpiles
The European Union is calling on member states to transfer Patriot air defense missiles from their own stockpiles to Ukraine, declaring the reinforcement of Ukrainian air defense an absolute priority, Babel correspondent reported on August 13.
The urgent appeal from Brussels comes as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of interceptors after US President Donald Trump refused to supply 300 Patriot missiles or allow their licensed production on Ukrainian soil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
European Commission spokeswoman Anitta Hipper confirmed the diplomatic push during a briefing in Brussels. She stated that EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas has directly appealed to all member nations holding relevant reserves to provide them to Kyiv, according to Babel.
Kallas is maintaining regular contact with EU governments to negotiate increased volumes and accelerate delivery schedules for the essential munitions.
Furthermore, the European Union is speeding up its joint weapons procurement procedures through the SAFE program , an initiative that includes Ukraine’s active participation to secure necessary defense equipment, Babel wrote.
The European push to secure air defense systems aligns with broader initiatives to bypass current production and supply bottlenecks. Last week, officials highlighted how EU SAFE loans could unlock non-EU Patriot missile purchases to quickly backfill Ukraine’s dwindling stockpiles.
The need for advanced interceptors remains critical as Russian forces continue to launch massive drone and ballistic missile barrages targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian centers. Patriot systems currently serve as one of the only platforms in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of reliably intercepting ballistic missiles.

Russia Plans to Abolish Border Zones With Temporarily Occupied Ukrainian Territories
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has announced plans to abolish border zones between Russian regions and the Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia, as well as on the Crimean Peninsula, according to the Russian outlet Agentstvo on August 13.
The planned changes concern Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh regions, as well as temporarily occupied Crimea. The FSB has prepared draft orders declaring its existing regulations establishing the border zones invalid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Until now, travel from Russia to the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine annexed in 2022 differed little from crossing the state border.
According to the documents, the proposed changes are justified by Russia’s claim that the occupied Ukrainian territories have been “incorporated” into the Russian Federation. Under the planned arrangement, the border zone would instead be established along what Russia describes as the external borders of the temporarily occupied territories.
In Crimea, however, the FSB plans to retain a border regime “within the boundaries of the Black Sea islands belonging to Russia.” The local FSB administration would determine the locations and times for entry and install warning signs.
The reported move comes as Kyiv continues to reject any settlement that would require Ukrainian forces to withdraw from territory under Ukraine’s control.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would not accept any conditions requiring its military to leave Ukrainian territory. Speaking at a press briefing, he stressed that defending the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is a constitutional responsibility of the state and its armed forces.
He also said Ukraine would not accept ultimatums or agree to surrender its territory, people, or homes, while acknowledging that parts of the country remain temporarily occupied by Russia.
Against this backdrop, Ukraine also plans to continue targeting Russia’s military infrastructure and support networks. Acting Defense Minister Major General Yevhen Khmara said Ukrainian forces would systematically degrade Russia’s military capabilities by striking critical infrastructure, naval assets, and key logistical networks.
He added that Ukrainian forces would continue targeting fuel, energy, and industrial facilities that support Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

When the earth moves: six major earthquakes of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:17:00 UTC
02:17:00 KST

When the earth moves: 6 major earthquakes of 2026
August 13, 2026
Is 2026 a particularly bad year for earthquakes? The number of extremely strong quakes so far this year is not, in fact, unusual.
Over the long term, around the world, there are an average of about 15 earthquakes per year registering above magnitude 7 on the Richter scale. By mid-August this year, there had been 10.
The devastation some of the quakes have wreaked has, however, been striking.
Venezuela: 2 quakes in just 39 seconds
On June 24, Venezuela was hit by an earthquake that proved to be by far the deadliest this year. A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed just 39 seconds later by an even stronger one of magnitude 7.5. The north of the country and the capital, Caracas, were the areas worst affected.
According to official figures, more than 6,300 people were killed in the double earthquake. The effects on the impoverished country's infrastructure have also been dramatic. Shortly afterward, a satellite-based assessment by researchers at Oregon State University provisionally concluded that more than 58,000 buildings may have been damaged or destroyed.
Philippines: Strongest quake of the year
With a magnitude of 7.8, the earthquake on June 8 off the southern coast of the Philippine island of Mindanao was the strongest of 2026 so far. It occurred at a depth of about 57 kilometers (35 miles), and was felt across large parts of the island.
At least 107 people were killed. But the fact that, despite the very high magnitude of the quake, far fewer people died in the Philippines than in Venezuela demonstrates that the strength of the quake does not necessarily determine the severity of the consequences.
Colombia: hundreds dead, despite quake depth
On August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia. The epicenter was in the Choco region, near San Jose del Palmar. Although the quake occurred at a depth of 100 kilometers (62 miles), the damage it caused was immense.
More than 250 people are currently estimated to have died. Landslides and damaged roads are hampering the search for victims buried beneath the rubble, as well as the provision of supplies to remote areas. After Venezuela, this quake is the most consequential so far this year for Latin America.
Tonga: Powerful quake, little damage
On March 24, the earth shook near the island group of Vava'u in the Pacific kingdom of Tonga. With a magnitude of 7.5, it was one of the strongest globally this year. But because there was no severe damage and no deaths, it received almost no attention from the media.
The quake occurred unusually far below the Earth's crust, at a depth of around 230 kilometers (143 miles), meaning that the tremors were significantly weakened by the time they reached the surface. To date, there have been no reports of deaths, or damage to infrastructure.
Japan: Strong undersea quake off Sanriku Coast
On April 20, there was an undersea quake off the northeastern coast of Japan. The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4.
This region, the Sanriku Coast area in Iwate prefecture, achieved terrible notoriety after the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami there in 2011, which also resulted in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. A tsunami warning was issued after this year's earthquake, too, but fortunately the region was spared the devastation of that magnitude 9 quake 15 years ago.
There was no major tsunami this time, but the quake illustrated once again how much Japan is affected by its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) volcanic belt runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean where several tectonic plates collide.
Afghanistan: Weak, but deadly
The earthquake in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhsham on April 3 only reached a magnitude of 5.8, which puts it right at the bottom of the list of the strongest earthquakes this year. Despite this, at least 12 people were killed, which is why it counts as one of the most significant quakes of 2026.
In poorer countries, even slight tremors can have deadly consequences. The risks are heightened by inadequate building construction, the difficulty of accessing remote areas and underdeveloped disaster response protocols.

Víctor Coyote dies: a life impossible to confine to music, comics and film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:16:49 UTC
02:16:49 KST

Víctor Coyote, the stage name of Víctor María Aparicio Abundancia, died on Thursday in Galicia in a cycling accident. He was 67 and leaves a bold four-decade career spanning music, comics, film and videos.
There were hardly any labels that really fit Víctor Coyote, and that was always his best calling card. Born in Tui in 1958, he died this Thursday in a cycling accident, leaving behind a career that began in late-1970s punk and ended, as he approached seventy, without ever having stopped reinventing himself.
His musical career took off in 1979 with the founding of Los Coyotes, the band he led alongside Fernando Gilabert and from which he took his stage name. The group emerged from 'psychobilly', but soon shifted towards Latin rhythms, becoming pioneers of that sonic crossover in Spain long before others brought it into the mainstream.
Their debut album, 'Mujer y sentimiento' (1985), put them on the map of the movida, a scene straddling Vigo and Madrid in which Víctor Coyote was one of the most restless figures. The band changed its name in 1988 to Los Coyotes de Víctor Abundancia and produced one of its best-remembered songs, 'Esta noche me voy a bailar', before finally splitting up in 1992.
Videos, comics and the Xabarín Clun
The break-up of the group did not mean a pause, but a change of format. By then Víctor Coyote had already spent years combining music with comics, contributing to the magazine 'Madriz' between 1984 and 1987, and he threw himself into directing music videos and drawing.
He directed the video for 'Milonga', by Los Rodríguez, and for 'Carmiña Vacaloura', a track that formed part of the soundtrack of the Xabarín Club and which remains lodged in the memory of much of a generation of Galicians. At the same time he published standalone comics such as 'Come yuca' (1998) and contributed to collective publications that cemented his place on the Spanish graphic scene.
A solo career impossible to pigeonhole
In 1995 he returned to the studio on his own with 'Lo bueno, dentro, disco', which yielded 'Jaguarundi', the theme tune for the Vuelta Ciclista a España that same year. From then on he went on releasing music, drawing and filming, without ever tying himself down to a single medium.
In a recent interview he described his own work as that of someone with "more eye than ear", and in 2024, when presenting his comic 'Si te falta calle', he explained that humour was an inevitable ingredient in his work, though never the only one: to capture life, he would say, you always need a little of it.
Víctor Coyote did not stop working or appearing in public in his final years. Last May he acted as a guide through his own career in an interview, and he was one of the main figures at the Festival de Cans, looking back over eight of his best-known works. His death this Thursday, in a cycling accident, brings to an abrupt close a career that, right up to the end, refused to sit still in a single line of work.

Russia is testing NATO's resolve - Sybiha
Kyiv • UNN
Andrii Sybiha stated that Russia is testing NATO's resolve by violating its airspace. He emphasized that strengthening Ukraine's air defense reinforces the Alliance's eastern flank.
Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha said that every violation of NATO countries’ airspace by russia is a test of the Alliance’s strength. Sybiha wrote this on the social network "X," reports UNN.
Details
russia is testing NATO’s strength. Each new violation tests the allies’ readiness, represents an attempt to test the limits of what is permissible for moscow, and raises the stakes ahead of the next provocation. Ukraine has already seen this pattern: when russia encounters indecision, it escalates the situation. When it encounters strength, it changes its calculations
According to him, the threats that Ukraine faces every day on a much broader scale are increasingly extending beyond our borders.
russian missiles and drones, sabotage, and other forms of hybrid pressure are components of one and the same strategy. Ukraine has unique combat experience in detecting, intercepting, and countering these threats and is ready to share it with its allies
He added that moscow would like the capitals of NATO countries to believe that strengthening their own defenses and supporting Ukraine are contradictory priorities.
In fact, they reinforce each other. A better-protected Ukrainian sky strengthens NATO’s eastern flank. A more decisive NATO response limits russia’s ability to escalate further. That is why strengthening Ukraine’s air defense is crucial for the security of the entire region. russia must understand that every attempt to test our collective resolve will make Ukraine and NATO stronger, better prepared, and more united—not the opposite
It will be recalled
Kremlin chief vladimir putin may try to "test NATO’s resolve with a limited attack on an allied country within the next few years," according to new U.S. intelligence reports that outline possible scenarios, "ranging from a cyberattack to a small-scale ground invasion."
