Air force to form dedicated UAV unit, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:20 UTC
01:38:20 KST

The air force is to form a dedicated combat drone unit early next year, a high-ranking military official said.
The planned air group would utilize multiple types of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), including the domestically developed Chien Hsiang (劍翔, “Rising Sword”) loitering munitions, which specialize in neutralizing radar systems, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The new unit would be tasked with preparing for potential long-range strikes against targets in China, enabling the air force to attack rather than passively defend Taiwanese airspace, they said.
Photo: Yen Hung-chun, Taipei Times
The Chien Hsiang was developed by the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST), Taiwan’s state-run defense research-and-development group.
The Air Defense and Missile Command has deployed about 200 Chien Hsiang loitering munitions in Taiwan proper and its outlying islands, the source said.
The drones can be deployed en masse in the Taiwan Strait to bait Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) forces into turning on their radars, which the drones could then target with one-way strikes, they said.
Such attacks would degrade the PLA’s capabilities for detecting and intercepting Taiwanese aircraft, allowing the air force to deploy its Lockheed Martin F-16s and AIDC F-CK-1 Ching Kuo jets, commonly known as Indigenous Defense Fighters, with less risk, the official said.
This tactic was tested in the latest Tien Lung (天龍, “Sky Dragon”) drills held from April 7 to 9, in which air force pilots took part in mock battles and simulated attack runs, the source said.
The planned UAV group centers on using swarms of inexpensive and expendable drones in asymmetric attacks to overwhelm enemy defenses, they said, adding that drones are significantly cheaper than air defense missiles.
The unit would combine existing Chien Hsiang drones with a newly procured attack system that uses off-the-shelf civilian components to reduce costs, the source said.
The new system is projected to cost several million New Taiwan dollars per unit, down from tens of millions, they said.
The unidentified system has satellite-positioning and image-recognition targeting capabilities, they added.
The official would not comment on whether the attack drone is the Mighty Hornet II (勁蜂二型) or newly imported attack drone.
Taiwanese forces participating in the ongoing Han Kuang exercise could be seen defending air bases with NCSIST counter-UAV systems and anti-drone guns against simulated saturation drone attacks.

Agency presents four farmers with owl-friendly label
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

Twenty-three agricultural workers have been approved to use the Australasian Grass Owl-Friendly Label for their agricultural products since the label was launched last year, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Pingtung branch said on Wednesday.
The branch had presented the label to four Kaohsiung-based agricultural workers who recently passed an Australasian grass owl-friendly farming course.
The Australasian Grass Owl-Friendly Label encourages agricultural workers to adopt eco-friendly field management approaches without using rodenticides, animal traps or herbicides, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency’s Chiayi branch
The goal is to minimize the impact of agricultural activities on Australasian grass owls and other ecosystems, it added.
The label has been granted to 23 agricultural workers who cultivate a variety of crops, including lemons, guavas, avocados, pineapples, rambutans, corn, rice and leafy vegetables, it said.
Among the four growers granted the label on Wednesday is Chen Mou-wei (陳謀韋), who operates a 16-hectare avocado orchard near the Nanzihsian River (楠梓仙溪) in Kaohsiung’s Chishan District (旗山), the branch said.
Chen applies his electrical engineering expertise to developing semi-mechanized field management and records his pesticide applications in detail in the traceability system, it said.
Another grower, Chen Tai-sheng (陳?昇), adopts organic farming to grow guavas on the badlands of Kaohsiung’s Tianliao District (田寮), the branch said.
He created a technique of warping the main stem of guava plants around a galvanized steel pipe to help them survive typhoons, as well as using pruned branches to surround guava plant trunks to retain moisture, it said.
Agricultural worker Chien Chun-fa (簡春發), who operates pineapple fields in Kaohsiung’s Dashu District (大樹), insists on not using herbicides or chemical fertilizers, the branch said.
Chien considers wild animals nibbling his fruit as “the rent paid to nature,” it said.
He also set up raptor perches in his fields to attract black-winged kites and crested goshawks, which hunt rats, the branch said.
Replacing pesticides with biological control techniques aligns with the principle of ecological integration, it said.
Lastly, Hung Chi-chin (洪麒欽), uses organic farming to cultivate avocados, mangoes and black persimmons near the Cishan River (旗山溪), the branch said, adding that Hung’s orchards document sightings of Australasian grass owls.
Agricultural workers are indispensable partners in promoting conservation of the critically endangered owls, it said, calling on the public to purchase products with the label to support eco-friendly farming.

Starlux said its direct flights between Taichung and Nagoya would begin on Oct. 25, with four flights each week in the initial stage via its A321neo aircraft.
With the addition of Taichung-Nagoya direct services, the airline’s Taichung-based aviation network would have 12 international destinations. The other 11 are: Tokyo, Kobe, Takamatsu, Okinawa, Miyakojima, Sapporo and Kumamoto in Japan; Da Nang and Phu Quoc in Vietnam; Busan in South Korea and Macau.
Photo: CNA
Nagoya serves as the gateway for travelers to explore central Japan, and its downtown area is rich in history, culture and local cuisine, Starlux CEO Glenn Chai (翟健華) said.
Through Nagoya, travelers can also access popular tourist destinations, such as Hida Takayama Municipal Ski Resort, Chai said.
Tigerair Taiwan, Taiwan’s low-cost carrier, said it would launch two new routes to Ishigaki and Komatsu next month, as it anticipates strong demand for overseas travel among residents of southern Taiwan.
The two new routes would bring the airline’s international routes from Kaohsiung to 11, it said.
Tigerair would then have a total of 45 international routes, with 19 operated exclusively by the airline, it added.
Tokyo, Osaka, Fukuoka, Okayama and Okinawa are among the most popular destinations for Taiwanese travelers, Tigerair said, adding that it expects demand to remain strong in the second half of the year.
It operates flights to Okinawa from Taoyuan, Taichung, Tainan and Kaohsiung, with an average load factor of 97.1 percent, it said.
Gooday Tours general manager Aron Huang (黃清涼), who serves as a specialist for Japanese tours in the Travel Quality Assurance Association, said 3.97 million Taiwanese traveled to Japan in the first six months of this year, up 20.9 percent from the same period last year.
Taiwan has emerged as Japan’s second-largest tourism source, preceded only by South Korea.
China remains Japan’s third-largest tourism source, although Beijing has urged its citizens to avoid travel to Japan.
Huang attributed the strong demand to the significant increase of flights to Japan, not only to Tokyo and Osaka, but to other cities as well.
The demand for Japan tours during the summer travel season remains strong despite the rising travel costs caused by airport tax hikes and inflation in Japan, Huang said.
Group tour costs are expected to slightly fall in the fourth quarter, following the summer travel season.
Tour prices could be even cheaper if people choose to travel a few days ahead of the nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28.
“As people might choose to stay and vote in the elections, travel agencies expect the demand for outbound tourism to drop and are more likely to offer special prices for tours,” he said.

EDITORIAL: AIT shows deepening Taiwan-US ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:16 UTC
01:38:16 KST

The American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) on July 28 posted on social media a picture of Taiwanese and US coast guard vessels sailing in formation, the first confirmation of the two countries’ combined patrols in waters near Taiwan.
The post showed the 4,000-tonne Chiayi-class vessel Taipei and 4,500-tonne Legend-class cutter USCGC Midgett sailing together in the Taiwan Strait, and said that Taiwan and the US coast guard were coordinating on shared maritime objectives, such as preserving maritime resources and interdicting illegal drug shipments.
“The US appreciates Taiwan’s partnership in maritime security and safety, and supports Taiwan’s meaningful contributions on global issues,” it said.
The two countries in 2021 signed a Memorandum of Understanding on Establishing the Coast Guard Working Group and have carried out several anti-smuggling and rescue exercises.
The AIT’s post came amid China’s escalating maritime “gray zone” coercions — such as harassing commercial ships, shadowing Taiwanese and international vessels, and conducting blockade rehearsals and “law enforcement” drills — which contravene international norms and have caused regional turmoil.
Other countries have condemned Beijing’s actions against its neighbors, but the AIT’s post aimed to deter China’s expanding presence in regional waters by showing the growing regional security cooperation between Taiwan and the US.
Hudson Institute China Center director Miles Yu, a China policy adviser to US President Donald Trump during his first term, said the AIT’s post was ‘the most important security development in East Asia this year.”
The joint patrol showed that the US does not accept China’s claim over Taiwan’s surrounding waters, and “affirms that Taiwan exercises lawful maritime jurisdiction in its own waters and those waters remain part of international maritime commons,” Yu said.
Although the US-China leaders’ summit in May and next month sparked concerns on Trump’s stance on the Taiwan issue, German Marshall Fund Indo-Pacific program managing director Bonnie Glaser said the post conveyed a message from Washington that “Taiwan is an important partner for regional security, and the US is committed to working alongside Taiwan to promote shared objectives.”
To other countries, it signals that they “could also benefit from working more closely with Taiwan,” Glaser added.
While the US’ national security strategy under Trump’s second term has emphasized a shift toward asking partners to share responsibility for their own defense and regional security, China’s maritime aggressions against Japan in the East China Sea, the Philippines in the South China Sea and Taiwan in the Taiwan Strait have given First Island Chain nations a common foe. Japan and the Philippines this year announced they would elevate bilateral relations to a “comprehensive strategic partnership,” which is obviously an alliance to counter shared security challenges from China.
Following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaishi’s statement that a Chinese attack against Taiwan could constitute a “survival threatening situation” for Japan, the Philippines’ president and secretary of national defense have also said that Manila would be involved if Beijing were to attack Taiwan, as its geographic proximity makes neutrality impossible.
Tokyo in its latest Defense of Japan white paper portrayed China’s military growth and coercion as the “greatest strategic challenge“ to Japan, detailed Beijing’s military operations and incidents around Taiwan and highlighted the growing military gap across the Strait as a matter of great concern to the region and the international community.
The report also for the first time devoted a special chapter on the modernization and reform of the Japan Self-Defense Forces and firmly asserted that Tokyo would reinforce its alliance with Washington.
Japan would also deepen partnerships with like-minded countries in the Indo-Pacific region and the EU “to uphold a rules-based international order against unilateral, coercive attempts to change the status quo,” it said.
Japanese destroyers sailing through the Taiwan Strait this year and last year, and Japan’s white paper and defense reforms reflect China’s failure in escalating its pressure campaign against Tokyo, the aim of which is to deter it from getting involved in a Taiwan contingency.
The joint patrol signals that a wider and more “paramilitary” maritime alliance is forming along the First Island Chain, with Taiwan at the center and the strategic anchor of the chain. Taiwan must enhance cooperation and partnerships with more like-minded countries to ensure stability and prosperity in the region and the Indo-Pacific area.

The TPP was formally established on Aug. 6, 2019. Thursday was its seventh anniversary and it marked the event at the party’s annual national congress meeting in Taichung on Sunday last week. It was also the week that the latest My Formosa public opinion poll was released, showing that the TPP’s approval rating had fallen 6 percentage points since the beginning of the year. The United States on Wednesday urged Beijing to end its “military pressure against Taiwan” after China claimed to have conducted naval exercises with an Indonesian warship in waters east of Taiwan.
According to the Eastern Theater Command of China’s military, its naval vessel Honghe and the Indonesian Navy frigate KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai-332 carried out live drills east of Taiwan Wednesday morning, including maritime communications, formation maneuvers, replenishment-at- sea, and a divergence ceremony.

Photo: CNA
Responding to a CNA inquiry, a U.S. State Department spokesperson said on background that Washington “urges Beijing to cease its continuous military pressure against Taiwan and instead engage in meaningful dialogue with Taiwan.”
“We call on other countries to encourage the peaceful resolution of cross-strait issues instead of amplifying Beijing’s destabilizing narratives,” the spokesperson added.
Separately, John Dotson, director of the Washington- based Global Taiwan Institute, said Beijing was pushing back against a growing “quasi-alliance” between Japan and the Philippines, driven by concerns about China’s increasingly assertive behavior and the possibility of a military crisis in the Taiwan Strait.
According to Dotson, Beijing has sought to cultivate its own regional partners, as reflected in joint naval activities with countries such as Russia, while also using the regional security situation as a pretext to expand its naval presence in waters east of Taiwan.
The joint drills with the Indonesian frigate appear to advance both objectives, he said.
“It’s a small step, but one that carries a lot of symbolism,” Dotson said.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned Beijing for disregarding international norms and responsibilities and escalating regional tensions.

Why the Middle East war still convulses the global oil market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

After more than five months of conflict, oil markets continue to surge and tumble over the latest developments in the US-Iran clash, including US President Donald Trump’s shifting pronouncements.
What is behind the market’s volatility?
While the potential vulnerability of the Strait of Hormuz has long been viewed as a risk, oil markets have still been caught off guard by Iran’s ability to largely close the crucial waterway.
“What really shakes the market are surprises... and the Hormuz closure was a shock,” said Jim Burkhard, head of global energy crude oil research at S&P Global.
Brent oil prices surged more than 13 percent in the immediate aftermath of the US-Israeli siege against Iran on Feb. 28. Since that time, prices have been jolted in both directions as the conflict has dragged on.
“Number one, it’s the complete unexpectedness, unfamiliarity with what we are seeing,” Bob McNally, president of the Rapidian Energy Group and a former White House energy adviser to former US president George W. Bush, said of the unprecedented curtailment of the Strait.
“There was this perception that the US would never allow it to happen,” McNally added.
About 20 million barrels per day of crude traverse the strait, about a quarter of global oil demand, making the supply shock “the biggest disruption in history,” McNally said.
Subsequent events have jerked prices in both directions. Markets were unnerved by the US move to blockade Iran’s ports, but subsequently buoyed by a June 17 agreement between the US and Iran to cease hostilities.
While the conflict has boosted prices overall, international benchmark Brent oil has averaged US$94 a barrel since the start of the fighting, well below the US$150-per-barrel level seen by some experts as possible.
One explanation is the market’s response to Trump, who has issued contradictory statements, but has often described a Hormuz resolution as within striking distance. Such statements have helped keep crude prices from rising more.
“The market believes and still believes that this crisis can and will end soon,” McNally said.
Optimistic statements by the president and other Trump administration figures such as Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent have often sent oil prices sharply lower, posing peril to traders on the wrong side.
“The oil market has sort of burned the bulls so many times you just don’t have bulls willing to go in and trade,” McNally said. “So all you have is people who are trading, especially these algorithmic traders who are just trading on headlines,” he added.
The Hormuz closure has lowered volumes by about 12.6 million barrels per day, JPMorgan Chase analysts said.
Some of this has been blunted by lower crude imports from China, while releases from commercial and government inventories have also offset the effects of lost supply.
In March, the International Energy Agency announced member governments would release 400 million barrels of oil, the largest emergency stock release in history.
The US, Canada and Brazil have been among the countries increasing output.
Middle East producers have maneuvered some shipments away from the strait. For example, Saudi Arabia shifted crude exports to the Red Sea, but that avenue has also been compromised by attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
While the fluctuations of crude prices generate most of the headlines, analysts have also highlighted the stresses on refined products, including gasoline.
“The most pressure in the world today is on refined products because there is generally enough crude oil out there right now, but there’s not enough refining capacity,” Burkhard said.
Diesel prices have doubled compared with February, while gasoline prices are up about 50 percent.
The Middle East conflict has also sidelined key energy infrastructure due to attacks, including some refinery capacity. Energy experts also point to Russian refinery outages due to attacks from Ukraine in that war.
Continued robust demand for petroleum products has led to a historic surge in refinery profit margins, resulting in huge earnings windfalls for large oil companies in the second quarter.

Air raid, Internet drills finish in north
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:12 UTC
01:38:12 KST

Air raid sirens rang out and streets emptied in northern Taiwan yesterday during annual air raid drills that also included the government limiting mobile Internet access to simulate what might happen in the event of a Chinese attack.
In this year’s 10-day Han Kuang war games, which end today, the military has practiced fighting a Chinese invasion and the government has also staged civil defense drills.
On Monday, the government held its first-ever mobile Internet “throttling” exercise in central Taiwan, with the exercise repeated in the northern part of the nation yesterday afternoon.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Lasting 30 minutes, mobile Internet speeds slowed dramatically, although fixed-line Internet and Wi-Fi were not affected.
The government had flagged the drills well in advance.
Police ushered people off the streets to seek shelter indoors during the mock air attack, with buses and cars pulling to the side of the road.
Photo: George Tsrong, Taipei Times
Earlier in the day, President William Lai (賴清德) visited an underground car park at Shuang Ho Hospital in New Taipei City that had been turned into an emergency ward, and a supermarket to see how provisions would be distributed in an emergency.
He was accompanied by senior foreign diplomats based in Taiwan, including US, Israeli and Canadian representatives.
Taiwan has been keen to learn from Israel about its civil defense operations.
“We are not facing regional geopolitical changes alone, but together with the shared concern and joint efforts of the international community,” Lai said of the presence of the diplomats.
At the hospital, the president inspected the emergency ward’s control zone, combat-readiness supply storage, blood donation station and core medical areas, including general wards, emergency dialysis units and intensive care units.
The hospital can convert its 3,504m2 underground parking lot into a fully functional underground medical center within 48 hours of receiving instructions, its medical team said.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
The military parts of the exercises also continued.
On Wednesday, the armed forces carried out an anti-blockade drill, using the navy and coast guard to simulate escorting a merchant ship.
The navy worked with coast guard vessels to complete the escort and security protection duties, while a minesweeper cleared a safe navigation channel and guided the simulated merchant vessel to port, the Ministry of National Defense said in a statement.
Photo: CNA
The Coast Guard Administration, which would have an auxiliary role helping the navy in time of war, said the port the ship was taken to was on the east coast.
It said it was the first time it had worked with the navy to hold an anti-blockade drill.
Early yesterday, the military held a defensive blockade drill in Taipei’s Wanhua District (萬華) aimed at preventing enemy armored units from advancing further into the heart of the capital.
The simulated battle took place on Guangfu Bridge (光復橋) and at intersections at both ends of the bridge.
The drill simulated a scenario in which enemy forces had carried out an amphibious landing and were advancing toward the capital.
Military police dressed in camouflage uniforms placed gabions and Jersey barriers on the bridge to block the enemy’s advance. They also secured the perimeter on the Taipei side of the bridge by deploying Czech hedgehogs, barbed wire and barricades along three sides of an intersection to create a “kill zone.”
Tour buses requisitioned from the private sector were also deployed as barriers under the military’s civilian force requisition plan.
Military police armed with T112 rifles simulated engagements with the opposing force, while attack drones simulated bombs being dropped from the air.

（By Eddy Chang, Taipei Times／台北時報張迪）
A technique that allows developers to shrink powerful artificial intelligence models into cheaper, more efficient systems has become the latest battleground in the intensifying US-China race for AI dominance. Known as model distillation, the method uses the outputs of a powerful AI system to train a smaller model that can perform some of the same tasks with fewer computing resources. “The first priority after the merger will be to bring the insurer back to health through capital injections,” E.Sun Financial chairman Joseph Huang (黃男州) told a news conference in Taipei ahead of a company earnings call.
E.Sun would inject NT$16 billion into Mercuries Life next month, followed by another NT$6 billion next year, Huang said.
Photo: CNA
The entire NT$22 billion capital increase would be subscribed by E.Sun Financial, with no preferred or common shares to be issued, he said.
The capital is aimed at boosting Mercuries Life’s capital base, with its Taiwan Insurance Capital Standard ratio expected to reach about 125 percent toward the end of the year, Huang said.
E.Sun Financial would expand Mercuries Life’s bancassurance business while maintaining its traditional insurance offerings, including participating policies, and accident and health insurance, he said.
Sales agents account for a significant share of Mercuries Life’s insurance sales, with unit-linked policies making up a large part of its portfolio, highlighting the potential for E.Sun to broaden the insurer’s distribution through its banking network, he said.
The group also plans to improve the insurer’s operating efficiency through organizational restructuring, process optimization and greater use of technology, he said.
E.Sun Financial president Chen Mao-chin (陳茂欽) said the group plans to initially place a small portion of Mercuries Life’s assets with E.Sun Securities Investment Trust Co (玉山投信) for management, with the mandate potentially expanded if the arrangement proves successful.
Mercuries Life had about NT$292.5 billion of assets under external management as of June, providing E.Sun Securities Investment Trust with scope to secure larger asset-management mandates over time, Chen said.
E.Sun Commercial Bank Ltd (玉山銀行) sells insurance products from eight life insurers, with Nan Shan Life Insurance Co (南山人壽) accounting for the largest share.
The lender would maintain its open-platform approach while gradually increasing the distribution of Mercuries Life products, E.Sun Commercial Bank president Lin Lung-cheng (林隆政) said.

Greenpeace calls for review of energy bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

Greenpeace Taiwan yesterday called for draft amendments to the Energy Administration Act (能源管理法) to be sent back to a legislative committee for review, and for new amendments that would include all of the more than 400 heavy electricity users under regulation.
The legislature’s Economics Committee on Wednesday last week passed the draft bill, which critics said falls short of expectations.
The Cabinet’s version would require energy users who have entered an electricity contract, with their contract capacity reaching a certain level, to install self-use power generation equipment and energy storage equipment.
Photo: CNA
However, the version of the bill passed by the committee would only require energy users with a newly established or expanded electricity contract to install self-use power generation equipment or energy storage equipment.
Greenpeace Taiwan climate and energy campaigner Lin Lien-kai (林煉凱) said the committee passed the revised bill soon after the Taipei-based Chinese National Federation of Industries on Monday last week suggested that the regulation be limited to energy users with a newly established electricity contract.
The approved draft amendments were like “copying and pasting” the federation’s suggestion and failed to include the more than 400 heavy electricity users, which account for more than 40 percent of the power grid, he said.
Lin said the bill has five main shortcomings.
First, energy users would be allowed to choose either installing self-use power generation equipment or installing energy storage equipment, but a combination of self-provided renewable energy with energy storage would be the most effective in promoting the use of self-generated electricity, he said.
The legal effectiveness was reduced, as not all of the more than 400 heavy electricity users would be included under the regulations, Lin said.
The bill neither excludes high-pollution energy nor encourages companies to prioritize the development of renewable energy, he said.
Fourth, the bill was passed without sufficient public participation, Lin said.
Lastly, the bill would have a five-year grace period, which might be too long and energy users might expand their capacity during the period to circumvent regulation, he said.
While the bill would be referred to a second reading, Lin urged lawmakers to send it back to committee for reconsideration.
The provisions should be revised to include all of the heavy electricity users and require energy users to prioritize renewable energy over polluting energy such as fossil fuels, he said.

Draft bill to combat crypto money laundering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:07 UTC
01:38:07 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday passed draft amendments to the Money Laundering Control Act (洗錢防制法) aimed at strengthening oversight of cryptocurrency-related activities and stablecoins to prevent them from being used for money laundering.
Under the amendments, providing virtual-asset services or third-party payment services without registration, as well as issuing stablecoins without authorization, would be designated as “specified unlawful activities” for the purposes of money laundering offenses.
The draft incorporates international standards by establishing a legal definition of a beneficial owner as a person who ultimately owns or controls a client or a transaction, or a person who exercises ultimate effective control over a legal entity or legal arrangement.
Photo: AFP
It would also authorize the central authorities overseeing relevant industries to establish inspection and identification measures for beneficial owners in consultation with other government agencies.
To strengthen cross-agency cooperation on money laundering prevention, the draft would allow government agencies to access necessary information on financial institutions and designated nonfinancial businesses and professions within specified limits.
It would also establish a mechanism allowing financial institutions and virtual asset service providers to share information with peers and entities in other industries when necessary to prevent money laundering or combat the financing of terrorism.
The draft amendments would be sent to the legislature for review before they can take effect.
At a post-Cabinet meeting news conference, Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) quoted Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) as saying that preventing money laundering is a critical foundation for combating crime and maintaining financial stability.
As criminal methods and means of transferring funds continue to evolve rapidly, legislation must also be updated in line with international standards and practical needs, Cho said.
He added that supporting measures and implementation rules should also be completed, while cross-agency cooperation and information sharing should be strengthened.

====================================================================================================

Taiwan’s punishing paradise: Surviving the Mabolasi Traverse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

Starting dramatically on a historic trail built by the Japanese above a hot springs town and ending unceremoniously on a muddy, leech-infested forest road after what could be your worst night’s sleep ever in the mountains, the Mabolasi Traverse (馬博拉斯橫斷) is full of challenge and reward. For fit hikers who can survive the former and still enjoy the latter, “Mabo” is the route for you.
UP, DOWN AND UP AGAIN
The first challenge of the trip: three days of uphill walking with a heavy backpack. From the hot springs town of Dongpu (東埔) in Nantou County, the route follows the Japanese-built Batongguan Traversing Trail (八通關古道) at first. This trail was built to cross the Central Mountains, joining west and east along a constant, gentle slope. Nowadays, this gentle slope is interrupted by several steep landslide detours, and the original meter-wide track is reduced to a narrow, crumbling mess in countless places.
Photo: Tyler Cottenie
Our group of three opted to cut off a day from the traditional eight-day itinerary, so instead of stopping after 15km at Guangao Lodge (觀高山屋), we pushed on. From here it’s only an hour to the Batongguan Meadow on the original trail, but it is officially closed due to severe landslide damage. We considered giving it a try, but in the end, we followed the official park detour: a grueling 400-meter ascent and steep drop back down to the meadow.
By the time we got to Zhongyang Gold Mine Cabin (中央金礦山屋), we had been walking for 14 hours and ascended nearly 2,000 meters carrying backpacks laden with seven days of food. Sleep came swiftly that night.
The route then splits from the Batongguan, passes the Baiyang Gold Mine Cabin (where most people spend their second night) and then reaches the spine of the Central Mountains. Another half-day’s walk along the spine gets you to the highest point on the trek, Mabolasi Mountain (馬博拉斯山), at 3,805 meters. We made it here on our second day, just in time for a gorgeous sunset looking out over the entire Central Mountain Range, with Snow Mountain (雪山) some 100 km away.
The following day we left our heavy gear in the cabin and set out for a day trip down to the next peak. Yes, down. Penju Mountain (盆駒山) is 800m lower than Mabolasi, but is a must-visit for most, as it is still (begrudgingly) part of the 100 Peaks of Taiwan.
After two days of carrying a 20kg backpack uphill, walking downhill with only a day pack was a relief. The punishing part, however, was the return trip back up in the afternoon heat. As we reached Mabolasi again just in time for another gorgeous sunset, the struggles of the day melted away, and we still made it over to the cabin before dark.
Shortly thereafter, we heard shouting outside: it was the couple who had been doing Penju today just behind us, now lost in the dark. We were able to find them and guide them back to the cabin, and were not surprised to learn they had no offline maps loaded on their phones.
ACROSS CRUMBLING CLIFFS
The following three days are the heart of the trek, over exposed peaks, crumbling cliffs and narrow ridges. The adrenaline rush from these sections is matched in intensity by the beauty of the scenery in this remote part of the country, where no trace of human activity exists away from the trail itself.
On day four we crossed the Wulameng Cliffs (烏拉孟斷崖), where a hiker fell to their death recently in snowy conditions. There are ropes set up here to help you along, but even with no snow on the ground, this section is a test of mental resolve and upper body strength, as the trail drops off at about 80 degrees on both sides.
Later on, after a steep climb on all fours up a scree slope in howling winds, we summited the next of the 100 Peaks, Malijianan Mountain (馬利加南山). The sky was a crisp winter blue and on a calm day this high perch would make for a great rest stop, but the wind was so strong we had a hard time standing upright for pictures without getting blown off, so we quickly moved on.
After a night at Malijianan Cabin and another serene morning along the ridge punctuated by dramatic cliffs, narrow spines and rope sections, we arrived at Mabugu (馬布谷), a wide valley of dwarf bamboo. Some people compress their itinerary, skipping Malijianan Cabin and coming all the way to Mabugu Cabin in one long day, arriving late. However, it’s highly recommended to plan a half-day of rest at Mabugu in the middle of the trip.
We were looking forward to this spot more than anything else on the itinerary, and after a tiring start to the trip, we felt we had earned the rest. The sky was clear and we were able to dry out all of our clothes and enjoy an afternoon basking in the warm sun. Two of us later took a side trail to Bugan Mountain (布干山), a nearby peak with an excellent view that surpasses many of the 100 Peaks.
Feeling well rested, we headed out early the next morning to catch the sunrise from the top of the next of the 100 Peaks, Maxi Mountain (馬西山). Not 10 minutes after leaving the cabin, however, we spotted two headlamps going up the steep side of the valley instead of following the correct trail along the valley floor. We hollered up at the people until they came back down and, sure enough, it was the same couple who had been lost three nights prior.
THE WORST FOR LAST
Beyond Maxi Mountain, the trail becomes less dramatic and continues to descend into Hualien County. Kaxipanan Mountain (喀西帕南山) is the last of the 100 Peaks, after which the trail drops steeply down toward the beautiful Taiping Valley (太平谷), another wide, flat, dry valley tucked between towering peaks. It’s all downhill from here, both literally and figuratively.
Not far below the valley, the trail joins the abandoned Zhongping Forest Road (中平林道), which eventually leads to the trailhead the following day, and then down to Yuli Township (玉里鎮) in Hualien. The forest here is much wetter and several necessary detours off the road are steep and slippery. The last night on a standard itinerary is miserable. There is no cabin, so a tent or tarp is necessary, and you’re likely to encounter leeches.
We avoided leeches by setting up camp under a tarp on a flat sand bar beside a river. Still, it was a cramped, wet night and any potential firewood nearby was completely waterlogged and unusable.
The next morning, we passed the other potential overnight spot, which we ironically named the “Mabo Marriott”. With one wall remaining on the first building, and three walls but only half a roof remaining on the building containing the old sleeping platforms, this dilapidated old forestry workers’ dormitory is practically unusable (though many still try). Bring a tent.
The rest of the trek down involves a lot of shortcuts and detours through steep, slippery forest, poorly marked in places and often infested with leeches. It’s hard to imagine how anyone can enjoy this descent, even in good weather. Thankfully, it’s only about a half-day walk to the 19km mark on the forest road, where a shuttle van can end your misery and take you down to the creature comforts you will have earned.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with
When Gary Melyan, a longtime Taiwan resident who died on July 7 at age 83, arrived in Taipei for the second time in 1971, he was a graduate student trying to complete a doctoral thesis on the Taiping Rebellion. Wanting to assemble some fellow academics for a regular meal, he initiated a Saturday lunch, which quickly shifted to Saturday dinner. Then, sometime in 1974 or 1975, it became a weekly Wednesday night meal. Melyan never finished his PhD, but the weekly Wednesday dinner, now known as the Wednesday Night Old Farts (WNOF), has continued for more than half a century

Registration opens Aug. 31 and ends on Sept. 4. The Central Election Commission (CEC) will vet the candidates and if they pass muster, the formal list of candidates will be released on Oct. 16. Election day is Nov. 28. Both parties are afraid of breakaway party members running as independents, challenging their nominees and splitting the vote. KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) is in overdrive, and the DPP has enlisted former president

Yuko’s experience was not unusual among the Siraya and other Pingpu (plains Indigenous) groups, who hid their Indigenous identity amid stigma and discrimination, leaving later generations unaware of their ancestry. The Executive Yuan yesterday called on all ministries and agencies to work together under the nation’s integrated diplomacy strategy to advance Taiwan’s first-ever dedicated healthcare subfund under APEC.
In May, Taiwan contributed US$1.5 million to establish APEC’s first dedicated healthcare subfund, targeting the region’s rapidly aging populations and widening gaps in access to care.
A memorandum of understanding formalizing the contribution was signed by Jonathan Sun (孫儉元), Taiwan’s senior official for APEC, and Eduardo Pedrosa, executive director of the APEC secretariat, on the sidelines of the second APEC senior officials’ meeting in Shanghai in May.
Photo courtesy of the Executive Yuan
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday forwarded the signed agreement to the Executive Yuan, which it then forwarded to the Presidential Office’s secretary-general to be given to the president.
According to the ministry, the subfund is the first healthcare-based subfund aimed at helping all economic bodies hold relevant meetings and events.
It asked that all ministries and agencies, alongside private companies, work toward a healthcare system that places patients at its core while utilizing artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies to resolve growing medical issues resulting from population structural changes.
Speaking after the Cabinet meeting yesterday, Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) quoted Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) as saying that Taiwan has made multiple contributions to APEC since joining the body in 1991, and that the subfund is the first under the body with a focus on healthcare.
Cho also said that the subfund’s establishment is the most significant proposal Taiwan has made in the past decade.
Cho thanked the ministry for its hard work to overcome politically motivated obstructions and obtain the unanimous support of all APEC members for the establishment of the fund.
The subfund leverages Taiwan’s strengths and advantages in digital medicine to help other APEC members, and is in line with President William Lai’s (賴清德) Healthy Taiwan vision, Cho said.
Cho asked that all government agencies and ministries work closely with private companies toward furthering the nation’s integrated diplomacy strategy.

Ministry urges Taiwanese to postpone Uganda travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

The government yesterday urged people to consider postponing travel to Uganda after Taiwanese were denied entry or had their passports confiscated by Ugandan immigration officers.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a travel advisory after a Taiwanese family of three, who live in Uganda for work, had their passports confiscated on Wednesday.
Although they were eventually allowed to enter Uganda and had no plan to leave in the short term, Ugandan immigration officials demanded that they submit Chinese passports bearing entry stamps before returning their Taiwanese passports, saying that the measure was part of Uganda’s enforcement of the “one China” policy.
Photo: Taipei Times
The Taiwan Representative Office in the Republic of Somaliland is working closely with the Taiwanese business association in Uganda to provide care and assistance to the family, the ministry said.
That was the latest incident in cases in which Taiwanese have had their passports confiscated by immigration officers at Entebbe International Airport. In one case, the person was deported.
“The Ugandan government has yet to officially announce any change to the visa policy for Taiwan. However, given that several Taiwanese recently encountered difficulties when seeking to enter Uganda, people should consider postponing the trip after cautiously evaluating the necessity and potential risks,” the ministry said.
There are 70 Taiwanese living in Uganda, and there are 35 Taiwanese-funded businesses in the country, it said.
“We express serious concerns over recent cases of Taiwanese being denied or obstructed entry at Ugandan airports. The Ugandan government should recognize that the Republic of China (Taiwan) is a sovereign and independent state, and is not subordinate to China. They should not impose improper entry restrictions on Taiwanese travelers, which would only harm normal exchange and economic benefits of both countries,” the ministry said.
Travel agents said that Taiwanese mainly visit Uganda for business purposes.
Separately, a travel agent advised people planning to visit north Africa to consider traveling to Tunisia instead, as Morocco has stopped issuing visa confirmation letters to Taiwanese tourists since July 20.
The ministry has stopped handling visa applications filed by Moroccans since July 30.
Success Travel general manager Vivian Chang (張雯雯), who also serves as a specialist for tours in Central Asia and Africa, said Morrocco was previously an add-on travel destination when people visited Spain and Portugal, but has over the past few years emerged as a popular destination for tourists seeking an in-depth travel experience.
About 5,000 Taiwanese visited Morocco last year, Chang added.
The unexpected visa policy change has affected 1,000 Taiwanese travelers who were scheduled to travel to the north African nation in the fourth quarter.
“To our knowledge, nothing is likely to change this year,” Chang said. “Some travel agencies allow tour changes under this circumstance, but some costs and fees are non-refundable. Airlines could also give partial refunds.”
“Compared with larger travel agencies, smaller travel agencies are likely to sustain more financial losses,” she added.
Success Travel estimated that only about 5 percent of people scheduled to travel to Morocco would switch to Tunisia instead, Chang said.
The incidents involving Taiwanese tourists in Uganda and Morocco are examples of African nations succumbing to pressure from China and imposing unreasonable requirements on Taiwanese tourists, travel agents said.
Another example is South Africa, which allows other tourists to file visa applications electronically, but requires Taiwanese to apply for visas via their diplomatic offices, they said.
In some countries, Taiwanese are forced to choose “Taiwan, China” as their nationality when filling in application forms, they added.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

Prosecutors yesterday said they have indicted a former Winter Olympian and 13 others for allegedly operating a cross-border heroin trafficking network, seeking sentences ranging from five years to life imprisonment.
The defendants were indicted under the Organized Crime Prevention Act (組織犯罪防制條例) and the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act (毒品危害防制條例), the Yunlin District Prosecutors’ Office said.
The Olympian, a 70-year-old man surnamed Wu (吳), was accused of directing the group’s operation via cellphone while bedridden with a serious illness.
Photo courtesy of the Yunlin District Prosecutors’ Office via CNA
Wu had represented Taiwan at the Winter Olympics in 1984, and has been bedridden over the past few years after undergoing a tracheostomy.
Prosecutors suspect he began the heroin trafficking and sales network last year to cover his medical expenses.
Three members, including a man surnamed Chen (陳), had allegedly traveled to Cambodia and Myanmar to smuggle heroin into Taiwan, but were arrested in January at the airport, they said.
After the arrests, Wu allegedly switched to using international parcels, instructing other members, including a man surnamed Su (蘇), to receive heroin shipments, and repackage them to be sold, prosecutors added.
Authorities arrested all 14 people in a series of operations in May, and seized cash and more than 1.6kg of heroin, prosecutors said.
Investigators alleged that Wu arranged for heroin to be transported into Taiwan four times, totaling more than 2.3kg, the estimated street value of which was more than NT$23 million (US$714,996).
The operation had seriously endangered public health, prosecutors said, asking the court to impose life sentences on Wu and two other defendants — a woman surnamed Tu (杜) and a man surnamed Yang (楊) — citing Wu’s role as the alleged ringleader, and the other two’s denial of the charges and failure to cooperate after being arrested.
Prosecutors are seeking prison terms of at least 15 years for three other defendants and sentences of at least eight years for the seven who confessed to the charges.
Another defendant, surnamed Lee (李), admitted to helping with money transfers and other matters, but denied any involvement in drug trafficking, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors have requested a prison term of at least five years for Lee, citing his lack of cooperation after being detained.

Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan, but cannot placate all his allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:05 UTC
01:38:05 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew skepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.
The Israeli leader is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.
The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up his coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory.
Illustration: Mountain People
US President Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.
With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.
On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.
The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and Israel Defense Force (IDF) Chief of the General Staff Eyal Zamir days earlier, Israeli media reported.
“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defense official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”
The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force — which has yet to be stood up — could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.
Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by US Central Command Admiral Brad Cooper.
He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported.
“The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theaters of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer said.
Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.
However, Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political maneuvering, at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Then-US president Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”
In May 2024, then-US president Joe Biden announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.
The administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes.
Last week, Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorizing attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger.”
Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand.
Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza could have bought him a bit of time, but US patience might not last until polling day in late October.
Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes.
Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper said.
It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by Netanyahu’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident.
“That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said.
The top envoy for the Board of Peace Nickolay Mladenov declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue.”
Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction.
Israeli attacks have continued, killing more than 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure.
The majority of Gaza’s surviving population lives in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished, food shortages are still widespread, with more than 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April next year, food security experts have warned.
Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.

China mourns Zhu while debating his painful reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:03 UTC
01:38:03 KST

The death of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji (朱鎔基) on Wednesday has set off a heated debate on social media over the true costs of his forceful reforms that helped transform the nation into an economic powerhouse, including the tens of millions of people those same policies left behind.
While state media has remembered Zhu as a tough, technocratic leader who pushed through needed changes that paved the way for rapid growth, Chinese social media users have painted a more mixed picture. Commenters have praised his leadership but also lamented the painful effects of his decisions, especially the restructuring of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) that led to mass layoffs across China’s industrial heartlands.
In the late 1990s, Zhu led a sweeping campaign to close or merge thousands of such unprofitable SOEs in nonstrategic sectors. The overhaul boosted productivity, helped clean up the banking system and positioned China to join the WTO in 2001, turbocharging two decades of export-led economic expansion.
Photo: Reuters
However, the social cost was enormous: As many as 40 million workers lost their jobs, and with them the housing and welfare benefits that came with state employment.
“Zhu’s policy drew criticism because he let the society’s most vulnerable groups bear the brunt of SOE reforms,” one user wrote in Chinese on social media platform Threads.
“Without a social safety net in place, this is no different from a warrior cutting off someone else’s arm,” the post added, twisting a famous Chinese metaphor that usually praises a reformer’s willingness to make painful sacrifices.
Such comments underline how the layoffs of that era have left a deep scar in China’s collective memory, even as the country went on to enjoy one of the fastest growth spurts in modern history before slowing in the past few years.
On Sina Weibo, a post that drew hundreds of likes recalled the psychological toll on a generation who grew up in that period.
“I learned the world is gray from a very young age, because I always heard that someone had died after being laid off,” the user wrote. “All the adults were afraid they would be laid off — they always looked worried.”
Other posts highlight what some see as survivor bias in today’s reassessments.
Middle-class Chinese who prospered from housing booms, private business and export manufacturing often praise Zhu as the face of a confident, upwardly mobile China. Those in regions that never found a new growth engine remain embittered, seeing little evidence that the country’s overall prosperity ever truly reached them.
To be sure, Zhu is still widely remembered in China as the symbol of a bygone era with reform being the central theme. Many posts also hail Zhu as a leader who appeared willing to take big risks to reshape the economy.
Even among those directly affected by his reform agenda, views are not uniform. Some laid-off workers and their children now acknowledge that the country’s entry into the WTO under Zhu’s watch ushered in what one Weibo user described online as “a golden era for China,” bringing jobs, rising incomes and unprecedented opportunities for many others.

16:38:03 UTC

The median cost of renting an apartment in Taiwan so far this year was NT$8,600 per month, up by 1.2 percent from September last year, the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday.
The top three most expensive places to rent in Taiwan were New Taipei City at NT$13,000 per month, Taipei at NT$12,500 per month and Taoyuan at NT$10,000 per month, Department of Land Administration head Lin Chia-cheng (林家正) told a news conference in Taipei.
The ministry reports on rent amounts every six months to provide accurate information to young Taiwanese seeking accommodation, a practice that started last year.
Photo: CNA
The cost of rent in Taiwan remained stable, as the median figure was the same or lower in more than 80 percent of administrative districts compared with the figures reported last year, Lin said.
The rent report this year features several refinements, such as breaking down housing options by age, he said.
Rents for units in buildings that were new to five years old, units in buildings that were six to 30 years old and units in buildings more than 30 years old were grouped separately, Lin said.
The report found that the rent for units in new buildings were 20 percent higher than the rent for units in buildings of middling age, which were 10 percent higher than the rent for old buildings, he said.
Apartments in large buildings furnished with elevators cost 20 to 30 percent more than those without, Lin said.
The report groups the rent per ping (3.31m2) of full-floor apartments and apartments that are subdivisions of a floor separately to give potential renters more detailed information, he said.
The report also excludes subletting, as the complex arrangements cannot be quantified accurately, he said.
Department of Statistics head Wu Pei-hsuan (吳佩璇) said the report revealed that more than 50 percent of households eligible for housing subsidies saw a 40 percent average rent reduction.
Economically or socially disadvantaged households could see rents reduced by more than 50 percent, she said.
The biannual report is meant to help young people find reasonably priced units, Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) said.

Contract electronics maker Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶) yesterday said PC shipments are expected to fall by 15 to 17 percent year-on-year in the second half of the year, as rising memory chip prices weigh on consumer demand.
Compal shipped 12.1 million PCs in the first half, down 14.2 percent from the same period last year, company data showed.
Compal expects full-year shipments to decline by a mid-teens percentage from last year’s 28 million units, Compal president Anthony Peter Bonadero told an online earnings conference.
Photo: Fang Wei-chieh, Taipei Times
Despite replacement demand for Windows 10, higher component costs are making enterprise customers and consumers more cautious about spending in the second half, Bonadero said.
Even so, Compal’s PC unit profitability has remained stable, thanks to a higher production share of artificial intelligence (AI) PCs and commercial PCs, increasing selling prices and improving operational efficiency, he said.
AI PCs account for about 50 percent of Compal’s PC shipments and the ratio is expected to rise as the market enters an AI PC refresh cycle, he said.
The firm also expects its server business to remain robust, with server revenue projected to grow by a high-double-digit percentage sequentially this quarter, he said.
Server revenue is on track to account for 10 percent of total revenue this year, he said, adding that AI servers accounted for about 70 percent of Compal’s total server revenue last quarter.
Compal’s AI server portfolio consists mainly of Nvidia Corp’s B300-based systems, most of which have moved into so-called “Level 10” production, Bonadero said.
The company plans to begin producing larger AI server racks in the first quarter of next year, he said.
Server orders last quarter were mainly from new cloud customers, with the momentum expected to continue through the second half, he said.
As new capacity in Taiwan and Texas comes online, Compal plans to diversify its customer base next year to include tier-1 cloud service providers and at least one major enterprise customer, he added.
Compal’s net profit last quarter grew 59 percent quarter-on-quarter and 549 percent year-on-year to NT$3.13 billion (US$97.3 million).
Earnings per share rose to NT$0.73 from NT$0.45 in the previous quarter and NT$0.11 a year earlier.
However, gross margin fell to 4.6 percent from 5.3 percent in the previous quarter due to higher memory prices, while operating margin slipped to 1.2 percent from 1.3 percent, Compal said.
The company said non-PC products accounted for 34 percent of its NT$238.3 billion revenue in the second quarter.
The ratio is projected to rise to 40 percent by the end of this year, it said.
Compal’s capital expenditure in the first half was NT$9 billion, including NT$6 billion to NT$7 billion on server-related investments in Taiwan and the US, while it plans full-year spending of about NT$18 billion, Bonadero said.

Taiwan basketball star Benson Lin Ting-chien (林庭謙) has returned home to join the TPBL’s Taipei Taishin Mars after six seasons in the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA).
At a press conference Thursday to announce his signing, Lin discussed his ambitions after returning to Taiwan.
Photo: Taipei Times
“I’m very excited and happy,” Lin said, adding that he hoped to contribute to Taiwan basketball and that his only goal with the Mars is to win a championship.
Lin’s return is particularly notable given that he is 26 and coming off his most productive CBA season
Taiwanese players from the so-called “golden generation” who returned home after playing in China generally did so later in their careers.
Regarded as one of the top guards on Taiwan’s men’s national team, Lin established himself as one of the country’s most successful players in China’s top professional basketball league.
He delivered the best season of his career in 2025-2026, averaging 19.6 points, 5.2 assists and 1.5 steals per game and earning All-CBA Second Team honors.
Lin will join a Mars team that went 11-25 in the 2025-2026 TPBL regular season, finishing sixth in the seven-team league.
The franchise has yet to win a title since it was established in the summer of 2023. Its best result came in its inaugural 2023-2024 season in the T1 League, when it reached the finals but finished runner-up.
Mars General Manager Chris Lin (林祐廷) said the club had been in contact with Lin since its establishment and held further negotiations during the offseason.
The two sides reached an agreement after finding that they shared the same goal of winning a championship, he said.
The general manager declined to confirm reports that Lin could earn up to NT$60 million (US$2 million) annually, saying only that he had signed a multiyear contract containing an overseas opt-out clause.
The Mars remain open to Lin playing abroad again and will not restrict such opportunities, he added.
“His value cannot be measured in money,” the general manager said. “His willingness to return and contribute to Taiwan basketball is what matters most.”
Returning home will also allow Lin to participate in rural outreach organized by the Lin Cheng-ming Charity Basketball Association, named after his late father, a renowned high school coach who died unexpectedly in July 2024.
For Thursday’s event, Lin wore the suit his father wore when guiding Neng Ren Home Economic and Commercial Vocational High School to its first High School Basketball League championship.
“I believe it brought him good luck, and I hope it will also bring the Taipei Taishin Mars good luck in the new season,” he said.

====================================================================================================

The Jason Arday affair must not spell the end for diversity. Here’s how – and why – we should defend it | Joseph Harker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:37:30 UTC
01:37:30 KST

This has not been a good fortnight for the concept of diversity and inclusion. The fallout from the Jason Arday affair has been an all-out attack, by the rightwing media and political classes, on institutional efforts to reduce inequality.
Arday was the Black academic who, in a fanfare of publicity, had been appointed a professor at Cambridge University in 2023. At the time, British institutions were still struggling to address the widespread issues of systemic racism thrown up by the murder of George Floyd three years earlier.
Last month Arday faced allegations of plagiarism over his PhD thesis, and amid massive scrutiny he resigned last week. Cambridge University has now announced an independent inquiry into its appointment procedures, but many academics already believe that Arday was given the job more for his remarkable backstory than for his academic ability. Arday was, they felt, not at the level you would expect for a professorial chair at such an elite institution. But he was the man who said he couldn’t talk till he was 11, and couldn’t read till he was 18; who had run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last third of them with a leg fracture. What an amazing story. Arday gathered headlines and media appearances. He became a walking advert for how an institution with such a poor record on diversity had progressed so far. Or had it?
I’ve been promoting diversity and inclusion for more than 25 years, and one of the stock responses I often hear is: “I’d love our organisation to be more diverse, but we don’t want to lower standards.” It trips off the tongue so smoothly, always accompanied by an apologetic faux-empathetic shrug.
Yet the response completely misunderstands what diversity and inclusion is about. If it meant lowering standards I’d never waste my time pushing it. Who could possibly believe in making their organisation worse? D&I is not about making a moral point that you believe in equality (though you should); it’s not about performing an act of charity because you feel sorry for poor, excluded minorities (though you might); it’s not even about a business case in the expectation of making more money (though you also might).
The point of D&I is that you bring people into your organisation with different life experiences and perspectives; you value them and listen to them (that’s why it’s called “inclusion”); and the outcome is that you make more informed decisions, so that your organisation better serves its customers. This may or may not translate into profits, but it definitely makes you better, and able to spot changing trends and changing patterns of behaviour more quickly.
Opening up your hiring to more diverse communities leads to more competition and therefore higher standards.
This is also why it’s important to make the distinction between positive action and positive discrimination.
Positive action is inclusive and offers training or short-term experiences to underrepresented groups, helping to level the playing field before they apply for permanent jobs. Positive discrimination (commonly referred to as quotas), excludes people from job applications, reduces the numbers who are able to apply, and therefore lowers standards.
Positive discrimination has always been illegal in the UK; its US equivalent, “affirmative action” was legal but provoked a huge backlash and is now in effect outlawed. Positive discrimination also leads to minorities in any organisation having doubt cast on their position, that somehow they’re second rate, the “diversity hire”.
The backlash over the Arday appointment has cast this shadow once again over a whole swathe of Black academics. Many of them are now furious at what Cambridge did. If the university had wanted to open the door for a Black professor, there are dozens of academics at the right level. The difference is that they wouldn’t have been such a PR hit. The message they’ve taken from Cambridge is that, if you’re Black, you only get a top job if you have a superhuman backstory. Level playing field? Really?
If Cambridge really were an inclusive institution it wouldn’t have been looking for the “quick fix” that the Arday appointment gave it: a superficial symbol that everything here is OK. Instead it would have been examining its recruitment processes, the retention and promotion rates of its minority academics, to see where the problems were and what could be done. Cambridge would ask: how can we identify true potential and what kind of support can we offer people from underrepresented groups to ensure they thrive in the institution? (This applies just as much to women, working-class people and those with disabilities.)
The past 18 months, since Donald Trump regained the US presidency, have seen huge political efforts to turn the clock back on equality and racial justice. Many companies have stood firm; but some have caved in and ditched their policies. The difference is that some understand why diversity and inclusion matters, and some don’t: there is ample evidence that diverse organisations perform better.
So what should be the lesson for progressives who believe in equality? If, after the past few weeks’ headlines, any institution feels under renewed pressure to ditch its diversity policies, the correct response is: “But we don’t want to lower our standards.”
- 
  Joseph Harker is the Guardian’s senior editor, diversity and development

01:31:14 KST

Elon Musk received over 2.5m times as much compensation at Tesla as the company’s average worker, according to a new report on the growing gap between top corporate executives and their workers.
Musk’s $158.3bn pay deal was an outlier but came as the gap between CEO and worker pay continued to grow. Excluding Musk, last year the average ratio of CEO to worker pay for the top S&P 500 companies was 312 to 1, up from a 285:1 ratio in 2024. With Musk, the average pay ratio was 5,387:1, according to the executive pay watch report released this week by the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US.
“In 2025, Elon Musk received the median Tesla worker’s pay every 4.23 seconds – less time than it takes to read this sentence,” states the report. “A majority of S&P 500 CEOs made more in one day than the median US worker made in one year.”
Average CEO pay, excluding Musk, was $22.8m in 2025, up from $18.9m in 2024. With Tesla accounted for, the average increases to $340.1m.
The report notes workers’ share of US national income has fallen to the lowest level since the second world war.
The report also looks at Donald Trump’s income in 2025. At $2.2bn, largely from his crypto holdings, Trump’s income rose nearly 254% from 2024. The median US worker would require 43,154 years to earn what Trump received in 2025.
“This is political grift unlike what we have ever seen in our lifetimes, perhaps ever, but it only tells part of the story of how CEOs and the Trump administration has rigged our economy to enrich themselves at the expense of working people,” said Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO’s secretary-treasurer.
“Trump’s radical budget bill that Republicans rammed through Congress last year, it made drastic cuts to healthcare, food assistance for children and families in order to give massive tax cuts for corporations and the wealthy.”
The report cited data demonstrating the economic struggles of most Americans; 33% of US adults have no retirement savings, 37% of adults do not have enough money to cover a $400 emergency expense, 26% of US adults have skipped medical care due to costs, and 23% of renters in the US have fallen behind on rent over the past year.
Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.
“As President Trump said, he has a lot of assets because he was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming President, which was why he was elected to office in the first place,” said a White House spokesperson in an email. “All of the President’s assets are in held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions. There are no conflicts of interest.”

Vertical Corridor for gas supplies from Greece to Ukraine remains on paper — politician
Unknown

2026-08-13

01:29:35 KST

ATHENS, August 13. /TASS/. The Vertical Corridor for natural gas supplies from Greece to Moldova and Ukraine remains largely on paper, Panagiotis Lafazanis, a Greek politician, former Energy Minister, and leader of the Democratic Movement for National Liberation (DIKEA) party, told TASS.
He noted that, in reality, "the agreement between Greece and the US, which was updated with the participation of other European countries to create a Vertical Corridor consisting of a network of strategic pipelines to deliver American LNG from Revithoussa to Alexandroupolis for regasification, and then to Ukraine via Greece, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, and Moldova, is not working."
"Of course, all of this is still mostly on paper, while major difficulties arise with its practical implementation. These are primarily related to the political and economic pushback from an increasing number of countries, parties, and popular associations dissatisfied with decisions that prolong and exacerbate the war [in Ukraine], are directed against Russia, deepen economic and social problems, and, primarily through expensive LNG, drive prices and the cost of living to even greater heights, further impoverishing society," Lafazanis said.
According to Lafazanis, "starting in early September, the DIKEA party will launch a large-scale initiative aimed at lifting the ban on Russian gas imports to Greece and Europe, fostering major public movements in this direction, and restoring relations of friendship and cooperation between Greece and Russia, as well as between European countries and Russia as a whole."
On January 26, the EU Council finalized a complete ban on Russian LNG supplies to the EU starting January 1, 2027, and on pipeline gas starting September 30, 2027. Meanwhile, the ban on LNG imports under short-term contracts took effect on April 25, 2026, and short-term pipeline gas supply contracts were set to expire by June 17, 2026.
The Vertical Gas Corridor is a project aimed at creating a route for liquefied natural gas supplies from Greece to Central and Eastern European countries, including Ukraine, Hungary, Slovakia, and other countries.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, it was the strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the 21st century. (PAP)

Wanted Polish ex-minister seeks safe conduct from breakaway Transnistria
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
18:29:16 CEST

Wanted Polish ex-minister seeks safe conduct from breakaway Transnistria
Marcin Romanowski, Poland's fugitive former deputy justice minister, has applied to a Warsaw court for a letter of safe conduct sent from Tiraspol in the Moscow-backed breakaway Moldovan region of Transnistria, a court official said on Wednesday.
Judge Anna Ptaszek, spokesperson for criminal cases at the Warsaw District Court, told PAP that the application arrived on August 4. Both the document and its envelope indicate that the mail was dispatched from Tiraspol. The application has been officially registered and the case is currently pending.
Judge Anna Ptaszek, spokesperson for criminal cases at the Warsaw District Court, told PAP that the application arrived on 4 August. Both the document and its envelope indicate that the mail was dispatched from Tiraspol. The application has been officially registered and a randomly selected reporting judge issued a directive on August 7 requesting the prosecution to provide an official stance on the matter and submit the case files.
National Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Przemyslaw Nowak confirmed that investigators have received a copy of the application, which was personally signed by Romanowski. In the document, the fugitive politician provided a specific, exact address within Tiraspol where he is currently residing. He declared that he is fully prepared to appear before the court or the state prosecutor on a designated date, but strictly on the condition that he is allowed to remain at liberty and respond to the charges without being placed in pre-trial detention.
The development presents unprecedented judicial hurdles. When questioned about legal precedents, Judge Ptaszek replied that the Warsaw District Court has no history of legal cooperation with law enforcement agencies in Moldova, and specifically none with the separatist Transnistria region. She added that given the complex political reality of the unrecognised, Russian-supported enclave, it is difficult to predict how local de facto authorities would respond to any formal requests for cooperation or extradition from Poland.
Romanowski faces 11 distinct criminal charges brought by the National Prosecutor's Office relating to his direct oversight of the Justice Fund between 2019 and 2023. He is a key suspect in a high-profile investigation into allegations that the fund, originally established to support crime victims and rehabilitate ex-offenders, was systematically hijacked for political and private gain. Specifically, prosecutors accuse him of participating in an organised criminal group and rigging state funding competitions to illicitly distribute public money.
The Warsaw District Court previously issued a European Arrest Warrant (EAW) and a domestic search warrant for Romanowski after law enforcement agencies failed to locate him. The former official had previously obtained political asylum in Hungary in December 2024. However, following a change of government in Budapest, Hungarian authorities revoked his refugee status and annulled his travel documents in early July, leaving his exact whereabouts unknown until this week.
