TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index continued its gains on Thursday, closing above the 46,000-point mark as trading volume increased.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index (TAIEX) closed up 503.41 points, or 1.11%, at 46,021.48. Turnover totaled NT$1.05 trillion (US$32.7 billion), compared with NT$858.7 billion in the previous session, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Among the index’s most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC closed 0.83% higher at NT$2,435. MediaTek and Delta Electronics recorded notable gains, rising 5.23% and 5.31%, respectively, to NT$4,225 and NT$1,885, according to Anue.
ASE edged up 0.81% to NT$626. In contrast, Foxconn fell 2.96% to NT$262.
Investors returned to passive component stocks following a recent pullback, as the sector remained supported by increased orders for AI servers, high-end industrial equipment, and automotive electronics. Industry leader Yageo, Walsin Technology, Kaimei Electronic, Tai-Tech Advanced Electronics, and Prosperity Dielectrics all reached their daily limits, according to Sinotrade.
Before the market opened, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) announced the results of its quarterly index review. Six Taiwanese stocks were added, which could potentially prompt funds that track MSCI indexes to buy the shares.
Memory chip leaders Nanya Technology, Winbond Electronics, and Phison Electronics were among those added, supporting buying interest in the sector. South Korean manufacturers have also shifted production toward higher-end memory products, reducing supplies of DDR4 products and lifting prices for Taiwanese firms.
Nanya Technology gained 6.53%. Phison rose 3.17%, while Winbond was unchanged.
Silicon wafer and related equipment stocks continued strong gains. GlobalWafers, Wafer Works, Formosa Sumco Technology, and All-Ring Tech all reached their daily price limits.
Silicon wafers form the foundation for chip manufacturing. Analysts estimate that the global silicon wafer supply shortfall could reach 8% by the end of this year, widening to 15% next year and 24% by the end of 2028, according to CTEE.
Information services provider Systex reached its daily limit after Taiwan Mobile announced plans to acquire common shares through a wholly owned subsidiary. Taiwan Mobile is targeting at least a 39% stake, which would bring its total ownership of Systex to more than 50%, according to CTEE.
Bicycle stocks continued their correction as investors took profits at higher price levels in the absence of fresh short-term catalysts. Giant Manufacturing fell 3.67%, while Merida Industry declined 8.36%.
Concord Capital Management senior manager Lu Chin-wei (呂晉維) said concerns over heavy spending by major cloud providers and its impact on cash flow had eased. Strong earnings from US AI companies also supported technology stocks, helping lift Taiwan’s market.
Senior analyst Chien Po-yi (簡伯儀) said turnover had also risen above NT$1 trillion, while the TAIEX remained above all major moving averages, which continued to trend upward in the short term. He expected the market to remain on an upward trend in the near term, according to CTEE.
However, Chien noted that the TAIEX had fallen nearly 9,000 points during its previous downturn before recovering 6,600 points, or more than 70% of the decline. As the index approaches its previous resistance level, the gap between the index and its short-term moving averages has widened, raising the possibility of a period of consolidation.
Market sentiment has recovered, led by passive component stocks and companies with solid second-half fundamentals. Chien said the market could remain on an upward trend as long as the TAIEX stays above its five-day moving average, and recommended optical communications, semiconductor materials and equipment, and passive components.

ROTTERDAM, Netherlands (AP) — An explosion at the Dutch port of Rotterdam on Thursday killed at least one person and injured several others, city police said.
Police said the blast at Europe’s biggest port happened late Thursday morning and that a crime scene has been set up to try to establish what caused it. In a post on social media, they said the explosion “appears to be a workplace accident for the time being,” without elaborating.
At the scene, Rotterdam police spokesperson Daan Valkenburg told The Associated Press that no definitive conclusions had been drawn and that “we are keeping all possibilities open.”
The explosion occurred at a refinery and fuel terminal operated by Gunvor Energy in an industrial section of the sprawling port. Dutch broadcaster NOS said that a maintenance team had been working on a section of pipes there.
Rotterdam’s emergency services coordinator also reported a major power failure in another part of the port and said that a transformer had caught fire under unexplained circumstances. Several companies halted their operations and evacuated workers.
By mid-afternoon, power was fully restored to the area, where a number of oil and gas companies are based. Emergency services later ruled out any link between the blackout and the explosion.

US unemployment claims rise but remain at healthy level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

12:53:02 UTC
21:53:02 KST

US unemployment claims rise but remain at healthy level
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. applications for unemployment benefits rose last week, but layoffs remain at historically healthy levels.
The Labor Department reported Thursday that 209,000 people filed jobless claims last week, up from a revised 200,000 the week before and higher than the 205,000 forecasters had expected. The four-week average of applications, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, was unchanged at 199,000.
The overall number of people collecting employment benefits the week that ended Aug. 1 dropped by 22,000 to 1.78 million.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and they’ve been at a historically low range of around 200,000 to 230,000 a week for the past year, suggesting that Americans who have jobs enjoy unusual job security. The U.S. unemployment rate is low at 4.1%, as the economy has proven resilient despite a spike in energy prices caused by the fighting with Iran.
“The labor market has yet to show any sign of wear and tear from the surge in oil prices since the start of the war with Iran and the global energy supply shock,’' Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics, wrote in a commentary.
The story is less encouraging for those trying to break into the job market and for those who lost their jobs and are looking for new work. Companies, scarred by worker shortages that followed the end of COVID-19 lockups four to five years ago, are reluctant to let go of staff; but they aren’t eager to take on new workers. Economists regularly refer to a “no hire, no fire’’ job market.
Last month, in fact, companies, government agencies and nonprofits together cut 23,000 jobs instead of increasing them, the Labor Department reported last week. So far this year, employers are adding 61,000 jobs a month. That is an improvement on the 9,700 they averaged last year — the weakest hiring outside a recession since 2002. The lingering effects of high interest rates and President Donald Trump’s erratic trade policies discouraged companies from hiring in 2025.
Still, hiring this year remains well below the 166,00 monthly jobs created, on average, in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed pandemic lockdowns.

Wholesale price inflation slows last month as gas, food costs fall

Unknown Publisher

Wholesale price inflation slows last month as gas, food costs fall
WASHINGTON (AP) — Wholesale inflation dropped last month as gas prices reversed some of their Iran war spike and other costs also cooled, a sign that consumer inflation could grind lower in the months ahead.
The Labor Department’s producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — rose 4.7% in July from a year ago, down from a much larger 5.5% increase in June. On a monthly basis, wholesale prices were unchanged from June to July, after they ticked down 0.1% the previous month.
The figures follows the government’s consumer price inflation report, released Wednesday, which also showed a modest cooling last month. Still, consumer prices have risen faster than wages for the past four months, underscoring the challenges many Americans have affording necessities such as rent and utilities. If prices continue to outpace wages, many consumers may be forced to dial back their spending in the coming months.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core wholesale inflation dropped to 4.2% in July compared with a year earlier, down from 4.7% in June. On a monthly basis, core prices 0.2%, down from 0.4% from May to June.
After falling in early July, gas prices then rose later that month and in early August, threatening to push inflation back up when August figures are reported next month.
“The soft (producer prices) reading for July points to reduced inflationary pressure for businesses in coming months,” said Ben Ayers, senior economist at Nationwide. “While the renewed rise in fuel costs is concerning, input costs beyond energy are cooling.”
Last month’s cooling gives Federal Reserve officials more leeway to avoid a rate hike when it meets next in September. Fed officials are debating whether they should raise their key interest rate to combat inflation, or keep it unchanged in hopes that inflation continues to cool on its own.
Wholesale prices can offer an early look at where consumer inflation might be headed. Economists also watch it because some of its components, notably healthcare and financial services, flow into the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge — the personal consumption expenditures, or PCE, index. That price index will be released in about two weeks.
The PCE index uses data from the consumer price index as well. With both those reports now released, economists forecast that when the Fed’s preferred gauge is issued Aug. 26, it will show yearly core inflation likely remained unchanged in July, at about 3.3%, unlike both the consumer and producer price indexes, which have slowed a bit. That could raise concerns among some Fed officials that inflation is too far above the central bank’s target of 2% and showing little sign of easing.
Fed officials are considering whether to hike rates after leaving them unchanged so far this year. Last week, the government said employers actually cut jobs in July, a sign of economic weakness that could discourage the central bank from raising borrowing costs.

Intelligence officials said that Russia is accelerating the creation of an LNG “shadow fleet”
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Intelligence officials said that Russia is accelerating the creation of an LNG “shadow fleet”
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is buying up old LNG carriers and building new ones to circumvent the EU embargo on LNG imports. The fleet has grown to 25 vessels, but experts doubt its effectiveness.
Russia is accelerating the creation of a "shadow fleet" to transport liquefied natural gas, preparing for the European Union's total ban on imports of Russian LNG, which will take effect on January 1, 2027. The Kremlin is buying up old gas carriers on the secondary market and commissioning the first vessels of its own production, UNN reports, citing the Foreign Intelligence Service.
Details
According to intelligence officials, more than 65% of Russia's LNG production comes from Novatek's projects — Yamal LNG and the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 — while another approximately 30% is supplied by Gazprom's Sakhalin-2. China remains the main buyer of Arctic LNG 2 products: according to experts' estimates, the cargoes are transported by 11 vessels with an average age of about ten years.
Unlike the oil "shadow fleet," which numbers more than a thousand vessels, building an LNG equivalent is considerably more difficult because of the high technological complexity of cryogenic gas carriers capable of keeping gas in a liquid state at a temperature of approximately –162 °C. Constructing a modern tanker costs up to $300 million, so Moscow is instead buying vessels more than 19 years old, which global shipping companies are already taking out of service.
EU increases pressure on Russian shadow fleet, tanker detained - Kallas22.07.26, 15:24 • 4662 views
Over the past six months, the fleet has been expanded by at least eight used gas carriers and two new vessels from the Zvezda shipyard in Bolshoy Kamen (Primorsky Krai). Most are registered to Russia-linked companies from Dubai, Hong Kong and Singapore. Overall, in 2026 the number of LNG tankers in the "shadow fleet" grew to 25 vessels — among the identified ships are Kosmos, Orion, Merkuriy, Luch, Arctic Express, Avacha and Chaivo, as well as the new Aleksey Kosygin and Konstantin Posiet.
Intelligence officials add that four more gas carriers are being built at the Zvezda shipyard, but sanctions are hindering the industry's development: six completed Arc7 ice-class gas carriers for the Kremlin's Arctic projects have been blocked at South Korea's Hanwha Ocean.
The "shadow fleet" will allow Russia to mitigate the consequences of the EU ban only partially. A full redirection of supplies to Asia will be hindered by a shortage of suitable vessels, the seasonality of Arctic navigation and a deficit of ice-class gas carriers. After the full embargo is introduced, Novatek risks accumulating unsold products, reducing production or selling LNG at significant discounts — but this will only strengthen the negotiating positions of China and other Asian buyers

SSU Exposed Russian Network That Was Hunting for F-16s and Mirage 2000s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:50:40 UTC
21:50:40 KST

The SSU’s military counterintelligence unit exposed a Russian military intelligence network that was gathering data on aviation infrastructure and F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighter jets.
This was reported on the website of the Security Service of Ukraine.
The network consisted of 14 individuals from various regions of Ukraine. Initially, Russian intelligence recruited a resident of Lviv who administered a Telegram channel about aviation and posted photographs of Ukrainian combat aircraft in pro-Kremlin chat rooms.
To carry out the missions, he enlisted 13 of his subscribers who had high-quality photography equipment and lived near the Defense Forces’ aviation infrastructure.
They photographed Ukrainian airfields, military aircraft, their crews, and technical personnel, and also recorded takeoff and landing times.
To do this, they used professional cameras, hiding in abandoned buildings or in open areas near air bases.
The photographic materials were stored in an online repository, access to which was provided by a resident of Lviv. From there, he forwarded them to his handler in Russia, whose identity the SSU has already established.
In addition, the agent ‘leaked’ flight schedules for combat helicopters to the Russians. This information was provided to him by a commander of a Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation squadron, who acted on his own initiative.
During searches of the suspects’ premises, authorities seized smartphones and digital photography equipment containing evidence of activities on behalf of the enemy, as well as photographs of Defense Forces aviation facilities.
The SSU also blocked four Telegram channels and 10 thematic groups where photographs and other data about the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ aviation units were being disseminated.
Currently, the detained agent, his accomplice, and a military servicemember have been notified that they are suspected of committing crimes against the foundations of national security.
In late July, the SSU reported the detention of FSB agents who attempted to eliminate several dozen Ukrainian servicemembers by organizing a ‘charity’ party for them.

Russia is trying to provoke panic over food shortages, but there is no reason for concern — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
The NSDC’s CPD assures that there will be no food shortages in Ukraine, despite Russia’s attempts to fuel panic. Logistics will be reorganized, and empty shelves are a temporary phenomenon.
Russian propaganda is trying to provoke panic in Ukraine over an alleged shortage of food products. However, there is no reason to panic, as there will be no shortage, UNN reports, citing the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine.
Details
Andriy Kovalenko, head of the CCD, noted that Russia is conducting a systematic campaign aimed at creating a food shortage in Ukraine, while simultaneously fueling panic so that people buy more than usual and the shortage increases.
Are there any reasons to panic? There are none. They are striking at logistics, but logistics is being reorganized. There will be no shortage. Some supermarkets have empty shelves, while others do not. Accordingly, this is a logistical shortage, not a food shortage. The logistical shortage, just as happened with fuel in 2022, will disappear; logistics will be reorganized, and the products will be on the shelves. Everything will be fine
In this situation, Kovalenko noted, it is important to "keep a cool head, since the enemy needs to create the illusion that the situation is out of control and that no one can cope with it."
Do not play this game. You will not be left without buckwheat, pasta, sugar, and so on. The products will be available; they are available. Warehouses are being dispersed to a certain extent, and certain non-public measures are also being taken so that logistics operates normally
Recall
Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Center for Countering Disinformation, stated that the temporary absence of goods in certain stores does not indicate a shortage.

Mecca Agreement does not set common enemy, aimed at cooperation, Turkey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:47:53 UTC
21:47:53 KST

ISTANBUL, August 13. /TASS/. The Mecca Agreement on Joint Defense between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan does not envision any single country as a common enemy - it is aimed at promoting regional security and stability, Turkish Defense Ministry official said.
"The goal is to create a more institutional and sustainable structure for the existing friendly and fraternal relations between our three countries in the field of defense and security. The main purpose of the agreement is to promote regional security and stability, develop military cooperation between our countries and strengthen our ability to work together against potential crises. This agreement is signed for defense purposes and does not define any countries as a common enemy or adversary," the official told reporters.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Agreement on August 7. It says that an attack on one of the countries will be regarded as aggression against all parties to the agreement.
The agreement provides for the creation of "strategic political and military mechanisms" with the participation of the defense and foreign ministers, chiefs of general staffs/army commanders, as well as coordination of actions between the three countries at the highest level. It also implies a phased development of military cooperation, including joint command and staff exercises and maneuvers involving the ground forces, Navy, air force and air defense. Another area of cooperation is the military industry.
"The goal is not only to supply military products and systems, but also to jointly develop and manufacture them, as well as to cooperate technologically," the Turkish Defense Ministry official said. "Cooperation in matters related to the development of unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare systems supported by artificial intelligence will be promising in this regard."
The official said that the Mecca Agreement "is not an alternative or competing structure to NATO. It is assessed as a mechanism that complements the international security architecture and contributes to the regional security and stability. As the mechanism develops, the participation of other countries in it may be considered if the necessary consensus is found."

EU experts on the ground in Ceuta amid fears of fresh migrant influx
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:47:31 UTC
21:47:31 KST

A team of EU migration experts is in Ceuta for a “first-hand assessment” of the situation, as reports warn of a potential new migrant influx on 15 August. Brussels, however, says its focus remains on protecting the EU’s external border at all times, rather than on any “specific date”.
The European Commission has deployed a team of migration experts to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, two weeks after around 80,000 migrants crossed into the territory from Morocco triggering an unprecedented humanitarian and political crisis, and amid reports that further large-scale attempts to cross into the enclave could be imminent.
Speaking on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Commission said the mission was intended to “understand the first-hand needs on the ground” and how the EU can bolster its support for the Spanish authorities.
Yet, the executive declined to say whether the visit would also cover preparations for a potential fresh influx, amid reports that a “forward call” is circulating on Moroccan social media urging migrants to make the journey again on the night of 14-15 August.
“For us it's not about a specific date. It's about reinforcing our borders and ensuring returns every day of the year,” another European Commission spokesperson said.
As many as 80,000 migrants are estimated to have entered Ceuta – the Spanish enclave home to just 83,000 people – by swimming across from neighbouring Morocco during the last two days of July, with around 100 people reported to have lost their lives.
The Spanish government says around 70,000 have since been returned to Morocco, and has hailed productive cooperation on returns with the government in Rabat.
The incident also triggered an unprecedented crisis for Madrid and exposed deep rifts between European nations.
Governments, notably Giorgia Meloni’s in Italy, found in the Ceuta crisis an opportunity to denounce Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s more lenient, more tolerant migration policies which, according to critics, undermined EU efforts to project solidarity and unity.
The tit-for-tat escalation between Rome and Madrid continues, with both sides now imposing exceptional border controls on each other. The Italian government has said it will continue to temporarily suspend the border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain until at least 15 August, citing expectations that Ceuta will be hit by a "new wave of migration".
EU cooperation with online platforms ‘bearing fruit’
The Moroccan Interior Ministry said Wednesday it was working to prevent a potential fresh wave and had increased security along its borders with both Ceuta and Melilla, the second of the Spanish territories located along Morocco’s northern coast.
The Spanish Civil Guard has already installed a maritime barrier, similar to that used along the sea border with Morocco off the coast of Ceuta, at Melilla’s southern breakwater.
The precautionary measures are in response to several reports that a coordinated online campaign is disseminating a call for another mass crossing on Friday evening.
Golden Owl, a digital intelligence company linked to the University of Alicante, has scoured social media platforms and identified an organised online operation behind the calls for further crossings. Spain's Civil Guard has also produced a six-page report examining the possibility.
The increased vigilance of social platforms is believed to have somewhat suppressed the call, with Golden Owl saying that the “15 August date has effectively disappeared from Facebook, driven by Meta enforcement”.
Both TikTok and Meta have activated a crisis protocol to set up a cooperation mechanism with fact-checkers, following calls by the EU’s tech chief, Henna Virkkunen, for enhanced monitoring and collaboration.
The European Commission confirmed that it would meet again with representatives from social media platforms on Thursday afternoon, adding that it was engaging with the platforms on a “daily basis” to streamline the work.
“Bringing in the fact-checkers will, in our view, make this work even more targeted and even more streamlined and coordinated in the context of this concrete crisis,” the spokesperson explained. “And what we hear is that this cooperation is proving highly effective and action is being taken by the platforms on this basis.”
The Commission also held a separate meeting earlier on Thursday that allowed an "exchange of information and discussion on the online dimension of the current crisis in Ceuta", with Spanish representatives also taking part.

This means that the IDF is willing to attack terrorists to thwart their attacks before it is too late.
Unlike the West Bank, where the military and Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency) tend to arrest these parties, the IDF cannot do so in Gaza. It cannot go in and out of areas controlled by Hamas in Gaza, meaning that airstrikes are still its preferred tool.
IDF strikes Hamas terrorists in Gaza Strip as BoP deals stalls
Currently, the IDF continues to eliminate Hamas fighters who approach the Yellow Line dividing the Israeli-controlled portion of Gaza from the Hamas-controlled section.
The IDF rejects allegations that it is holding its soldiers back from defending themselves. Although not explicit, the implication has been that the US is on board with the IDF’s current approach until Hamas starts to disarm. Hamas has yet to even begin the disarmament process.
On Wednesday, the IDF undertook its first preemptive strike against a Hamas official since the late July deal. Shortly after that deal, the US essentially instructed Israel to stop attacking Gaza; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu complied.
Since then, there had been a limited number of instances where the IDF killed Hamas fighters near the border when they presented an immediate threat. Wednesday’s airstrike was the first to break that trend. It was against a Hamas terror cell commander in northern Gaza, who was nowhere near the border and did not pose an imminent threat.
The IDF said he was killed because he was planning to order or carry out future terrorist attacks. The United States did not condemn the attack.
The late July deal was supposed to lead to Hamas beginning the process of handing over its weapons. Israel’s airstrike was, in a sense, a reminder of that deal. The US, for its part, looked the other way to remind Hamas that it could easily remove its restraint on Israel.
It is also possible that the cabinet and the IDF ordered the airstrike in response to Hamas’s recent planning of a potential large-scale military drill. Notably, Israeli officials received public criticism for not firing on Hamas.
Earlier on Wednesday, the IDF issued a statement noting that while the Hamas drill never took place, an airstrike signaled that Israel would not approve it.

Satellite images confirm damage to two Russian missile frigates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:46:26 UTC
21:46:26 KST

- Satellite imagery released by Vantor on August 12 shows fire damage near the Kalibr missile launchers of Russian frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov at Novorossiysk.
- Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the strike damaged four Russian warships overnight on August 12, describing its assessment of the damage as preliminary.
New satellite imagery released by Vantor on August 12 shows visible fire damage on two Russian frigates at the Kalibr cruise missile launchers, the clearest independent look yet at the aftermath of Ukraine’s overnight strike on the naval base at Novorossiysk.
The imagery covers the Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov, both Project 11356R frigates that serve as key Kalibr missile carriers for Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. Each vessel carries an eight-cell vertical launch system for the missiles, which Russia has used repeatedly to strike targets across Ukraine. Journalist Jake Epstein published the Vantor images on X, noting that both frigates appear to have their forward missile banks affected by strikes and fires, though he did not characterize the vessels as sunk or confirm the ships are permanently disabled.
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the previous day that Defense Forces struck four Russian warships at Novorossiysk overnight on August 12, identifying the vessels as Admiral Essen, Admiral Makarov, the Project 21631 small missile ship Buyan-M, and the Project 22160 patrol ship Vasily Bykov. The General Staff described its assessment as preliminary and said the extent of damage was still being determined, a caveat that Wednesday’s satellite imagery has not fully resolved.
The Ukrainian OSINT group Exilenova+ had separately assessed the same general area of damage before the Vantor imagery circulated, identifying strikes near Admiral Makarov’s Kalibr launchers and its rear superstructure, where the ship’s radar systems are mounted, and a similar pattern of launcher-area damage on Admiral Essen. The group’s assessment, along with the newer Vantor imagery, converges on the same conclusion: the visible damage clusters specifically around each frigate’s missile launch cells rather than across the hull broadly.
What the imagery does not establish is how severe that damage actually is. The images show what several analysts have described as a short-duration fire near the launchers, consistent with a drone strike rather than a larger explosive impact, but the underlying condition of the launch tubes, missile inventory, and adjacent electronics cannot be determined from satellite photography alone. A brief fire at a missile launcher does not by itself indicate whether the vertical launch cells were destroyed, disabled, or left functional beneath visible scorching, and it remains possible the ships sustained secondary damage from fragments thrown by the initial detonation.
Repair timelines for damage of this kind are difficult to predict from imagery. Modern warship missile systems integrate dense electronics, wiring and sensor equipment around the launch cells, and even limited fire damage in that area can require extensive diagnostic work before a shipyard can determine what needs replacing. Neither the Russian Ministry of Defense nor Russian state media had issued a public damage assessment for either frigate as of Wednesday.
The strike fits a documented pattern for both ships. Ukrainian forces have previously claimed to have hit the Admiral Essen on March 2, 2026, and the Admiral Makarov on March 6, 2026, according to reporting from the Maritime Executive, though neither of those earlier claimed strikes was confirmed to have caused damage comparable to what Wednesday’s imagery shows. Novorossiysk became the Black Sea Fleet’s primary operating base after Russia relocated much of the fleet there in response to repeated Ukrainian strikes on facilities in Russian-occupied Crimea, a shift that has not insulated the fleet from continued Ukrainian reach.
Beyond the two frigates, Wednesday’s broader satellite coverage and OSINT analysis pointed to damage across Novorossiysk’s port and Black Sea Fleet infrastructure. NOELreports, an open-source analyst who reviewed the Vantor imagery, identified additional damage at the naval base extending to a Krivak-class frigate and other vessels, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday that Kyiv used a combination of long-range drones and other weapons in what he called a successful operation against Russian fleet vessels in the bay. Zelensky’s account listed a large landing ship and a corvette among the vessels struck, in addition to the two Grigorovich-class frigates.

Selçuk Bayraktar (L) poses with students during a Teknofest event.
Top executives from Turkish defense contractor Baykar and veteran industrialist Mustafa Rahmi Koç emerged as Türkiye’s highest individual taxpayers for the 2025 tax year, official revenue data showed on Aug. 13.
According to figures released by Türkiye’s Revenue Administration following an evaluation of 2025 income and corporate tax declarations, Baykar Chairman Selçuk Bayraktar claimed the top position on the nationwide individual taxpayer list, declaring 2.99 billion Turkish liras ($62.6 million) in income tax.
He was followed in second place by his brother, Baykar Chief Executive Officer Haluk Bayraktar, who declared 2.50 billion liras ($52.4 million). Together, the two defense executives generated a combined individual income tax liability of 5.49 billion liras ($115 million).
Mustafa Rahmi Koç, honorary chairman of major industrial conglomerate Koç Holding, ranked as Türkiye’s third-highest individual taxpayer.
State-run lender Ziraat Bank topped Türkiye’s corporate tax rankings, reporting a high of 70.39 billion liras ($1.47 billion) in tax liability for the 2025 tax period.
The individual tax success of Selçuk and Haluk Bayraktar marks their fifth consecutive year at the peak of Türkiye’s top 100 individual taxpayer list, spanning from 2021 through 2025.

‘Funny Games,’ ‘The Piano Teacher’ and More: Michael Haneke Retrospective in Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:45:47 UTC
21:45:47 KST

From Aug. 15 to 23 in Kyiv, at the Zhovten cinema, a retrospective of prominent European director Michael Haneke’s films titled VIDEO will take place – a series of screenings of the Austrian filmmaker’s key works.
The program includes the scandalous “Funny Games,” and Cannes Film Festival Grand Prix and “Palme d’Or” winners – “The Piano Teacher,” “The White Ribbon” and “Amour.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The films will be screened in their original language (German, French) with Ukrainian subtitles.
The main theme of the retrospective, according to the organizers, is embedded in the title VIDEO, which literally means “I see.”
Haneke, one of the most prominent European directors of recent decades, worked on the edge of shock and deep drama, revealing the nature of audience complicity in the events on screen. His films are permeated with reflections on the essence of violence, the crisis of the Western worldview, human alienation and isolation from the outside world.
Haneke’s cinema does not allow one to remain a neutral observer, so his works have always been at the center of attention at leading European film festivals.
Film Screening Program Schedule
August 15, 18:00
Funny Games (1997) – retrospective opening film
                                                                                                                                                                         
GANNA: ‘I Want Ukrainian Folk Music to Be Heard for Its Beauty, Not Because of War’
A film-scandal, during the premiere of which at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, a third of the audience left the session. “Funny Games” seemed so cruel to the public that the director was even accused of sadism. Critics argued that it is impossible to criticize the exploitation of violence on screen with the “most violent film of the decade.” At the same time, it was this film that gained cult status and prompted the public to reflect on what changes are happening in cinema and mass culture with the tacit consent of the viewer.
August 16, 18:00 and August 21, 19:00
Benny’s Video (1992)
One of Haneke’s first films, which brought him recognition in Europe and outlined the main themes that the director would return to in his subsequent work. The film tells a story of a teenager’s morbid fascination with violence captured on a video camera. Without taking his eyes off the lens, the boy gradually leans towards a crime that he seeks to “shoot” on video.
August 19, 18:30
The Piano Teacher (2001)
                                                                                                                                                                         
“The Piano Teacher” is the winner of the Grand Prix of the 2001 Cannes Film Festival and the winner in three main categories (best director, best actress and actor). This adaptation of the novel of the same name, by Nobel laureate in literature Elfriede Jelinek, centers on a Vienna Conservatory teacher (Isabelle Huppert), who develops a deviant relationship with her student, which destroys the established order of her life and reveals its “dark” side.
August 18, 18:00 and August 20, 18:00
The White Ribbon (2009)
                                                                                                                                                                         
Winner of the 2009 Cannes Film Festival “Palme d’Or,” “The White Ribbon” tells the story of a village teacher who finds himself in the midst of strange events on the eve of World War I. However, the secrets of the small village turn out to be not what they seem.
“The White Ribbon” is considered one of the most important in the director’s career, exploring the nature of 20th-century catastrophes and the origins of human inability to resist true evil.
August 18, 18:00 and August 22, 19:00
Amour (2012)
The victory of “Amour” at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival made Haneke only the sixth director in history to become a two-time winner of the “Palme d’Or.” “Amour” tells the story of an elderly woman’s sudden severe illness and her husband’s helplessness in the face of the inevitable.
August 23, 18:00 Happy End (2017)
The director’s farewell film, “Happy End” is a kind of crossover that combined all the key themes of his work into a bizarre canvas about a wealthy bourgeois family whose members have neither love nor a sense of community. Only a desire to end their own lives as quickly as possible.
In addition, on Aug. 21 at 11:00, within the framework of the retrospective, an open talk with philosopher Oleksandr Filonenko will take place, focusing on the specifics of film viewing and the nature of violence. Admission is free.
The general partners of the retrospective are Visa and Raiffeisen Bank. The project is also supported by the Austrian Embassy in Ukraine and is being implemented in partnership with the Zhovten cinema. The screenings will be accompanied by short introductory speeches before the films by the organizers of the retrospective – the KRAY project. This is an independent research film project founded in 2023. The project works with auteur cinema through public screenings in Kyiv and Kharkiv, discussions, reviews, and translations.
After each screening, there will be a discussion of the film with speakers, as well as an opportunity for the audience to share their impressions of what they have seen.
Full information about the event is available on the website, Telegram, and Instagram.

Global electric vehicle sales rose in July due to surging demand in Europe
Kyiv • UNN
Global electric vehicle sales rose by 9% to 1.85 million in July, while demand in Europe increased by 33%. In China and North America, sales fell by 5% and 27%, respectively.
Global demand for electric vehicles rose for the fifth consecutive month in July, driven by a sharp increase in sales in Europe, while sales in China and North America declined, according to data from consultancy Benchmark Mineral Intelligence released on Thursday. Reuters reports, writes UNN.
Details
Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids rose 9% year-on-year to 1.85 million vehicles in July. A total of 11.5 million such vehicles have been sold since the beginning of the year.
These figures demonstrate the growing divergence between the major electric vehicle markets. In Europe, demand is being supported by subsidies, while the U.S. market has been affected by the cancellation of federal tax credits for electric vehicles, and Chinese automakers are increasingly relying on exports to drive growth.
Sales in Europe rose 33% to 450,000 vehicles, with growth since the beginning of the year reaching 28%.
High growth rates persisted in Europe's largest automotive markets, many of which have reinstated electric vehicle subsidy programs over the past 18 months
In July, electric vehicle sales in France, Germany and the United Kingdom rose by 81%, 46% and 43%, respectively.
Meanwhile, sales in China fell 5% to 980,000 vehicles.
In North America, sales fell 27% to 140,000 vehicles after electric vehicle tax credits in the United States expired.
Sales in the rest of the world rose 97% to 280,000 vehicles.

Eesti Pank to issue Hiiumaa‑themed €2 coin
Eesti Pank will issue a special‑design €2 coin honoring Hiiumaa in 2027, featuring the island's Kõpu Lighthouse.
The central motif of the coin is Hiiumaa's landmark, the Kõpu Lighthouse, surrounded by sea waves, with the light beams reflecting the striped pattern of Hiiumaa's traditional folk skirt. This pattern is an important part of the island's identity, symbolizing continuity and resilience, and representing the security of the home island.
The design is by Kaupo Kangro.
The Kõpu Lighthouse was completed in its original form in 1531 and is the third‑oldest operating lighthouse in the world.
One million coins dedicated to Hiiumaa will be minted and released into circulation through retail channels. The coin will be valid as official legal tender throughout the euro area.
Hiiumaa, known for its distinctive nature and long maritime history, will open Eesti Pank's new coin series dedicated to Estonia's counties. The aim of the series is to highlight the diversity and cultural uniqueness of Estonia's regions.
Image of the coin design was updated on 14 August.

Turkiye lays out ‘mechanisms’ of defence pact with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
Unknown

Turkiye lays out ‘mechanisms’ of defence pact with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
Three nations to group ministers, hold joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation under the pact signed last week.
Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will group senior ministers, hold joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation under a military pact signed between the regional powers last week, Turkiye’s defence ministry says.
The three countries on August 7 signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, which stipulates that an armed attack against any member would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO’s Article 5 collective defence clause.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What are Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan’s joint military capabilities?
- list 2 of 4Where does Iran stand on Saudi-Pakistan-Turkiye pact?
- list 3 of 4Which other countries could join the Turkiye-Saudi-Pakistan defence pact?
- list 4 of 4The Mecca pact is not just another regional alliance
At a weekly briefing in Ankara on Thursday, the Turkish defence ministry said the pact’s fundamental goal was to ensure defence and military ties were put on a “more institutional and sustainable” footing.
“Under the accord, strategic political and military mechanisms plan to be established involving the Defence Ministers, Foreign Ministers, and Chiefs of General Staff/Armed Forces Commanders, and that coordination among the three countries will be conducted at the highest level,” it said.
The ministry added that joint military exercises involving land, naval and air forces, as well as air defence and unmanned systems were planned, in addition to deeper defence industry cooperation.
“The aim is to provide not only product and system supply, but also joint development and production, technology cooperation, and sustainable maintenance and logistics support,” it said, adding that unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence capabilities would be prioritised.
Turkiye, which has NATO’s second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion — with Egypt as a potential candidate — and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
The ministry also said Turkiye was participating in meetings in Jeddah aimed at establishing an international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping.
On developments in the Middle East, ministry spokesperson Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said lasting peace and stability in the region would be possible if Israel ends its occupation and attacks in Gaza and Lebanon.
He said Israel continues attacks that have deepened the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, as also reflected in United Nations reports.
“Israel’s rejection of the 15-point Gaza Plan has been another indication that it is pursuing a policy of regional expansionism. On the other hand, despite the framework agreement that was signed, Israel similarly continues its attacks and military activities in southern Lebanon,” Akturk said, referring to the plan proposed by the United States.

Egypt denies link to ship targeted off Yemen, condemns Red Sea attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:42:10 UTC
21:42:10 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Lina Altawell
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
Egypt denied Thursday any link to a ship targeted off Yemen earlier this week, while condemning attacks on ships and maritime navigation in the Red Sea.
The Transport Ministry said reports linking the targeted vessel to Egypt or its ports were false.
The denial came after media outlets and social media platforms reported that Yemen’s Houthi group had targeted a ship off the Yemeni coast and that the operating company’s address was in Alexandria, northern Egypt.
“The vessel was flying the Tanzanian flag, owned by a Yemeni national and operated by a company based in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates,” the ministry said.
It added that the ship was not registered with Egyptian shipping chambers and had not received a license to conduct maritime agency work through Egypt’s maritime transport and logistics sector.
“The ship had never entered Egyptian ports, was not heading to Egypt and did not carry any cargo belonging to Egyptians,” the ministry said.
Separately, Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said Cairo “condemns the targeting of ships in the Red Sea.”
It cited a Yemeni commercial ship flying the Tanzanian flag that was attacked Tuesday with missiles while sailing off Yemen’s coast south of Mokha port in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as a Saudi oil tanker targeted on July 25.
“Such attacks represent a serious threat to the security and safety of navigation in the Red Sea,” the ministry said, adding that it is one of the world’s most important international waterways.
Egypt renewed its “categorical rejection of all acts targeting ships and civilian facilities or threatening the security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and international waterways.”
Attacks in the Red Sea often reduce traffic through Egypt’s Suez Canal, causing financial losses for Cairo as ships divert to alternative routes to avoid security risks.
Last week, two ships caught fire at Egypt’s northern Damietta port after being targeted by a drone in an attack not claimed by any party. Cairo is still investigating the incident.
Since July 20, tensions have escalated in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden after the Houthis announced a “naval blockade” on ships linked to Saudi Arabia.
Three days later, Riyadh said one of its ships had come under attack and, the following day, carried out strikes on Houthi sites in Yemen’s western Hudaydah province, saying they were used to threaten maritime navigation.
Saudi Arabia also announced the formation of a defensive naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including the US, Yemen, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan, Sudan, Morocco, the Maldives, Bangladesh and New Zealand.
Since 2015, Saudi Arabia has led a coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government, while Iran is accused of supporting the Houthis, who have controlled provinces and cities, including the capital Sanaa, since 2014.

Anti-Israel progressives benefit from lack of pushback in primaries - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:41:28 UTC
21:41:28 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- Anti-Israel progressives benefit from lack of pushback in primaries - analysis
Anti-Israel progressives benefit from lack of pushback in primaries - analysis
The exception to Tuesday’s not-good-at-all results for Israel supporters was in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, where democratic-socialist Francesca Hong lost to David Crowley
One of the biggest lessons from Tuesday’s Democratic primaries is that when the old guard pushes back on the far left, or at least declines to get behind it, there’s still a chance of victory.
Another is that it's one thing to be anti-Israel. It's another to completely go off the deep end.
In a critical Senate primary in Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan whipped centrist Rep. Angie Craig.
Flanagan has accused Israel of “genocide” and asserted that she would have voted to cut off military aid to the Jewish state.
Meanwhile, Craig was among the fewer than half of House Democrats who voted to oppose severing defense aid, and Flanagan hit Craig on the latter’s support for Israel and previous endorsements from AIPAC, even as the pro-Israel group did not endorse her or directly contribute to her campaign this time around.
Suggested articles
- Hey Israel, don't be so sure about your support among Republicans | India Naftali
- Michigan: Anti-Israel candidate Abdul El-Sayed win the Senate Democratic primary | i24NEWS
- House Democrats split over Massie amendment to cut Israel aid | i24NEWS, Henry Kirshner
Flanagan moves on to face former national sportscaster Michele Tafoya, who easily won the Republican nomination. But even with high name recognition, Tafoya, who is making her entry into politics, faces an uphill climb given Minnesota's blue bent.
Craig’s struggles were reflected in her own district. Former state Sen. Matt Little, who ran furthest to the left and the harshest on Israel, handily defeated a pair of centrists for the Democratic nomination for that House seat.
Among those moderates was state Sen. Matt Klein, an advocate for Israel.
Little is favored to win against Republican nominee Eric Pratt, a state senator, in a relatively moderate district that Kamala Harris carried by only six points in the 2024 presidential election.
AIPAC-endorsed Rep. John Larson lost his reelection bid in a Connecticut House race, falling heavily to former Hartford mayor Luke Bronin. Larson, who has struggled with health issues, will see his 14-term House career in the state’s most populous Jewish district come to an end.
Larson, like Craig, had voted against the majority of House Democrats on the Israel aid issue, and AIPAC raised some $130,000 to try to extend his term.
Bronin, meanwhile, said he’ll oppose offensive weapons for Jerusalem, while keeping Iron Dome support intact.
The exception to Tuesday’s not-good-at-all results for Israel supports was in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, where State Assembly member Francesca Hong, aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, fell to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in the Democratic primary.
Hong, though, didn’t just take on the establishment on Israel, but on everything, essentially running on a DSA platform, including defunding the police and even canceling Thanksgiving.
Polls showed her leading, but outcry from Democratic officials, including sitting Gov. Tony Evers, appeared to bring attention to her extreme positions, potentially saving the race for Crowley and for Democrats intent on hanging on to the governor’s seat.
Even progressive stalwarts like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez didn’t speak out on Hong’s behalf.
It brought into stark contrast the way Michigan officials handled the Senate race there, where earlier this month, anti-Israel radical Abdul El-Sayed defeated Israel-backer Rep. Haley Stevens, in what many view as a national bellwether.
Few officials there went to bat for Haley, and even those that did were loath to criticize El-Sayed. Their prescience, or reckoning, will come in November, when El-Sayed faces former Rep. Mike Rogers, in a state where a Republican hasn’t claimed a Senate seat in 32 years.

Minister Talvitie to meet EU ministers of culture in Oulu

Minister Talvitie to meet EU ministers of culture in Oulu
Minister of Science and Culture Mari-Leena Talvitie has invited EU Member States to an informal meeting of culture ministers in Oulu on 14–15 August 2026. The invitation has also been extended to Ukraine, providing an opportunity for dialogue on all-important cooperation in the cultural sector. The meeting is being held to celebrate Oulu’s year as European Capital of Culture 2026.
The main theme of the meeting is how to protect artistic freedom and cultural rights in the age of artificial intelligence. Countries taking part will have the opportunity to share their experiences of effective cultural policy measures. The informal meeting will be attended by representatives from 15 countries, including Ukraine’s Deputy Minister of Culture, along with the European Commission.
As part of the parallel programme, the participants will visit AaltoSiilo, a concrete industrial building designed by Alvar and Aino Aalto. The repurposing of AaltoSiilo is a key legacy project of Oulu2026 and part of the European Commission’s New European Bauhaus (NEB) initiative. The participants will also be introduced to other important Capital of Culture sites, including Central Library Saari and Children’s Cultural Centre Kotilo. In addition, they will learn about the local food culture at Kesäillan kattaus, a communal food event.
“Culture is everything that brings us together and makes our communities stronger. This idea is directly linked to the original aim of the European Capitals of Culture initiative: to promote mutual understanding among Europeans and celebrate the cultural features we share. I am delighted that we can be part of Kesäillan kattaus – a kilometre-long dining table that is one of the highlights of the Oulu2026 year,” says Minister Talvitie.
Ukraine will have a strong presence throughout the weekend. On Friday, Minister Talvitie will open an exhibition celebrating the twin town relationship between Oulu and Odesa. The exhibition is organised by the City of Oulu and the Embassy of Ukraine in Helsinki. During the weekend, the Minister will also hold bilateral talks with Ukraine’s Deputy Minister of Culture Tetyana Filevska. At their meeting, the ministers will discuss Finland’s efforts to help Ukraine safeguard its cultural heritage and support the cultural sector.
The City of Oulu and the Oulu Cultural Foundation are involved in arranging the meeting.

With half of FIFA confederations revolting, can Infantino survive?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:39:17 UTC
21:39:17 KST

- Former FIFA governance chief Mark Pieth calls situation ‘very serious,’ says Infantino has ‘lost the support of Asia’
- FIFA governance commentator Herve Verhoosel says surviving a vote, retaining political authority to lead ‘are not the same thing’
The revolt against FIFA President Gianni Infantino by half of the world’s football confederations is widening, raising questions about whether he can secure enough votes to win another term.
UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf sharply escalated their confrontation with FIFA on Monday, accusing its leadership of a “fundamental breach of trust” and “deception” over the handling of an abandoned proposal to sell a stake in the FIFA World Cup to private investors.
In their joint statement, the confederations rejected the suggestion that the controversy amounted merely to a communications or procedural failure, arguing instead that the attempt represented a serious failure of judgment. They also called for an independent review.
The confrontation comes at a sensitive moment for Infantino, who announced in May that he would seek another term in 2027.
FIFA’s electoral arithmetic may still favor a president capable of building support association by association. Each of its 211 member associations has one vote, meaning opposition from confederation leaders does not automatically translate into votes against Infantino.
Votes versus political authority
Herve Verhoosel, a former senior UN official who now writes and comments on FIFA governance, told Anadolu in a written statement that the political calculation behind those votes has changed.
Once a confederation has publicly declared a “fundamental breach of trust” with FIFA’s leadership, he said, "it becomes considerably more difficult for its individual associations, particularly smaller ones, simply to take the opposite position."
“They still have their vote. But the political cost of that vote has changed,” Verhoosel said.
For Verhoosel, the larger question is no longer simply whether Infantino can assemble enough individual votes to remain in power, but whether he would retain sufficient authority to govern an increasingly divided organization.
“A president may still be able to assemble enough individual votes to survive. But surviving a vote and retaining the political authority to lead are not the same thing,” he said.
If a substantial part of FIFA no longer trusts its leadership, Verhoosel argued, "every major decision risks becoming another confrontation, every vote another test of loyalty and every initiative another battle between blocs."
“That is not sustainable -- and, more importantly, it is not in the interests of world football,” he said.
Verhoosel said the question facing FIFA’s 211 associations could therefore become larger than whether they support or oppose Infantino.
He added that the associations may ultimately have to consider whether maintaining the status quo is still in FIFA’s best interests.
 
Infantino made 'mistakes,' acted 'disrespectfully'
Mark Pieth, former chair of FIFA’s Independent Governance Committee, told Anadolu in a written statement that the situation is “very serious.”
“Of course he can try to survive with individual votes from Associations, but he has made mistakes; just look at Jordan,” Pieth said.
Pieth was referring to a recent dispute involving Jordan Football Association President Prince Ali bin Al Hussein, a former FIFA vice president.
Prince Ali accused FIFA and Infantino of “blackmail” last week, saying Jordan had faced unresolved issues including World Cup-related costs and unpaid Arab Cup prize money. He alleged that he was verbally told during the World Cup that endorsing Infantino would “go a long way” toward helping the Jordanian association.
Jordan, which qualified for its first World Cup in 2026, had not previously endorsed Infantino, and Prince Ali said it would not do so.
Two days after Prince Ali made the allegation, he said FIFA had paid the outstanding prize money to Jordan’s players and coaching staff. He welcomed the payment but said it did not change his concerns about FIFA’s leadership or his position that Jordan would neither endorse nor vote for Infantino.
FIFA did not publicly comment on the blackmail allegation.
Pieth said Infantino had “acted disrespectfully, including to many non-European associations.”
“This is one reason why he has lost the support of Asia,” he added.
The AFC’s role in the current confrontation is particularly notable because the Asian confederation had backed Infantino’s bid when he announced his intention to seek re-election earlier this year.
The three confederations -- out of a total of six -- are now challenging FIFA. But Infantino’s political fate ultimately rests with national associations voting individually rather than confederations voting as blocs.
That leaves him room to rebuild alliances before the 2027 election, but in a political landscape that has shifted considerably in a matter of months.
With the nomination deadline for the 2027 FIFA presidential election approaching in November, the question is therefore not only whether Infantino can assemble the votes for another term, but whether a president facing open resistance from half of FIFA’s continental confederations can retain the trust and political authority needed to govern world football.

South Korea's Incheon becomes world's busiest airport for international passengers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:38:09 UTC
21:38:09 KST

Faisal Mahmud
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
South Korea's Incheon International Airport ranked first globally for international passenger traffic in the first half of 2026, claiming the top spot for the first time since opening in 2001.
The airport handled 38.39 million international passengers between January and June, up 6.3% from the same period last year, Yonhap News Agency reported Thursday, citing Incheon International Airport Corp. (IIAC).
Preliminary data from Airports Council International covering 1,234 airports placed Incheon ahead of London Heathrow, which handled 37.79 million international passengers, and Singapore's Changi Airport, with 34.53 million.
Incheon has steadily climbed the global rankings, moving from 10th place in 2002 to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024, when it handled 70.67 million international passengers.
IIAC officials said shifts in global aviation patterns, including weaker transit operations at major Middle Eastern hubs amid the US-Iran war, may have redirected some Europe-bound transfer traffic through Incheon.
Transfer passenger numbers at Incheon jumped 18.1% year-on-year to 4.24 million during the six-month period, while transfer traffic on European routes surged 63.2% to 210,000 passengers.
 
Foreign travelers also accounted for a record 44.4% of Incheon's total passengers in the second quarter.

Mecca pact ‘not a rival to NATO’: Defense Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:36:10 UTC
21:36:10 KST

Far from being an alternative or rival to NATO, the newly established alliance between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is purely defensive and designates no country as an adversary, a Defense Ministry spokesman stressed.
“The main objective of this agreement is to contribute to regional security and stability, enhance military cooperation between our countries and strengthen our ability to act jointly against potential crises,” Zeki Aktürk told reporters at a weekly briefing on Aug. 13.
“This agreement is for defensive purposes and does not define any country as a common enemy or adversary,” he stated.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7, in an attempt to redesign the entire security architecture in the Middle East. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Pakistan Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also held a trilateral meeting to discuss regional developments.
Aktürk said the agreement will pave the way for increased cooperation among the three countries and cement it in a more institutionalized and sustainable manner. The founding countries will establish strategic political and military mechanisms and gradually develop military coordination through exercises, training and other activities, he suggested.
“Defense industry cooperation is one of the key elements of the agreement. This includes not only the supply of products and systems, but also joint development and production, technology cooperation and the provision of sustainable maintenance and logistical support,” he explained.
The pact is neither an alternative nor a rival to NATO, but rather a complementary structure within the international security architecture that contributes to regional security and stability, the rear admiral stressed.
“Once the structure has matured, the admission of other countries will be assessed if a necessary consensus is reached,” he added.

Israeli strikes in Gaza kill two people, first fatalities in more than a week, medics say
CAIRO, Aug 13 - Israeli airstrikes killed two Palestinians, including a senior police official, in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, in the first reported fatalities in more than a week as the Israeli military scaled back its targeted attacks in the enclave under U.S. pressure.
Palestinian medics said the first strike targeted two people riding on a motorbike, in a western area of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip. One person was killed and the other was wounded, they added.
The Israeli military said in a statement that the Khan Younis airstrike targeted a Hamas commander planning an attack on its troops.
Later on Thursday, an Israeli drone launched three missiles against a vehicle driving in western Gaza City, killing the head of the Gaza City police force, and critically wounding two other people medics and witnesses said.
The Hamas-led interior ministry also confirmed in a statement the "assassination" by Israel of police colonel Jamal Abu Kmail.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment.
Israel had stepped up attacks on members of the Hamas-led police force since an October ceasefire began, killing dozens of them, according to security and health officials.
TRUMP GAZA PLAN
U.S. President Donald Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilization Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave.
On Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of Trump's latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government, even as Israel's military had effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the U.S. president.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan to avoid a resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal and halting attacks.
On Wednesday, the Israeli military said in a statement that a man was hit in an aerial strike in order to remove a threat to Israeli military troops. Gaza medics said one person was critically wounded in the attack in Beit Lahiya town, in the north of the enclave.
Israeli fire has killed more than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza, most of them civilians, since a U.S.-backed ceasefire halted two years of full-scale war in October.
It is unclear how many of those killed might be militants since Hamas does not usually disclose information about dead fighters.

Allied forces move military power across the Baltic

Warships escorted vessels carrying allied military equipment through Latvian territorial waters and into port during Lion Protector 26, the Joint Expeditionary Force exercise now running across Northern Europe, the Latvian Ministry of Defence stated.
The exercise began on 3 August and runs until 12 October, covering Northern Europe, the North Atlantic and the Baltic Sea region. Its opening activity, designated Baltic Express, is built around the rapid coordination and movement of forces across the region.
Rapid movement is a key part of credible deterrence. 🚢🚛🛡️#BalticExpress demonstrates how @JEFnations can coordinate and move forces across Northern Europe, strengthening military mobility, interoperability and readiness in support of #NATO’s deterrence and defence.… https://t.co/ahvmCBSzp5
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) August 12, 2026
According to the Latvian ministry, their Armed Forces worked with the JEF to escort the vessels safely, oversee their entry into port and handle the unloading of equipment and its onward movement to deployment locations.
NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said rapid movement is a key part of credible deterrence, and that Baltic Express demonstrates how JEF nations can coordinate and move forces across Northern Europe, strengthening military mobility, interoperability and readiness.
Moving heavy equipment into the Baltic states is the problem the exercise exists to solve. The region is connected to the rest of NATO by sea and by the Suwalki gap, the stretch of Polish and Lithuanian border running between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, and reinforcement in a crisis would depend heavily on ports and the roads and railways leading inland from them.
Baltic subsea cables and pipelines have been damaged repeatedly since 2023, including the Balticconnector gas pipeline and several telecommunications cables, and NATO stood up Baltic Sentry in January 2025 to increase patrolling in response. Suspected shadow fleet tankers have been detained by regional navies, and GPS interference across the region has been attributed by several governments to Russian sources.
The Joint Expeditionary Force is a British-led grouping of ten Northern European nations: the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It operates outside the NATO command structure but is designed to complement it, allowing a smaller group of countries with common interests in the High North and the Baltic to act faster than an alliance of thirty-two members can.
Lion Protector 26 covers the maritime, air and land domains from the Arctic to the Baltic. Latvia describes it as complementing NATO’s vigilance and deterrence measures while strengthening the ability of participating nations to deploy forces rapidly.

Economy minister rejects proposed restrictions on nicotine products
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:34:00 UTC
21:34:00 KST

Economy minister rejects proposed restrictions on nicotine products
Economy Minister Erkki Keldo declined to approve a draft bill aimed at curbing the use of nicotine products among young people as the proposed changes could have a significant impact on sellers and importers.
The restrictions proposed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Ministry of Justice would allow nicotine pouches, nicotine strips and nicotine sprays containing no more than four milligrams of nicotine per gram to be sold in Estonia. The aim is to reduce the use of nicotine products among young people.
Erkki Keldo sent a letter to the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs on Wednesday informing it that he had declined to approve the draft bill. Keldo said the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications supports protecting the health of children and young people and curbing the illegal sale of nicotine products, but considers it important that measures restricting freedom of enterprise be sufficiently justified and proportionate.
"The changes proposed in the draft bill could significantly affect manufacturers, importers, wholesalers and retailers of nicotine products operating in Estonia. The explanatory memorandum does not adequately assess the extent of these impacts or provide a convincing justification for the proposed maximum nicotine content of 4 mg/g for nicotine-containing products related to tobacco products," Keldo said.
He noted that the draft bill's maximum nicotine content of four milligrams per gram is based on Latvia's approach, but said this was not sufficient justification for restricting freedom of enterprise.
"The explanatory memorandum does not indicate the nicotine content of nicotine pouches and other products covered by the bill currently on the Estonian market, what proportion of products currently marketed legally would comply with the proposed limit or how many businesses and products would be affected by the change," the economy minister said.
He is also dissatisfied that the draft bill does not include a comparative analysis of approaches taken by other EU member states or explain why Latvia's regulations are the best model for Estonia.
Keldo said the explanatory memorandum needs to be supplemented with a comparison of different options. The impact of the limit on the health of children and young people, the risk of accidental poisoning, businesses, the functioning of the legal market and consumer behavior should also be analyzed.
The data presented in the explanatory memorandum concern products containing e-cigarette liquid, but does not address the impact of the changes on nicotine pouches, strips, sprays and heated nicotine sticks.
"We ask that the impact assessment be expanded to separately cover all product categories regulated by the draft bill and the requirements proposed for them," the minister said.
Keldo also wants the impact of the changes on Estonian manufacturers, exports, employment and regional businesses to be examined, along with their impact on the legal market, illegal trade and tax revenue.
"Possible substitution behavior must also be analyzed, including whether some consumers could switch to products with unregulated contents or to other tobacco and nicotine products and what impact this could have on achieving the draft bill's public health objective," Keldo said.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications is also dissatisfied with a provision in the draft bill stipulating that products may not contain substances that produce a flavor or aroma other than tobacco or menthol and that only substances listed in a specific regulation may be used to provide those flavors. However, the explanatory memorandum does not explain why those particular substances are considered suitable or what costs businesses could incur in reformulating existing products.
Keldo said the bill's relationship with the planned update of the European Union's legal framework for tobacco and nicotine products should also be assessed.
The Ministry of Social Affairs has previously said that people are starting to use nicotine products at increasingly younger ages. While young people previously tried nicotine at ages 15 or 16, they are now doing so at around age 11. Nicotine pouches and e-cigarettes are the most common products used by those starting out.
Just over one-fifth of the nicotine products currently on the market comply with the requirements proposed in the draft bill. Around 60 percent of products would have to be reformulated, while nearly one-fifth would have to be removed from the market.
Several European countries have tightened restrictions on nicotine products in recent years. Latvia raised the minimum age for purchasing tobacco and nicotine products to 20 two years ago. No such proposal is currently under consideration in Estonia.
The new rules are planned to take effect in 2028, although the exact date will be determined as the draft bill moves through the legislative process.

Why do women need 12 times their salary to buy a home, when men need only eight?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:33:29 UTC
21:33:29 KST

A consistent pay gap and more difficulties in saving for a deposit compared to men are some of the factors holding women back from home ownership.
Home ownership has become much more challenging globally in the last few years. Rising interest rates, persistent inflation and the ongoing cost of living crisis seen in many parts of Europe have made this dream considerably harder to attain for several young people.
Soaring property prices and stagnant living wages have added another layer of complexity to this problem too.
According to the European Youth Portal, more than 10% of young Europeans aged 20 to 29 spend more than 40% of their disposable income only on housing costs. This is far above the standard 30% affordability benchmark.
However, women, especially younger, single women, could be at an even greater disadvantage when contemplating buying a home in Europe and the UK, leading to the rise of the gender housing gap.
Why is it more difficult for women to become homeowners than men?
One of the biggest reasons women, especially single women, are more likely to struggle to buy homes than men is due to the persistent gender pay gap still being seen in the UK and several European countries.
In 2024, the gender pay gap in the EU stood at 11.1%, while a Trades Union Congress report released in February this year estimated the UK’s gender pay gap to be 12.8% currently.
Women are also likely to face lower lifetime earnings and higher rates of part-time work, mainly due to more child-rearing, household and caregiving responsibilities, which can severely impact their career progression.
Combine that with the fact that women are less likely to ask for a pay rise according to the European Central Bank, and this creates a vicious cycle that can be very hard to break out of.
As such, they are likely to find it more difficult to save for a house deposit, stamp duty and other repair, renovation and maintenance costs, apart from a mortgage, that usually come with home ownership.
More women are also likely to reduce deposit savings due to financial pressures, while also delaying life milestones such as weddings and starting a family to prioritise saving for a house than men.
The Women’s Budget Group has found that women need over 12 times their annual salaries to be able to buy a house in England, while men need just over eight times. This gap can increase even more when it comes to house prices in key hubs like London.
According to a recent survey by specialist bank Aldermore, 33% of women consider saving for a deposit the biggest obstacle to home ownership, compared to 20% of men.
Similarly, rental costs are likely to hit women harder than men, the survey found, with 76% of women sharing that these costs are a struggle, compared to 67% of men.
As older and middle-aged women are significantly more likely to live alone than men, they also lose dual-income household benefits, making any significant savings and mortgage approvals even more challenging.
This is especially as European women are more likely to experience steeper drops in household incomes after divorces, compared to men.
Splitting a joint marital home can also leave the woman with insufficient capital to re-enter the property market as a sole buyer, redirecting her instead to an ever more competitive rental market.
One of the biggest economic barriers to female home ownership is also that women are likely to get lower maximum loan amounts from mortgage lenders, compared to men, due to these lower per hour and annual salaries.
In many cases, despite having a stable or relatively high income, mortgage holders may view women with part-time or freelance jobs as higher credit risks, which further decreases the chances of loan approval.
Several times, women also face a confidence and knowledge gap in the property market, due to lower financial literacy levels. According to the European Central Bank, only 15% have high financial literacy, compared to 27% of men.
They can also be much more dismissed by brokers, mortgage approvers and estate agents during the buying process, which can make the whole process feel much higher-friction.
Another less considered issue is that several new properties also frequently lack affordable, secure, multi-room housing for single-parent family units, which are overwhelmingly headed by women. This can often lead to them putting off a home purchase for longer, while sticking with renting.

Downing Street did not rule out the possibility of renting places in foreign prisons on the 10th of August, but a spokesman for Burnham’s office said that the government is currently focusing on building additional capacity in the country’s domestic system.
