But you are basically… these are tiny little bits of brick, if you like, in the normative building, the normative environment. I mean, I started life with MSF and thought all this is rubbish, all this diplomacy stuff is absolute… there's another word I'd use for it, but not on air. What I have learnt over the years, though, is that you build the normative environment word by word, and, you know, that the kind of statements that ministers come out with around Gaza, okay, they will have been hard fought every single word about that. And as a P5 member – and we can have our questions about whether it's right or wrong that we're a P5 member, etc. etc. etc… – the bottom line is that people pay attention to the UK's position, and it changes the normative environment fractionally. So, if I can respectfully suggest, don't underestimate the power of words. But you know…
Tammam Aloudat
No, no, I’m not. My worry is at the, I mean, if I was a Palestinian or Sudanese, I'd contest that this is a major victory, given how slow and how late. But even in the tactical sense you've talked about, it is a change. Kier Starmer has not given anything near that. But who on earth knows? You know, you build this for 10 years, and then the next elections you have Nigel Farage and you're back to sub-zero. How much can we go incrementally, slowly building normative frameworks that an extreme right-wing politician [can] come and demolish with no regrets, as Trump did with USAID, and as potentially a, you know, a Reform UK might do with whatever is built until then?
Colum Wilson
I mean, you're talking about the nature of the times and why this moment in time represents a watershed, and I'll defer to here to Christina who's seen through many, many rounds of reform from the inside of the system. But you know, in my, my recollection of previous reforms, have been that they were against a backdrop where we were increasingly doing technical shifts to the perimeter, to the edges of the humanitarian system against a backdrop that was more or less stable. Now, two things have happened that has made the last two years absolutely tumultuous. The first thing is that the international geopolitical world order has shifted in ways that even the most pessimistic foresight products that FCDO was producing at the time had not anticipated. So the shifts are mega. And the second thing is, we've got– or that includes, I should say, a move to a realism, international relations realism that is really, really stressing our humanitarian frameworks. And the second is, of course, the recognition that our system is no longer fit for purpose, set against this shifting background, and therefore this now presents a moment of time, in time where we have an opportunity, like, this is a once in a generation opportunity. The time when I left FCDO, in fact, you know, you, you blink once and the whole world melts down, but this is basically the moment that we've been waiting for for all these years.
Christina Bennett
So if that's true, Colum, what you say is that we are at a major inflection point that's the one chance in a generation to make these fundamental shifts that we've all been talking about but have yet to make. You've talked about the fact that change is already happening on the ground. How then do you harness the power of governments to be able to enable that change? And do you think powerful donor governments will allow that reform to happen, or will they see a movement towards solidarity, a movement toward righting injustices as a threat to their ability to control?
Colum Wilson
Yes, I think is the answer. I do see a battle for the heart of humanitarianism ahead. In fact, it's already playing out. You know, the question of solidarity is quite interesting and now being tossed around as an alternative framework to govern and shape what we support and do. But I think that you're going to end up with a rump system that is essentially the same shape as the one we have at the moment, because it won't be able to shift quickly enough or in the right direction fast enough. But it will be small. I'll come and answer your question about what governments can do in this, but around that, you're going to get alternative models: regionalised, national models that centre sovereignty at regional or national level, that centres civil society. And by the way, this is not something that's going to happen in the future. It's happening now. At the best, you could end up with a confederated sort of global system that supports humanitarianism. At worst, you could end up with a fragmentation that so shakes the normative frameworks that they cease to be meaningful. Now, question about what, if you could call them ‘traditional bilateral Western donors’ can do in this melee: I think what they have to do is to smell the coffee and work with an agility that they're going to find very, very difficult. And I would say that there are some donors, and I'd call them middle-tier Western donors, that are already moving in this direction. But I don't think the principal big donors are going to be able to move fast enough in this direction, and they're going to become a little bit of an anomaly. They're going to be left behind. The new frameworks and ways of working will be being determined out in the rural areas of Somalia, and in the rural areas of, I don't know, Bangladesh, rather than in Geneva, and London, and Washington.
Tammam Aloudat
Is that a good or a bad thing?
Colum Wilson
Oh, it's interesting. I hadn't thought of attaching a judgement to it, but if you put me on the spot, I think it's a good thing. Because it's, basically we are shackled to Maslow's hierarchy, our entire humanitarian system. If you actually ask people what they want, they don't talk about the bottom tier of Maslow's hierarchy, and that fundamentally is what should be guiding us. So it's a question of agency. And if you use the servicing of people's agency as a principal driver, you are already building in all sorts of tensions with the existing centres of power.
Tammam Aloudat
Let me ask you, when you were an FCDO, how much does a government know, or consider, or factor in, or even care about what actually people, like… How much of it is a technical, or political, or agency calculation on behalf of the people that are affected?
Colum Wilson
Well, the first thing is you've got to be quite careful, and you'll forgive me for just correcting the assumption that FCDO is a single entity – it's got lots of people in it, and all those people have different perspectives. And what I can tell you is that there's a hardcore of humanitarians in there – I was fortunate, privileged enough to be one of them – that understand the way that things go. But the idea of leeching power away from the centre, from the donor control, is fundamentally going to be problematic. This is something, I'm not the first person to say this. You know you guys write about it the whole time, Christina lives the dream by transferring power out. We understand that. But fundamentally that is going to be problematic. So what you have is a lot of very, very good humanitarians who understand the technical ramifications, who understand the moral point of doing this, but are to some extent constrained by realpolitik of humanitarianism as an instrument of, if you like, power, global power.
Christina Bennett
We've talked about a lot of dynamics today. We've talked a lot about the history of the power of donor governments. If you were in control of the UK's humanitarian policy today, suspend disbelief, what would be the first thing you would do?
Colum Wilson
If you go into this imaginary world of views where it's decoupled from national interests, so that's the first thing to get out there, is you can set a policy frame that favours support for, if you like, all the stuff that's happening that would form ultimately a confederacy rather than a centralised system. So a way of supporting the growth, a thousand flowers blooming out there, and it comes down to a few important policy levers. One of them is cash. The cash revolution hasn't, hasn't been completed. We're only on 21 per cent or whatever it is now, and that's declining since last year. The second is moving away, wholescale, from the grant model. There's two reasons for that. One is it's no longer fit for purpose, there isn't enough money to hand out. And secondly, it is a major affront to people's dignity. So what we need to do is to start using the limited ODA that we've got to leverage other money, and insurance is a very good example of that. So I would be saying, well, you need to explain why you're responding, why you're not putting insurance frameworks in place beforehand. The third area is extensive use of the ecosystem of pooled funds, and that doesn't just mean CERF or country-based pooled funds. And I'm using the words really carefully: the ecosystem. So, feminist pooled funds, women's pooled funds, local civil, civil society pooled funds – that entire ecosystem. Obviously you’ve got to work out how the checks and balances work, etc., and that's not a small thing, you know. That's got to be reconciled with Daily Mail readers and whatnot back at home. But fundamentally, that represents a way of solving the wholesale-retail problem that is at the heart, one of the technical reasons why large scale support for localisation is quite difficult from big donors. So those, I've given you three policy levers. I would reframe the UK's humanitarian approach in those terms.
Christina Bennett
You’ve painted a picture of this federated ‘let a thousand flowers bloom’ ecosystem, and there are some who think that that is the future of aid. But what we also have alongside it: some very, very powerful interests re-centralising, pulling back from this idea that there is a, there is an ecosystem and going back to funding the oligopoly that has been the humanitarian enterprise for some time. If you were the UK government now, what would you do to influence those larger and smaller donor governments to move in the direction that you've explained to us?
Colum Wilson
Well, the first thing is, one of the issues that I have with FCDO – and I'm sure I don't think I'm going to upset anybody by saying this – is that FCDO, along with a lot of other top-tier bilateral donors, is risk-averse, bureaucratic, and highly path-dependent. So the first thing to do is to embrace an agility and willingness to look outside and understand what is going on across the rest of the constellation, the humanitarian ecosystem, as it's been framed out there, and understand that there are alternatives out there. The second thing I'd do – and this is something that gave me a lot of sleepless nights when I was in the previous role – was to mobilise donors around that agenda. Now that sounds easy enough, but as I said to you earlier, it was very difficult to get a coherent message out of donors because they're fractured by their own national interests. And you know, particularly with the rise of, sort of, populist governments across Europe, that's become even more intense. So you know, the German framing of humanitarianism in its recent strategy is quite interesting in that respect because it, it coasts very closely towards supporting national interest. So you've got all this problem going on. So then what you look for is new and emerging and middle-tier donors who have the agility, don't come with the geopolitical baggage necessarily, and whatnot. And I think that is the next centre of power that we need to invest in to try and mobilise towards shifting the system.
Tammam Aloudat
Just for our listeners' clarity, when you talk about the middle-tier donors, are we talking about Belgium, Luxembourg, Australia, or are we talking about new donors? What should we think about when you mention that?
Colum Wilson
It's a bit of both. There are some very innovative donors out there that are quite small. I mean, Swiss is one of them. Irish Aid, very very interesting what they're doing. Then there are what I'd call emerging donors. Again, it's a bit of a pejorative term, but you know countries where we used to go in and do old-style humanitarian support, like Bangladesh and Indonesia, they don't have the same frame. They don't have same framing of humanitarianism as we do. Whose humanitarianism is it anyway? But you know, can you imagine a coalition of those member states putting forward alternative models and supporting an alternative way of doing things. Yes, it represents a different centre of power, but it's either ignoring that or it's trying to support it in a constructive way. And I'd be in for the latter.
Christina Bennett
This episode has been about reform from above. Do you think that reform of the system, by the system, or from its, its patrons, the donor governments, is possible or desirable? And is ultimately the future of humanitarian action better off without them? Better off without those patrons that have been the major players in the system to date?
Colum Wilson
So you can't wish them out of existence. Let me answer your first, your second question first. You can't wish them out of existence. This is why I think where we're going to end up, if we scrolled forward and imagined ourselves sitting around this table in 20 years' time, what would we see? This is this idea of kind of rump system that I mentioned before, surrounded by a kind of a constellation, if you like, of alternative centres of power that, to a greater or lesser extent, are coherent, but not necessarily. So that's the future I think where it's going to end up for pragmatic reasons, because you can't undo the structures that we've got. The power is too entrenched. But to come to your first question, then, about whether a complete reset, if I can use that word, or a complete sort of white-sheet-of-paper reform is possible: the answer is no. And by the way, getting to that new configuration that I've described is going to be heavily, heavily contested, and it's going to be fought over the whole way. If you ask me whether the system can self-reform – and this is why the question about the World Humanitarian Summit 2026 I think is relevant – I don't think it can self-reform. I think it's too embedded. I think we had a political moment in 2016. Probably wasn't a powerful enough political moment, but you wouldn't be able to get that political moment again. And I think that reflects the fact that actually the system is too heavily embedded to be able to do fundamental self-reform. It won't, it won't wish itself out of existence.
Christina Bennett
So, as someone who's familiar with the system, what advice do you have for those working outside the system? Those movements that have emerged in countries like Sudan, like Myanmar, like other places that have something to give to the system, that are able to shift it from below, but that have to contend with powerful governments’ resistance to that locally-led change?
Colum Wilson
Well, I mean, again, I don't have a silver bullet answer here, and it's probably stating the bleeding obvious, but it's basically not waiting for the system to catch up. Trying to influence the existing system, the one that's so embedded where we can, but in the meantime, just getting on with it. And, you know, whether that's bringing weather forecasting in the last mile to people in Sudan, or whether it's bringing microinsurance to ground level in war zones, just get on with it, and then move it to scale. And that's going to require non-traditional alignments and partnerships. Again, it's a little bit of a hackneyed phrase, and you know the Global Partnerships Conference was nominally all about that. So you know, it's with the private sector, it's with philanthropies, and it's leveraging then into these places that sometimes are not necessarily comfortable to go into. So there isn't any big revelations there, Christina, but I think it is something to do with agility, and just not hanging around, and just walking the walk as well as talking the talk, because that's the only way it's going to shift.
Christina Bennett
Thanks for that, Colum. Thanks for being with us today and for taking all of our questions.
Colum Wilson
And thank you very much.
Tammam Aloudat
That was Colum Wilson, former head of the FCDO’s humanitarian department. Next episode, we continue our discussion on how humanitarianism is changed from the top-down, this time from the point of view of a government that traditionally receives aid.
Abdihakim Ainte
The aid cut could be a blessing in disguise. This could be a moment, a defining moment where countries such as Somalia to see the current challenges and turn the current challenges into an opportunity, and look them inward rather than looking outward.
Christina Bennett
To our listeners, we’d love to hear from you – How can humanitarian action remain values-driven in a more transactional world?
Tammam Aloudat

In the Lviv region, a 54-year-old man is suspected of systematically sexually abusing a minor girl who, together with her two biological sisters, had been placed in his foster family for care. According to the investigation, the unlawful acts continued for about a year

Sexual assault survivors in Lithuania face long waits for help – and lost evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:37:01 UTC
20:37:01 KST

By Urtė Šlevaitė, LRT TV, LRT.lt.
People who have survived drug-facilitated sexual assault in Lithuania say they are being let down by a system with too few specialist services, no reliable way to preserve evidence, and long waits for care. The country’s social security ministry says changes are coming, but for now, campaigners say, survivors are often left to navigate the process largely on their own.
“A black screen, then nothing”
Ten years ago, comedian and human rights advocate Vita Žiba was sexually assaulted after being drugged. She says it took her a while afterwards to understand what had happened to her.
“First of all, you barely remember anything, because those drugs are usually designed specifically to suppress memory. I just remember having one drink, then another, and then – a black screen. The next thing I remember is being in some room, I don’t even know where, with some man’s hands all over me,” she said.
When Žiba shared her story on social media, she received an outpouring of support – within a week, roughly 800 women had come forward with their own experiences of sexual violence. But she also faced abuse online.
“A lot of older men wrote things like ‘you had it coming’, ‘it’s your own fault’, or ‘you should be grateful someone wanted you’,” she said.

UN: 437 civilians killed in Ukraine in July, Kyiv among hardest-hit cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:37:00 UTC
20:37:00 KST

UN: 437 civilians killed in Ukraine in July, Kyiv among hardest-hit cities
This is according to a report by the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine published on August 13, Ukrinform reports.
"HRMMU verified that at least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 per cent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 per cent increase compared with July 2025," the mission said.
The report's authors noted that Kyiv was among the hardest-hit cities. At least 54 civilians were killed and another 202 injured in the capital in July.
"With at least 54 civilians killed and 202 injured, Kyiv was one of the hardest hit cities in Ukraine in July as Russian armed forces significantly increased the use of ballistic and cruise missiles. Russia launched at least 429 missiles in July, more than double the number in June. Many of the missiles struck Kyiv," the mission said.
Danielle Bell, head of the HRMMU, said the number of civilians killed and injured in Ukraine had been rising every month this year.
"That trend accelerated sharply in July. The number of civilian casualties in July was the highest we documented in a single month since March 2022," she said.
Long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remained the leading cause of civilian casualties in July, accounting for 38 per cent of the total (183 killed and 967 injured). Civilian casualties from aerial bombardments (105 killed and 753 injured) increased by 143 per cent compared with June 2026 (45 killed and 308 injured), with glide bombs becoming the second leading cause of civilian casualties. Short-range drones near the frontline caused 27 per cent of casualties (111 killed and 710 injured).
"Together, these attacks are driving up civilian casualties across different regions of Ukraine," Bell said.
Overall, since February 24, 2022, OHCHR has verified at least 16,874 civilians killed, including 820 children, and 51,273 injured, including 3,126 children.

A 12-year-old dies in occupied Kherson Oblast where no hospital or ambulance is left, Ukrainian official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:34:00 UTC
20:34:00 KST

A 12-year-old with a high fever died without medical care in Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast, Hola Prystan official in exile Svitlana Linnyk told Ukrinform on 13 August 2026.
No medicine or medical worker was available locally, and the child’s mother could not reach an ambulance pickup point, she said.
The child's reported death comes amid a wider humanitarian crisis in Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast. UN and OSCE monitors found drone attacks, mines, and movement restrictions obstructing medical aid and evacuations around Oleshky and Hola Prystan, two occupied communities across the Dnipro from Kherson city. About 6,000 civilians, including 200 children, remained in and around the two communities as of May. Similar medical shortages span occupied Ukraine, while access to free medicines has been tied to having a Russian passport.
The Hola Prystan community where the child died has no operating hospital or rural medical post, Linnyk said. Only two pharmacies remain: one in the city of Hola Prystan and another in the nearby village of Nova Zburivka. Both are selling their remaining supplies.
The nearest hospital is in Skadovsk, an occupied Black Sea port about 60 kilometers by road from Hola Prystan. Nova Zburivka’s ambulance has not operated since 2025.
Russian occupation authorities have distributed no humanitarian aid for at least eight months to villages surrounding Hola Prystan, or for over a year in the city itself, Linnyk said.
Linnyk said a Moscow Patriarchate priest occasionally brought supplies but gave them only to Russian passport holders. This reflects a broader pattern of tying basic services in occupied Ukraine to accepting Russian citizenship.
Ukrainian children face a medical system stripped bare
The medical dangers surrounding the 12-year-old’s death are not confined to Hola Prystan.
In April 2025, Ukraine’s National Resistance Center reported that occupation officials were administering vaccines to children under six in Luhansk Oblast. It described the vaccines as uncertified and of unknown origin.
That November, the Center said a Russian inspection found Crimea’s main children’s hospital lacked breathing bags and cardiac monitors. It said infant mortality on the occupied peninsula had risen 9% over the previous year.
Aid comes with a Russian passport
Hola Prystan is not the only occupied community where access to care has depended on Russian citizenship.
In 2023, Russian-installed officials in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast threatened to deny medical care to residents without Russian passports. A 2025 Kremlin policy later tied free medicines for chronic illnesses to Russian citizenship.
Ukraine’s Health Ministry reported in July 2024 that Russian forces had destroyed 214 medical facilities. It said the full toll remained unknown because authorities had limited access to occupied territories.

A tour boat carrying 115 people caught fire off the coast of Fethiye in southwestern Türkiye, triggering a rescue operation after passengers, including children, jumped into the sea wearing life jackets to escape the flames.

The blaze caused extensive damage to the tour boat, which later began to sink. Despite the dramatic scenes, no fatalities were reported in the initial assessment.
Authorities said rescue and medical operations continued until all passengers had been accounted for. The cause of the fire remains unknown, and an investigation has been launched to determine how it started.

US warns Israel against permanent occupation of south Lebanon
The United States has warned Israel against turning its occupation of southern Lebanon into a permanent military presence, saying such a move would violate the framework agreement reached with Beirut and undermine Lebanon's sovereignty.
The unusually direct rebuke from Washington came after Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz declared that Israeli forces would not withdraw from Lebanese territory and had been ordered to prepare for a long-term presence in areas Israel has designated a "security zone".
A senior US State Department official said in a statement sent to Israel's Channel 12 seeking a response to Katz's remarks that Washington expected Israel to abide by the commitments it made under the US-brokered framework signed in late June.
"A permanent military presence in southern Lebanon is inconsistent with the commitments set forth in the framework, or with the long-term peace and security of both countries," the official said.
The official also reaffirmed Washington's "full support for Lebanon's territorial integrity and sovereignty", drawing a clear line between the agreement negotiated by the United States and Katz's declaration that Israeli troops intend to remain on Lebanese soil.
The State Department official stressed that the framework provides a conditions-based pathway towards a gradual Israeli withdrawal, tied to the verified disarmament of Hezbollah and dismantling of its military infrastructure.
"The Lebanese Armed Forces are currently implementing the first pilot areas, and the United States will continue to support the full implementation of this process," the official said.
Israel has publicly framed its occupation of Lebanon as necessary to secure its northern border, but senior Israeli officials have repeatedly advocated the seizure and colonisation of Lebanese territory and the expansion of Israel's northern borders.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for Israel's northern frontier to be moved to the Litani River, while Katz has threatened Lebanon with the "loss of territory". His latest declaration that Israeli forces will remain indefinitely has further fuelled Lebanese fears that the occupation is intended to become permanent.
During a tour of occupied Lebanese territory on Wednesday, Katz said Israeli troops would remain in the so-called "security zones" in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza.
"We will not move from here and we will not withdraw," Katz said.
He said he had instructed the Israeli military to make the administrative and operational preparations required for a prolonged deployment.
The language echoed Israel's earlier occupation of southern Lebanon, when it maintained a self-declared "security zone" for nearly two decades before withdrawing in May 2000.
Katz also spoke openly about the destruction being carried out in the occupied area, saying Israeli forces were demolishing homes and alleged "Hezbollah infrastructure".
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Wednesday condemned Israel's "systematic destruction" of homes and infrastructure in the south, saying it violated international law and was intended to prevent displaced Lebanese residents from returning to their land.
The Israeli statements come as negotiations over implementing the June framework remain deadlocked, particularly over the sequence of Israeli withdrawals and the Lebanese army's deployment in the south.
Lebanon has sought further Israeli withdrawals to allow its army to move into additional "pilot zones", while Israel has made further redeployments conditional on the verified disarmament of Hezbollah and dismantling of its infrastructure, while introducing a widening list of unrealistic and unserious demands.
These include the transfer to Israel of remains from Jewish cemeteries in Beirut and Sidon, information on 11 Jews who disappeared or were killed during Lebanon's civil war, and answers over the fate of Israeli airman Ron Arad, who disappeared in Lebanon in 1986.
The impasse has persisted despite the Lebanese army beginning implementation of the framework in the first pilot area. Lebanon has pushed for the same model to be expanded, with Israeli forces withdrawing and the Lebanese army moving in, but Israel has resisted opening additional zones.
Lebanese army commander General Rudolph Haykal raised the obstacles facing the military during meetings this week with US Major General Joseph Clearfield, who heads the military coordination group involved in implementing the agreement.
According to Lebanese accounts of the meetings, Haykal pointed to continuing Israeli attacks, bulldozing and destruction as among the principal difficulties facing the army as it attempts to deploy and carry out its responsibilities in the south.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has sought greater American pressure on Israel to withdraw, raising the issue during his July visit to Washington and talks with US President Donald Trump.
The latest comes ahead of another expected round of US-mediated negotiations in Rome in early September.

The head of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Faiq Zidan, arrived in the Syrian capital Damascus on Thursday for talks on Daesh terrorists transferred from Syrian detention facilities to Iraqi prisons.
Syrian Justice Minister Mazhar al-Wais received Zidan upon his arrival, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
The visit aims to discuss several issues of mutual concern, “most notably the file of Daesh terrorist detainees who were transferred to Iraqi prisons,” the news agency said.
On January 21, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the transfer of 150 Daesh terrorists from a detention facility in Syria’s northeastern Hasakah province to Iraq as part of a plan to relocate 7,000 detainees.
Baghdad declared victory over Daesh on December 10 2017, after retaking all Iraqi territory captured by the terrorist organisation following three years of intense fighting.
The group, however, continues to operate in Iraq’s northern, western and eastern provinces and carries out sporadic attacks. Iraqi forces continue security and military operations against its remaining cells.

The spread of pro-Kremlin narratives about Ukraine and strikes on russia is being recorded in the Czech Republic — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
The Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council is recording the spread in the Czech information space of claims about the negative consequences of Ukraine's strikes on russia. These narratives are being disseminated by resources that Czech researchers classify as sources of pro-Kremlin propaganda.
In the Czech information space, claims are being circulated about the alleged negative consequences of Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory and the futility of supporting Ukraine. Such messages appear on resources that Czech research organizations associate with disinformation and pro-Kremlin propaganda. This was reported by the National Security and Defense Council’s Center for Countering Disinformation, UNN writes.
The Center is recording the spread of pro-Russian narratives in the Czech information space through a number of resources affiliated with Russian propaganda
In particular, claims are being promoted that strikes deep inside Russia allegedly "worsen Ukraine’s strategic position and provoke further escalation of the conflict," and that "the only thing Ukraine and its partners have achieved is worsening Ukraine’s tragic fate," among others.
The resources spreading these narratives, predominantly of an far-right ideological orientation, belong to the segment of quasi-media outlets and information platforms that independent Czech research organizations systematically classify as sources of disinformation and pro-Kremlin propaganda.
By using such resources, the Kremlin is trying to influence public opinion in the Czech Republic, foment hatred toward Ukrainians in the country, and obstruct the provision of assistance to our state

Israel trucks out Gaza’s rubble to ‘hide genocide’ and ‘redraw the map’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:29:32 UTC
20:29:32 KST

Israel trucks out Gaza’s rubble to ‘hide genocide’ and ‘redraw the map’
The Israeli military is carting away millions of tonnes of rubble – including from cemeteries and known locations of human remains – in what rights groups say is an effort to erase war crimes evidence.
Israel is carrying out a massive, organised operation to crush, mix and transport millions of tonnes of rubble out of the Gaza Strip, according to human rights groups and monitors.
The Israeli military’s systematic reshaping of the urban landscape comes against a backdrop of a staggering human toll, with at least 73,387 Palestinians – mostly children and women – killed since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 411-year-old boy shot by Israeli forces in Gaza
- list 2 of 4US strikes in Yemen killed 153 civilians in 2025, says Pentagon review
- list 3 of 4Israeli strikes in south Lebanon a ‘violation of international law’: PM
- list 4 of 4Palestinian women in Gaza face legal hurdles in divorce struggles
This removal of rubble could be an attempt at demographic engineering and erasing evidence of the genocide, the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor has said, in a report entitled Gaza Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment.
Obliterating the truth
The report estimates that there are approximately 68 million tonnes of rubble across the Gaza Strip, much of the result of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on the enclave.
At least 10 million tonnes of rubble have already been removed, crushed or moved from their original sites within areas under Israel’s unlawful military control, which encompass about two-thirds of the enclave.
About 400 heavy pieces of excavation, crushing and transport machinery are also working to demolish the remaining structures in Gaza.
Debris is being loaded onto nearly 100 Israeli trucks daily, which are leaving the Gaza Strip for undisclosed sites within Israel and the occupied West Bank.
Budour Hassan, a researcher at Amnesty International, told Al Jazeera that this could be a calculated attempt to destroy evidence of crimes committed by Israel during the war.
“The bulldozing is an integral part of all attempts to destroy the lands in Gaza City and in the Gaza Strip in general,” Hassan said.
“The real fears are that these operations are taking place with the aim of obliterating and hiding evidence.”
Preventing access to evidence of crimes is a direct challenge to the International Court of Justice, Hassan said. The ICJ is currently overseeing a genocide case against Israel brought by South Africa and supported by numerous other nations.
“The occupation systematically works to obliterate evidence and destroy the features of the crime,” she added.
Mohammed Salha, director of the NGO Network in the Gaza Strip, believes the debris being moved out of the enclave contains missile fragments, ammunition, and personal belongings – crucial for future accountability.
“The occupation is moving the rubble, fragmenting it, and moving it into the Green Line to obliterate the evidence and facts,” Salha told Al Jazeera.
“Naturally, there are thousands of martyrs under this rubble, and moving this rubble with their remains means a deliberate destruction of the crime scene that contains the basic evidence that exposes the occupation’s commission of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.”
Urban engineering
The mass removal of rubble could serve a distinct military and colonial purpose. Euro-Med Monitor reported that the large-scale crushing and removal of rubble destroys land boundaries, house foundations and street networks, stripping Palestinians of the physical markers of ownership and deepening ethnic cleansing in Gaza. This sets the stage for efforts to re-establish Israeli settlements in Gaza.
Retired Brigadier General Elias Hanna, a military and strategic expert, explained to Al Jazeera how geography is being used against the population as an extreme form of collective punishment.
“The building and the geographical area have become part of the battle and part of the weapon itself,” Hanna said.
“When the Israeli enemy destroys and bulldozes, this bulldozing falls within the policy of collective punishment; that is, you create a new urban engineering and a new phase and a different shape for the social and security environment to punish those who resist and punish the civilian incubator at the same time,” Hanna said.
This strategy of urban engineering aims to permanently alter the ecosystem of the enclave by preventing the return of Palestinians to their homes and making the destroyed areas in Gaza unliveable or unbuildable, Hanna added.
The daily tragedy
The removal of ruins also means that the bodies of missing people, estimated by Gaza’s civil defence in July 2026 to number about 8,500, could be gone forever.
Using heavy machinery without prior forensic surveys risks crushing or scattering these remains, severely infringing on the rights of families to know the fate of their relatives.
Abu Asim, a Palestinian citizen whose family members remain buried in the eastern areas of the Gaza Strip, now designated as behind a military “Yellow Line“, shared his agony with Al Jazeera.
“My family’s story is that their body parts were scattered in the streets, and some of them are still to this day under the rubble of the house, and their remains have not been brought out,” he said.
“We lost them, and the first tragedy was their martyrdom, and the second and daily tragedy is the absence of these graves and the absence of the evidence with which we will try this occupation for these crimes and atrocities.”
Rescue efforts have been entirely paralysed in areas seized by the Israeli military.
Samir al-Mana’ama, a lawyer with the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that during the war, Israeli authorities seized an area of approximately 70 percent of the eastern Gaza Strip.
“[The Israeli military is] preventing the access of rescue crews to recover the bodies of the martyrs, and it is also tampering with the rubble areas and moving them from one place to another, which leads to a clear and explicit violation of the provisions of international humanitarian law and international human rights law,” al-Mana’ama told Al Jazeera.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of civil defence in Gaza, highlighted the impossibility of their mission.
“In the available areas where we move now, things are very difficult and complex,” he told Al Jazeera. “So how about the situation if the matter requires coordination to enter the areas located inside the Yellow Line, which requires special equipment, coordination, and securing … the nature of our work there.”
Even known resting places of the dead have not been spared, Salha said, with historical burial sites included in this campaign of erasure.
“Reports and human rights documentation state that the occupation completely or partially destroyed more than 93 percent of the cemeteries in the Gaza Strip,” Salha said. “Neither stone, nor human beings, nor even the dead in their graves have been spared from the occupation.”

China extends anti-dumping duties on Indian optical fiber for five years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:28:17 CST
20:28:17 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- China will continue to impose anti-dumping duties on imports of single-mode optical fiber originating from India for five more years starting Aug. 14, 2026, the Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday.
This decision was made following a review of the anti-dumping measures, which was initiated in August 2025 at the request of China's domestic industry, the ministry said in a statement.
If the anti-dumping measures were terminated, the dumping of single-mode optical fiber from India would likely continue or recur, potentially causing ongoing or renewed harm to China's domestic industry, according to the ministry's expiry review investigation.
Under the extended measures, anti-dumping duties on the imported products range from 7.4 percent to 30.6 percent.
China imposed anti-dumping duties on single-mode optical fiber imports from India in 2014 and extended these duties for another five years in 2020.
Single-mode optical fiber is mainly used in high-speed, long-distance and access network transmission, and is widely applied in long-haul trunk lines, metropolitan area networks, cable television and fiber-optic access networks. ■

Unknown Publisher

19:28:14 CST
20:28:14 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Unhealthy air quality was detected across 11 areas in Malaysia on Thursday, according to data from the country's air quality monitoring system.
The northern Borneo state of Sarawak was badly affected, with the Semarahan district recording the highest air pollutant index (API) of 183, followed by Serian (182), Kuching (176), Sarikei and Sri Aman (158), and Mukah and Sibu (152), according to data from the Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System.
In Peninsular Malaysia, four areas recorded unhealthy readings: Johan Setia (154) and Shah Alam (101) in Selangor state, as well as the capital Kuala Lumpur (131) and administrative capital Putrajaya (104).
Fifty-five areas recorded moderate API readings.
According to the country's air quality rating, an API reading of zero to 50 is "good," 51 to 100 "moderate," 101 to 200 "unhealthy," 201 to 300 "very unhealthy," and 301 and above is "hazardous."
Meanwhile, the Malaysian Meteorological Department National Weather and Earthquake Operations Centre senior director Maqrun Fadzli Mohd Fahmi told Bernama that although rain is forecast to occur in several places, it is not yet able to restore air quality on a large scale. ■

====================================================================================================

Chinese researchers uncover "ripple" structures in Milky Way
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:27:56 CST
20:27:56 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have identified widespread corrugated structures in the Milky Way for the first time, offering fresh observational evidence for understanding the galaxy's three-dimensional architecture and dynamic evolution.
The finding, from a team at the Purple Mountain Observatory (PMO) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was published on Aug. 7 in the journal Nature Astronomy.
The Milky Way's overall shape resembles a warped record, with one side bent upward and the other downward, a large-scale deformation known as the "warp." However, systematic observations and quantitative studies of finer vertical structures within the galaxy have long been lacking.
The team analyzed more than 30,000 molecular clouds in 3D, using carbon monoxide (CO) spectral-line survey data from the PMO's 13.7-meter millimeter-wave telescope, said Sun Yan, associate researcher at PMO and the paper's first and co-corresponding author.
CO is a key tracer of cold molecular gas, the raw material for star formation. The sample covers about half of the Milky Way's outer disk, reaching up to roughly 26 kiloparsecs from the Galactic center.
Based on these samples, the team constructed the first global warp model of the molecular gas outer disk. After subtracting the large-scale warp background, they detected clear, wave-like vertical undulations, or corrugations, in the residual structure.
"These corrugations appear as large-scale vertical deviations of the disk, likely originating from bending waves excited by external gravitational perturbations," Sun said.
"They may well be the 'ripples' propagating through the outer disk as a result of gravitational disturbances caused by satellite galaxies, such as dwarf galaxies, flying past the Milky Way," Sun added. ■

He added that Iran's other conditions had been conveyed to the United States through mediators.
Rezaei also referred to ongoing negotiations between Iran and Oman over the designation of a new route through the strait, saying a potential agreement between the two countries "will be an issue separate from the strait's closure."
Iran tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory. ■

Britain's main political parties chose not to field candidates in the contest, leaving Farage to face a field largely made up of independents, smaller parties and novelty candidates.
Then-Foreign Secretary, now Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the by-election "shouldn't be happening" and accused Farage of throwing a "political tantrum" as a distraction.
"Nobody is going to get drawn into what is a political stunt by Nigel Farage because he wants to duck and dive around the rules that apply to everyone," she told BBC last month.
A survey released last week put Farage on 73% among decided voters, with Count Binface second on 20% and the remaining 32 candidates sharing 7%.
Polling stations are open from 7 am local time (0600GMT) until 10 pm (2100GMT).

====================================================================================================

Who is Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's new security chief with an Interpol Red Notice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:27:40 UTC
20:27:40 KST

Mohsen Rezaei is one of the Islamic Republic's founding military figures, a four-time failed presidential candidate and the subject of an Interpol Red Notice over the 1994 Buenos Aires bombing that killed 85 people. Here is what we know about Iran's new security council chief.
One of the founding figures of Iran's IRGC Mohsen Rezaei has been appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council — giving one of the country's most controversial senior figures formal authority over the institution responsible for Tehran's strategic decisions.
The appointment was made in a presidential decree signed by Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday.
Hours earlier, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had separately appointed Rezaei as his personal representative on the council.
With nearly five decades at the top of the Islamic Republic's security and military apparatus, Rezaei, 71, succeeds Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a veteran IRGC commander who resigned after around four months in the post and was appointed as a political adviser to Khamenei.
Right after his appointment was announced, Rezaei has said publicly that Iran will not open a second shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz, that US warships entering the strait will be targeted, and that the war must end and Iran's frozen assets must be released before Hormuz can be reopened.
Who is Mohsen Rezaei?
Rezaei, whose birth name was Sabzvar, was born in 1954 in Khuzestan province into a Bakhtiari tribal family.
Initially a political activist against the rule of Shah Reza Pahlavi in the early 1970s, Rezaei was arrested by the shah's intelligence agency SAVAK and imprisoned in Ahvaz.
He was one of the founders of the Mansouroun militant group, which helped lay the groundwork for the Mojahedin of the Islamic Revolution Organisation.
After the 1979 revolution, Rezaei joined the central council of the Islamic Republic and served on a 12-member committee that drafted the IRGC's constitution.
In September 1981, at the age of 27, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appointed him commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Guards.
Rezaei held the position for 16 years — making him one of the longest-serving military commanders in the history of the Islamic Republic — before stepping down in September 1997.
He then became secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council, the body that resolves disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council and sets broad state policy, for nearly 24 years.
He was appointed deputy president for economy under President Ebrahim Raisi in 2021, a post he left in June 2023.
Despite this record of institutional prominence, Rezaei has run for president four times and lost each time. In the 2021 election, he received 3.4 million votes — fewer than the number of ballots deemed invalid in the vote.
The bombing of the Jewish centre in Argentina
Rezaei's name has been associated internationally with the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people and injured hundreds in the deadliest terrorist attack in Argentina's history.
In 2007, Argentine prosecutors sought arrest warrants for nine people in connection with the attack, including Rezaei, then IRGC commander. Interpol issued a Red Notice against him that remains in force.
Tehran and Rezaei have consistently denied any involvement in the attack, describing the allegations as politically motivated.
The case has nevertheless had practical consequences: Argentina protested his appointment as deputy economic president in 2021, previously objected to his attendance at the inaugurations of Nicaraguan presidents, and asked Qatar to arrest and extradite him during a visit to Doha — a request that was not carried out.
Operation Karbala-4
The most controversial episode of Rezaei's military command domestically was Operation Karbala-4, a December 1986 assault during the Iraq-Iran war intended to retake parts of the Faw area that was detected and repelled by Iraqi forces, resulting in heavy Iranian casualties, including frogmen units.
In 2015, the remains of 175 divers who had participated in the operation, reportedly buried with their hands tied, were discovered and identified.
Rezaei's subsequent claim that continuing the operation after it had been compromised was a deliberate deception ahead of the larger Operation Karbala-5 — or the siege of Basra, the largest military offensive of the war — drew sharp criticism from former officials, journalists and social media users.
Qassem Soleimani, then Quds Force commander, contradicted the account by saying Karbala-4 had been the primary operation all along.
Another controversy surfaced in November 2011, when Rezaei's eldest son Ahmad, who had previously defected to the US and given media interviews criticising senior Islamic Republic officials, was found dead in a Dubai hotel room.
Dubai police attributed the death to an overdose of antidepressants. Rezaei's family and the Expediency Council secretariat rejected that conclusion and described the death as suspicious. The cause of Ahmad Rezaei's death has never been conclusively established.
War, succession and regime in flux
Rezaei's appointment comes after one of the most turbulent periods in the Islamic Republic's history.
The US and Israel launched broad strikes against Iranian military targets on 28 February, killing Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Defence Minister Mohammad Reza Ashtiani and around 40 senior military and security commanders.
Ali Larijani, who had been secretary of the Supreme National Security Council since August 2025 and was regarded by many analysts as Iran's most powerful figure on the eve of the war, was killed in a subsequent wave of Israeli strikes on Tehran.
Zolghadr then succeeded Larijani in that role. Under the constitution, an interim council of President Pezeshkian, judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Ejei and a Guardian Council-appointed cleric managed the country's leadership functions until Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as the third ayatollah on 9 March.

Indigenous rangers, scientists map vulnerable reefs in northern Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:27:37 CST
20:27:37 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- A two-year collaboration between Indigenous rangers and scientists has produced the first comprehensive scientific baseline of coral reefs around the Groote Archipelago in Australia's Northern Territory.
The study documented the seafloor composition of five reefs surrounding Groote Eylandt using underwater remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) in waters that can be challenging to access due to saltwater crocodiles and marine stingers, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
The surveys found coral cover ranging from 5 to 47 percent across the sites, with reefs dominated by hardy massive corals rather than branching varieties more common on other reefs, said the study co-authored by Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers and UTS researchers.
Fieldwork in early 2024 coincided with an environmental stress event. Satellite data showed elevated sea temperatures before the event, although they were not at levels typically associated with severe coral bleaching. Ranger surveys subsequently identified mass coral bleaching at several sites.
The findings challenge assumptions that remote or marginal reefs are naturally resistant to heat stress, said UTS Associate Professor Emma Camp, senior researcher of the study published in the journal PLOS One.
"Remote reefs like these have too often been treated as an afterthought in conservation, despite how important they are to the communities who rely on them," Camp said.
The project combined traditional Indigenous knowledge with modern technology, with local rangers guiding scientists to key reef sites and receiving training to operate ROVs and drones, researchers said. ■

Supplier says subcontractor ordered non-fire-retardant nets before Tai Po blaze
Documents released by independent panel investigating the deadly Wang Fuk Court blaze detail Gain Profit’s orders for non-compliant nets
The statement from supplier Lam Kee Construction Materials was among the documents released on Wednesday by the independent committee investigating the causes of the fire in November, the city’s deadliest in decades.

The ministry said that in a series of intelligence operations in Khash, four members of the two cells were arrested, while two others were killed in clashes with security forces.
According to the statement, the two trained operatives had been dispatched to Iran by terrorist-Takfiri groups affiliated with the US-Zionist enemy intelligence services.
The ministry said the cells had intended to carry out operations aimed at destabilizing Sistan and Baluchestan and targeting economic infrastructure in the southern parts of the province, but were identified and dismantled before taking any action.
In a separate operation, intelligence forces also dismantled a four-member organized gang involved in violent crimes and disrupting public order and security in Zahedan.

Antwerp diamond sector rejects link between Trump ring and tariff exemption
BRUSSELS, Aug 13 - The Antwerp diamond sector has rejected allegations there was a link between an 18-carat gold ring encrusted with 321 diamonds recently gifted to U.S. President Donald Trump and the exemption of Europe's diamond industry from new tariffs weeks later.
"The discussion about U.S. import tariffs was entirely separate from (the gifted ring)", the Antwerp World Diamond Centre, which represents the Belgian city's diamond sector, said in a statement on Wednesday.
• The statement follows a letter by two Democratic senators demanding answers from both AWDC and David Gotlib Luxury Cufflinks, which had gifted the ring, warning that the gift raised legal questions under U.S. federal bribery law and could result in criminal penalties for the companies.
• "The ring was designed and gifted on the occasion of the official celebration of 250 years of American independence, organized by the U.S. Embassy in Belgium. Without that celebration, there would have been no ring," the AWDC statement said.
• David Gotlib Luxury Cufflinks was not immediately available for comment when approached by Reuters and there was no immediate response from a PR representative or via LinkedIn.
• The sector had secured 0% tariff in September 2025 but when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's tariff law, he pivoted to a 10% global tariff for 150 days which AWDC said also affected the diamond sector.
• AWDC said that when new tariffs were announced, the sector had pushed for the 0% tariff to be implemented again but that this was "entirely separate" from the gift.
• The ring was presented to the U.S. ambassador in Belgium by the AWDC president and Gotlib on June 28 as a gift for Trump in honour of the 250th anniversary of the U.S.
• On July 24, the Trump administration officially exempted European natural diamonds from new Section 301 tariffs, restoring the industry's prior 0% tariff access.
• The White House has denied any favours to special interests. A spokesman has said that the decision to exempt the diamond industry from new tariffs merely upheld the Trump administration's previous agreement to provide preferential treatment for diamonds under a U.S.-European Union trade deal signed in Scotland last July.
• An administration official said the diamond ring was federal property, and if the president wanted to keep it, he would have to pay the government market price for it. REUTERS

Major financial crime probe targets leadership of Islamic group

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:24:01 UTC
20:24:01 KST

Turkish authorities on Aug. 13 launched an operation targeting the leader and senior figures of an Islamic religious community known as the “Süleymancılar,” following the detection of substantial suspicious financial transactions allegedly linked to money laundering.
The order’s leader, Alihan Kuriş, and 48 others were among wanted suspects as part of the operation led by prosecutors in the capital Ankara.
The case is centered on “organized financial crimes,” with suspects facing allegations including corruption, money laundering, the orchestration of unusual cash flows through high-capital companies and irregularities involving commercial transactions.
More than 100 billion Turkish Liras (over $2 billion) were transferred abroad through certain individuals and companies believed to be affiliated with the organization, local media said, quoting an investigation report.
International money transfers have come under scrutiny, with allegations of transactions involving links to Israel reportedly being investigated as part of the probe.
As part of the investigation, searches were conducted at a total of 123 addresses across 17 provinces, authorities said.
The locations searched included premises belonging to 33 companies.
Local media reports emphasized that the operation was not being conducted on the basis of the community’s social or religious activities.
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi told NTV that the group’s activities “became more clandestine” after Kuriş assumed its leadership in 2016.
Çiftçi also said the community built a $70 million headquarters in Cologne, Germany and that authorities believed its activities could eventually be relocated there.
The minister added that authorities were working on the operation for a long time.
The community traces its roots to Süleyman Hilmi Tunahan, who founded the religious movement that later became widely known in Türkiye as the “Süleymancılar,” a term referring to followers of Süleyman.
In the early 1990s, it was estimated to have around 2 million members in Türkiye, though its current membership count is not exact. The community has opened religious courses, student dormitories, foundations and companies in several countries.
The movement has been continuing to maintain an extensive network of activities.

US-China, the economy, and a burial dispute: What is at stake in Zambia’s election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:23:03 UTC
20:23:03 KST

US-China, copper, and a burial dispute: What is at stake in Zambia’s election?
Zambians are voting in presidential, parliamentary, and local elections on Thursday, with incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second five-year term as a bitter dispute over the burial of his predecessor and longtime rival, Edgar Lungu, continues to overshadow the campaign.
Although 14 presidential candidates are in the race, the contest is widely seen as primarily pitting Hichilema against opposition figure Brian Mundubile, a former senior member of the government of late President Lungu.
Nearly 8.8 million people are registered to vote, according to the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). Under the Constitution, a presidential candidate must receive more than 50% of valid ballots to win outright; otherwise, the two leading candidates proceed to a runoff.
What has happened since Zambia's 2020 default?
Following the country’s 2020 debt default, Zambia signed a $1.3 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) debt restructuring program though it is reported to owe China, Lusaka’s largest creditor, some $6 billion. However, the standard of living for ordinary citizens remains heavily strained due to painful fiscal austerity measures, high inflation, and severe climate shocks like regional droughts.
Speaking after casting his ballot in central Lusaka, Kantumoya Derrick Mpaka, a Zambian national who studied at the Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia (RUDN University), told RT that voting there had been peaceful and orderly.
“People are very civil. Everyone is calm. There is no chaos whatsoever,” he said. Mpaka described the election as highly unpredictable but said he expected Hichilema to prevail by a narrow margin, stressing that this was his “personal assessment” rather than an “endorsement of the incumbent.”
Who is Hakainde Hichilema?
Hichilema, 64, is a businessman and leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND). He won the presidency on his sixth attempt in 2021, defeating Lungu by nearly one million votes.
His first term has focused on repairing an economy damaged by Zambia’s 2020 sovereign default. The International Monetary Fund says agreements cover approximately 94% of the external debt targeted for restructuring and that Zambia has made substantial progress toward macroeconomic stability.
Who is Hichilema’s main challenger, Brian Mundubile?
Hichilema’s main rival Mundubile, 55, is an accountant, lawyer, and former lawmaker. Under Lungu, he served as Northern Province minister and government chief whip. He later became leader of the opposition in parliament.
Mundubile has criticized Hichilema’s economic and human rights record and promised Zambians a larger share of the country’s copper wealth. His political background suggests greater continuity with the China-friendly policies of the Lungu era, during which Beijing financed major infrastructure projects.
He is running for the presidency under the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity banner while leading the Tonse Alliance. The coalition was originally formed around Lungu and brought together several parties seeking to remove the UPND from power.
Mundubile’s most notable political achievement has been reaching an agreement with part of the divided Patriotic Front movement. Makebi Zulu, an ally and former lawyer of Lungu, is his running mate. However, several other opposition figures, including Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe, are running separately, meaning the anti-government vote remains fragmented.
How is Zambia’s economy performing?
On Wednesday, the Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry said investment in critical sectors has increased gross domestic product (GDP) from $19 billion to $40 billion since 2021, generated 7.8% growth, and produced a positive trade balance. The Zambia Statistics Agency, however, put annual growth at 3.8% in 2025, followed by a 7.7% year-on-year expansion in the first quarter of 2026.
Mpaka told RT that the figures do not reflect many voters’ circumstances. “On paper, our economy is doing okay, but in reality people are suffering, especially in rural Zambia, where people are living in poor conditions,” he said, citing a wide gap between rich and poor. High food costs, unemployment, and electricity shortages remain major concerns.
How important is Zambia to the global copper industry?
Hichilema has also introduced free primary and secondary education, recruited tens of thousands of teachers, and attracted billions of dollars in mining investment. A February 2026 World Bank Group report ranks Zambia as Africa’s second-largest and the world’s ninth-largest copper producer. Rising demand for minerals used in electric vehicles and clean-energy technology has intensified international interest.
In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe accused Washington of linking a proposed five-year health package worth up to $2 billion to a critical-minerals agreement favoring US companies.
What’s Hichilema’s foreign policy about?
In foreign policy, Hichilema has strengthened relations with the US and Europe while maintaining extensive economic ties with China. Beijing remains a major creditor and investor in Zambia’s mines and infrastructure, including a planned $1.4 billion renovation of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway.
Relations with Moscow have also continued. In a December interview with RT, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe described Russia as an “all-weather” friend and characterized bilateral ties as a “strategic partnership,” highlighting cooperation in education, energy, and trade.
Does Zambia favor the East or the West?
Andrey Maslov, head of the Center for African Studies at Moscow’s Higher School of Economics, told RT on Thursday that regardless of the election results, any leader of Zambia will follow a multilateral policy.
“Larger than any country in Europe, Zambia anchors two rival transport, logistics, and resource strategies: The US seeks to draw Zambia’s resources toward the Atlantic Ocean via Angola, while China finds it more advantageous to develop the Tanzania-Zambia corridor,” he said. “The country itself is attempting to balance these interests and benefit from these contradictions.”
Maslov noted that Washington might view Hichilema as capable of containing China’s expansion and preventing Zambia from aligning with alternative centers of power. However, the expert predicted that any Zambian leader would pursue a multilateral foreign policy while remaining mindful of public opinion, including opposition voters.
"Zambia is traditionally perceived as a source of copper and cobalt for global markets. Its role is, however, gradually evolving – for instance, the country has already become an exporter of electricity," Maslov adds.
Why is the burial of EdgarLungu controversial?
Former President Edgar Lungu died while receiving medical treatment in South Africa in June 2025, but his remains have not been buried following a dispute between his family and the Zambian authorities.
The government sought to repatriate him for a state funeral at which Hichilema would preside. Lungu’s family opposed the plan, saying the former president did not want his longtime rival involved in his funeral.
In June, South Africa’s Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that the government had not established a legal right to override the family’s wishes. Lusaka subsequently said it would not appeal.
The dispute has nevertheless entered the election campaign. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, who previously acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson, have promised to give the former president a dignified burial if elected.

Human Rights Watch says the Taliban detained 6 staff of a women’s and children’s rights group
ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities have “forcibly disappeared” six staff members of a local organization working on women’s and children’s rights, a U.S.-based advocacy group said, following a separate U.N. report that two Afghan employees of its mission in the country were detained.
The reported detentions come as Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers prepare to mark the fifth anniversary of their return to power on Saturday.
The six men — employees of the Women and Children Legal Research Foundation — were detained on July 18 after they were told to come to their office to retrieve confiscated laptops and phones, Human Rights Watch said in a statement released late Wednesday. Their families were given no information about their whereabouts, their condition or possible charges.
Human Rights Watch called on the Taliban to allow family and lawyers to visit the detained and for them to be “immediately released unless they have been charged with a recognizable offense.”
The statement came after the U.N. said two Afghan members of its political mission were detained on Sunday in the western city of Herat by the Taliban’s General Directorate of Intelligence. The U.N. mission has not been informed of the charges against the two men or been able to visit them, U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq told reporters.
The mission has called on the Taliban “to ensure compliance with the privileges and immunities of the United Nations and its officials,” Haq said.
There was no immediate comment on the two incidents from the Taliban, which seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as U.S. and NATO forces withdrew from the country after two decades of war.
Shortly after taking power, it barred girls from secondary schools and later extended the restrictions to higher education, employment and other sectors, effectively excluding women and girls from public life.
“The Taliban seems to consider any effort to assist women and girls a threat to their abusive rule,” said Macarena Sáez, women’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “They should immediately provide information on the six staff members’ whereabouts and release them if held unlawfully.”
Human Rights Watch said the detention of the six employees came a month after the security forces searched and sealed their office in Kabul and interrogated staff members about their work.
The U.N. mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, said Thursday it had no information on the reported six detentions or whether the two incidents were connected.
The detentions come as a humanitarian crisis in the poverty-stricken Asian nation is worsening and as Taliban forces are engaged in cross-border fighting with Pakistani forces. Clashes escalated sharply in February when Afghan forces launched a raid into Pakistan in retaliation for Pakistani airstrikes inside Afghanistan. Islamabad later declared it was in “open war.”
The U.N. mission’s mandate from the U.N. Security Council includes promoting and supporting humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people, promoting human rights, equality for women and girls, inclusive governance and economic stability.

As Abdul El-Sayed breaks a barrier, anti-Muslim vitriol surges on multiple fronts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:23:02 UTC
20:23:02 KST

As Abdul El-Sayed breaks a barrier, anti-Muslim vitriol surges on multiple fronts
Abdul El-Sayed made history this month in Michigan by becoming the first Muslim nominated by the Democratic Party to run for the U.S. Senate. But elation among many of his fellow Muslim Americans was tempered by awareness of persisting and widespread anti-Muslim sentiment across much of the nation.
Some Republicans, including President Donald Trump, swiftly began referring to the nominee by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, while depicting him as a danger to America. “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,’' said U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., in a post on X.
El-Sayed says such attacks betray a weakness in those who launch them.
“We all pray for the same things. ... We want what’s good for our kids and our families,” he told MS NOW after his primary victory. “They’re going to use Islamophobia, because their ideas are tired.”
The vitriol extends far beyond the political class. Tensions related to anti-Muslim sentiment have heightened in several communities around the country, where some residents have bitterly opposed proposals to build new mosques.
“American Muslims have made incredible political and societal progress in recent years,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, national deputy director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR. He cited increased visibility in entertainment and sports and the election of Democrat Zohran Mamdani as New York City’s first Muslim mayor.
“But there also is a very concerted backlash to this progress,” Mitchell said. “You’ve seen this in the resurgence of anti-Muslim hate and rhetoric, the targeting of mosques.”
A Dallas suburb is a flashpoint
McKinney, Texas, a large suburb in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, is one of the flashpoints. Despite angry anti-Islam remarks at a heated city council meeting on Aug. 4, the council voted unanimously to approve a site plan for the McKinney Islamic Association’s proposed new mosque, classroom building and gym.
Among those urging the council to give the plan fair treatment was George Fuller, a former mayor of McKinney, a nonpartisan position. Opponents of the mosque project booed him, and some shouted “traitor” as he left the council chamber. One woman could be seen on video physically accosting him.
“I have never witnessed so much hate, anger and lack of humanity in our beautiful community gathered in one place as I did today at City Hall,” Fuller later wrote on Facebook.
During the hearing, which lasted more than four hours, the speakers included U.S. Rep. Keith Self, a Republican whose district includes McKinney. To loud applause, he urged the council to reject the mosque proposal.
“I know you’re in the accommodation phase, but the intimidation phase follows quickly,” Self said. “Child marriage. Honor killings. Don’t tell me it can’t happen here.”
Fuller also went to the microphone, evoking the broader phenomenon of divisive political rhetoric.
“Sadly, we live in a time when some have discovered that the easiest way to gain attention or win elections is not by offering solutions but by manufacturing fear, dividing communities, demonizing neighbors and turning misinformation into a political strategy,” he said.
In North Carolina, anger flares over approval for a new mosque
The scenario was similar in Mooresville, North Carolina, when town commissioners held a public comment session on Aug. 3 about a proposed mosque that had already been approved, with early phases of construction underway.
Angry residents at the meeting voiced hostility to Islam and assailed the commissioners for not being more forthcoming about the project as it took shape over previous months. One speaker cited violence in Nigeria by Islamist extremists as a reason for concern in Mooresville. Another depicted Islam as “a political regime with the ultimate goal of takeover in regions and nations.”
CAIR’s regional manager, Al Rieder, issued a statement denouncing “the hateful and conspiratorial anti-Muslim rhetoric” that surfaced at the meeting and expressed concern about the safety of Muslims in the area about 25 miles (40 kilometers) north of Charlotte.
“Muslims are your neighbors, your doctors, your teachers, your local politicians, your police,” he said.
A few hours after the public meeting, the town commissioners released a summary of the mosque project, which calls for a two-building Islamic center on a parcel acquired in 2019 by a local Muslim organization.
The commissioners said that the parcel is in an area zoned to allow religious assembly and that the mosque proposal was handled the same way as a proposal for a new church.
“All decisions must be based on adopted ordinances, objective standards and legal requirements, which do not allow for different rules for different religious groups,” the commissioners said. “We encourage all members of our community to remain respectful in their discussions and interactions as this project moves through the appropriate processes.”
In Oklahoma, Muslim leaders fight against the rebuff of a new mosque
A mosque controversy has been raging for many months in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, Tulsa’s largest suburb.
Back in January, at a stormy meeting attended by hundreds of people, the city council voted 4-1 to reject a rezoning proposal by the region’s Islamic Society to build Broken Arrow’s first mosque. Before the vote, dozens of residents voiced anti-Muslim views while opposing the project.
Council members who rejected the mosque had raised concerns about its potential impact on infrastructure such as roads, sewers and flood plain management.
But the Islamic Society is persisting with its quest. On Aug. 3, it filed a lawsuit against the mayor and four councilors, alleging that the vote reflected “a wave of bigoted opposition from members of the community and local politicians.” The lawsuit contends that the council violated state and federal laws governing religious land use, treating the mosque proposal differently from other comparable rezoning requests.
“They did not want a mosque in their city. They did not want Muslims here,” said Meghan Murphy, an attorney with CAIR’s Legal Defense Fund, at a news conference announcing the lawsuit. ”So they made up a reason, and in doing so they violated the law.”
Some see a terrorism threat while others see baseless scaremongering
Opposition to mosque construction isn’t a new phenomenon: In Murfreesboro, Tennessee, an effort launched in 2010 to block a mosque project dragged on for more than three years. The mosque was built anyway as the case moved through the courts, but members of the Muslim community faced public protests, vandalism, arson and a bomb threat during that span.
The latest anti-mosque campaigns coincide with a broad wave of anti-Muslim rhetoric from Republican officeholders over the past year. In Congress, several bills were introduced targeting sharia, the moral and spiritual framework that guides Muslims in prayer and ethical conduct. Some Republicans say they’re concerned about growing Muslim populations in major cities and potential ties to terrorism — fears that CAIR and other civil rights groups say are unfounded and being exploited for political purposes.
Republican governors in Texas and Florida have endorsed efforts to shut down CAIR, saying it has ties to terrorism. CAIR has denied the allegations and filed lawsuits calling the governors’ efforts unconstitutional.
Muslim American leaders view the vitriol as political scaremongering.
“Every election year, we expect a rise in anti-Muslim hate,” said CAIR’s Mitchell. “It’s been worse this year than it has been in years.”
